Katalog Berita (Halaman 24/57)

#6652. A Guide to Ceramics That’s Also a Lot More Than That

How to Make a Pot, a new book by Maggie Boyd, a ceramic artist in New York, is a how-to book that works for clay newbies and veterans, as well as those who are only vaguely interested in clay, given that, at its heart, the book is a meditation on life and art.

It is broken into two parts. Part one explores what a pot is and what it means to make one—reminding you that art is a way to interact with the world—while part two, covering the technical side, gets into how every pot is an experience, and that expertise is the result of many well-intentioned but imprecise turns. It’s not a spoiler to say that Boyd’s book is about how we hold the world and care for it, a future hidden in every piece of fresh wet clay.

How to Make a Pot is very smart and fun and serious, as was its author, who—when Vogue talked to her the other day in her studio, in Bushwick—was wearing a vintage 1930s baseball jersey and making pots.

Maggie Boyd: I was teaching a class for friends in my studio—it was a secret little speakeasy class—because I had a lot of friends who wanted to learn ceramics. One of the people who ended up taking the class, who kind of instigated it, was my friend Caleb, who said, “Listen, you should write a book.” And I said, “You know, I’m not sure, but I think I have a book that I wrote already in my brain.” I’ve been teaching for about 15 years and I’ve been working with clay for over 20 years, so everything that is in there is these collected observations from trying to figure out how to explain a process that is so lengthy and cumbersome and dependent on timing and pressure and a sensitivity to the material. There’ve been so many attempts to try to clarify that process for people.

Part one of the book had me thinking of that great line by M.C. Richards, the Black Mountain College ceramicist and writer, who said: “Poets are not the only poets.” It is a series of drawings with very few words, and I am wondering about what made you want to start a how-to book with drawings as opposed to, say, technical diagrams and step-by-step instructions?

Well, I regularly speak in metaphor. I explain things with drawings, all that stuff, and the way that I teach ceramics is through drawing and basically interpretive dance moves! And I hadn’t seen a book that approached teaching ceramics in this way. So the first part is almost like a prayer or meditation or primer—a spiritual primer before you actually even touch the clay. And the point of that is to resensitize the reader, because I think that especially with—well, I hate to name any of the social media platforms, but I feel as if that one platform has made it so that people are like, “Oh, you can make clay really fast! You can make money at it—it’s a business!” There are all these things that it has sort of taken away from the magic of pushing a material that moves.

Yes, because we are so inundated with the search for the ultimate point of productivity. We’re a grind culture. We’re like: How do we turn the most beautiful, calm, mystical experience of interacting with material into profitable business immediately? And that shifts the way we relate to the material. And I wanted to slow us back down.

Because everything tells us that easier is the best way, which reminds me of a conversation I overheard the other day: two ceramicists were talking about the world being taken over by AI slop. It’s a discussion being had these days by so many people making things: drawings, films, clothing, or even sentences.

I’ve been thinking about this non-stop lately because everyone’s always saying, “Oh, AI just makes everything easy. It streamlines everything and it takes away all this effort.” And to hear this makes me so sad because that is the point for me, the effort. I like doing this. I want to do it. AI would take away that experience with the material. There’s so much magic when you interact with the material or a person, and you can’t do that with AI. That’s not the effort I want removed from my life.

Part of the effort, it seems to me, is learning the hard way that, for example, at around 212 degrees, if there is moisture in a piece it will, no matter how potentially wonderful, explode. Right?

It’s a circle of failing and trying. Clay is a rigorous material to understand and you need a lot of help and a lot of tips and a lot of support and a lot of pre-discovered knowledge. So part two is just me telling you what I’ve learned and what worked for me, knowing that it will be imperfectly described and not everything will apply to you. You take whatever you can from everything you read. And what I’ve learned from doing ceramics for so long is every time I go and I talk with a new artist about a new thing, I learn something from them. Because we’re all approaching this material and it has so many forking paths of possible approaches that I’m always like, “Oh, that’s how you do it.” And it always shifts. So in that way, I don’t feel like I need to know everything because I just know what I know. And hopefully that’s helpful.

Was it difficult to describe, say, how to turn a pot on a wheel? Something that is so seemingly simple but complicated? What was the real triumph for you in, I guess, achieving an explanation?

The triumph is when you have a skill that is so innate and just in your body and then you translate that into words, step by step. It’s such a wild writing exercise. Try it at home! Write how it is to take a fork and bring food to your mouth. It was such an eye-opening experience to understand what how-to manuals do. I had to step outside of myself. Sometimes I would even video myself doing something so I could watch and realize, Oh, that’s the order I do it in!

Do you remember the first ceramic piece that you ever made in your life?

In grade two—that’s what you say in Canada, not “second grade”—we got to work with clay, real clay, for the first time. Not Play-Doh, but clay that was going to go in a kiln. And I made a dragon. And I remember I made a super long neck and these, like, Bart Simpson-looking eyes and pinch spikes all the way around along its tail. And I remember I was like: Maybe I’m kind of good at this? Like, I had this sense really early that I understood working with this material.

This tall dragon that was so beautiful, and then I remember that I glazed the whole thing in a forest green, and I loved that it had green eyeballs that matched its skin! Later on, it got lost, so I actually remade it from memory when I was 23, for my dad. I remember because when I made it before, it said: “Maggie, age 6.” And then the second time I wrote: “Maggie, age 23.”

I’ve read about the “Projects Class” at the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design, where you attended; it involved artists from all over—everyone from Lucy Lippard to Dan Graham to Sonic Youth—collaborating with the school, or even sending up proposals for the students to execute.

I showed up and I completely threw ceramics out the window. Because I was like, okay, well, obviously I’m going to be a performance and sound installation artist who lives in a gallery and then maybe secretly sleeps at school and, you know, does all the stuff that you need to do to get your art school yah-yahs out. I took every possible class and had no intention of graduating. I just wanted to stay forever.

Luckily, I got hired to do the after-school programming at this place, the George Dixon Center, a public housing project in Halifax. So I kind of pulled this skill out of retirement and started teaching. And then people in the neighborhood wanted to take classes, and then I was teaching kids that were about four years old. The teacher before me was saying, “Kids are not allowed to touch the wheel until they’re 11 years old,” or whatever. And then as soon as she left, I said, “All right, kids, get on the wheel!” And it was totally crazy and so amazing. I had something that people wanted to learn that I could share. From that point on I was always teaching ceramics.

How did your art school theoretical studies and your pot-making studio skills connect? Did the two skill sets blend together at some point?

I think for a long time they felt separate, and it’s taken until kind of recently for them to fuse comfortably. I thought of [ceramics] as sort of my trade skill, something I could do. I can throw a pot. I can do cups for restaurants. And I just kept getting hired and hired, and really all I wanted was to have a way to be in a studio. Yes, there was this side of me that just wanted to, you know, do all the experiments and sounds and all this stuff, but I started to think that the art world also wants these two instincts to be at odds. And we buy into that because, you know, commerce is king, and it defines things for us instead of our intuition.

Your pieces seem to be as much functional as they are experiments—wondrous functional experiments—which is to say, I guess you resolved something?

I just stopped believing in the hierarchy that was constructed through commerce and the art world. And I just understood that the most important aspect of being an artist is following the impulse to make, because it’s a question that you solve with any answer, and it doesn’t have to have a truth. So you just get to follow this incredible line of thought and that’s the whole point. That could become a pot or painting or drawing or a dance or a nap or whatever—they’re all just the same person asking the same questions and trying to answer them in different ways.

By the way, what happened when the four-year-olds got on the wheel?

OK, the difference between adults and children is that children, if you get them at the right point, have absolutely no fear about making a mistake. They are so fearless and they have so little self-criticality. They’re just pure curiosity and cause and effect. And so, yeah, kids on the wheel is sometimes, “How fast can this thing go?” and “How far can I spray this clay?” Like, pretty good questions, though hard questions to clean up. But they’re just so involved in making, whereas when you teach adults, you have to try to sort of break them back down. Sister Corita Kent, she says: “Don’t try to create and analyze at the same time.” So that’s what children don’t need help with, and it’s exactly what an adult often needs help with. And then, well, if you learn to decipher a pot, a pot will show you who you are.

In terms of part two of How to Make a Pot, what are you reading to continue your never-ending ceramic education?

The Ceramic Spectrum by Robin Hopper, second edition. It is the definitive reference book on glaze.

And for the lay person, such as myself: What, exactly, is a glaze?

So a glaze is a glass-like coating that goes on top of a clay body, that fuses to the surface. It is made up of stabilizer, glass, and flux to make it melt, and its combinations of those three ingredients [dictate] how it holds color, or its opacity or clarity or transparency and all that.

And what are Hopper’s insights into glaze?

He is talking about how experience is so much more important than calculation in glaze-making. It’s just a really great overview of how to make colors and glazes and how to experiment. He values knowledge that is experiential, and it’s so cool because I feel as if glaze-making, in particular, is this gatekept thing—you have to understand the chemistry and how to do the chemical equations. And he just makes the point, which I feel like people need to remind themselves of with almost all things that they make, bread or anything, that this is something that has been part of humanity since long before we had computer programs that broke down the chemical analysis of something.

What have you read recently, or what have you been listening to while you work in the studio at this moment?

A lecture by Anne Carson on Homer’s Odyssey and Le Mépris, the film by Jean-Luc Godard. I used to say my two favorite movies were The Lion King and Le Mépris.

Ah, a film about an artist making a film, and having to deal with the studio’s purely commercial demands, which is what Godard himself was dealing with in dealing with an American producer; the insistence, first off, that Brigitte Bardot be nude!

Yes, and Carson is talking about how to be an artist. Or, really, about the seller versus selling. But until I heard her lecture, I didn’t understand that the Americans asked that he have nudity in the film, and that Godard said, “Oh, so what I’m going to do is I’m going to double down on this thing that you’re asking me to do and actually, like, rub it in your face.” Carson says Godard makes art out of selling out. She says he makes a spectacle of compromise. And she says that Brigitte Bardot just wins. I love that. The film’s so good. It’s how to be an artist, or when do you realize, Oh, they’re just going to want you to make the same thing.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6651. Kylie Cantrall Wants to Be Your Modern-Day Carrie Bradshaw

After all, the rising star has a single named after the Sex and the City character.

Last night at the Moxy Downtown Los Angeles, rising pop star Kylie Cantrall teased her next project. “It’s gaggy. It’s giving 21,” she joked onstage during a small, intimate performance. “I actually haven’t written any ballads so far. I’m healed.”

Cantrall, who is perhaps best known for portraying Red, daughter of the Queen of Hearts, in the Descendants film series, has had a banner year. The L.A. native just wrapped a nationwide tour, appeared on Fox’s The Masked Singer, is set to perform at iHeart’s Jingle Ball, and dropped her EP Valley Girl Problems. A standout on the release is “Carrie Bradshaw,” which examines the similarities between Cantrall and the iconic Sex and the City character, played by Sarah Jessica Parker. “I think my fashion sense has been influenced by Carrie,” Cantrall says. “Also, she’s just kind of a mess, but she keeps it together on the outside. That’s honestly how I feel about myself. The choices are questionable, sometimes. Choices in dating, questionable.”

At the show, Cantrall played four tracks, including “Carrie Bradshaw.” She took pictures with her fans, signed vinyls, and, for one fan, even signed their chest. The experience is a part of a larger effort to use music as a connector at the Moxy, which has also hosted Ayra Starr at its London property. The brand unites artists with their fans in private settings and gives travelers the opportunity to relax with a musical backdrop. “I’m so excited to be here at Moxy,” Cantrall told ELLE before taking the stage. “I love doing these little underplays and acoustic shows, because it’s a different side of myself that I feel like people don’t usually get to see.”

Ahead of her performance, Cantrall sat down with ELLE to discuss Valley Girl Problems, her acoustic set, and new music on the horizon.

Full production, dancers, props. It’s always very razzle-dazzle, Kylie the performer, but I feel like this is more Kylie just the singer and songwriter. I like getting to showcase that aspect.

Honestly, I get nervous for it all. I think I put so much thought and care into every show, so there’s always a pressure I put on myself. But I feel like once I get out there and see the cuties’ faces, it feels chill. I know so many of them. We have more of a friendship bond.

It’s everything. What’s really special about me and my fan base is that we’ve really grown up together, because a lot of them are my age now. They had maybe started watching me from YouTube or from my first Disney show when I was 13 and have stayed along with my journey. It’s crazy. Our bond is kind of familial at this point.

I think they’re quite different. It’s so different playing a character. Of course, with someone like Red, I’m very grateful I got to play a character that I felt like had a lot of me in it already. But, Kylie the musician, Kylie the artist, that’s completely, 100 percent raw me. I have so much freedom to take risks and experiment. With Valley Girl, I feel like that perfectly encapsulated the person I was a couple months ago when I wrote it. I’ve changed so much since then. I’m just excited for the next project that’s going to reflect who I am now as a 21-year-old. I want all of my bodies of work to reflect the person I am in whatever chapter that is. It’s like a time machine. It’s very powerful in that way.

No. I listen to it so much when I’m creating it, and obviously it’s just nonstop before it comes out. The minute it comes out, it feels like I have no control over it whatsoever. It’s not mine. It’s for everyone else. I have to have that kind of separation. If I am still listening to it after it’s been out, I’ll start to pick things apart and be like, “Oh, I wish I did that. Oh, I could have done this differently.” Then, you have people’s criticism or opinions also in your brain when you’re listening to it, which can taint the way you view it. I was so proud when I finished it. I knew how I felt once I submitted it to the label and was like, “Okay, this is the final product. Here you go.” I just want to remain in that place.

It’s always the vocal fry—holding the ends of my words for a long time. Definitely the way I talk. I guess hiking and matcha are also kind of a worldwide thing at this point, but for some reason growing up I always felt like that’s such a Valley thing. In the Valley, it’s either matcha cafes or Pilates studios and fruit carts on the corner, and that kind of encapsulates the Valley for me.

So excited. At the top of the year, I wrote in my little manifestation journal, I’m going to perform at Jingle Ball this holiday. It was before it was even a topic of conversation. I just threw it out there because I was like, I really want to do Jingle Ball just to be a part of a lineup. I’ve watched every single Jingle Ball since I was seven years old. The fact that I’ll get to share the stage with Katseye, Olivia [Rodrigo], the Jonas Brothers, Adéla, these are all artists that I look up to. I’m just excited to be in that orbit.

I was probably enjoying my days off for the first two days when I got back home from tour. Then, the third day I was like, “Okay, I’m ready to get back out.” I’m already thinking in my head what the new set list is going to be with the new songs that I’m recording at home right now and getting ready for the next album. My wheels are turning.

New York had a crazy energy. The New Yorkers know how to pull up and show some love. And, of course, L.A. I got to end the tour here, so there was something that felt very full circle about getting to come home and celebrate with my friends and family that all came out to the show, and a lot of my L.A. fans who are here tonight at the Moxy. It’s also just so fun anytime I get to do anything in L.A. It’s all my closest fans, and all my first pop-ups I had ever done were always here in L.A. A lot of my foundational fans that have been with me, they’re all here.

I’m just taking a lot of inspiration from my life right now, as a 21-year-old who’s going out and just kind of embracing this next chapter. It feels like I have all the freedom in the world. I’m just excited to kind of show people maybe a little more of a wilder side. A little more messy, a little less curated. Kylie, outside of the work I’ve done or the image, the narrative, whatever that may be. Here’s who I am right now. I like to have fun. I like to go out. I’m going through it all the time, but I get to pour it into my music, whether it’s just discovering my kind of identity in this era, dating, or all the things I’m learning about myself. It’s all going to be poured into this record.

I’m a Cancer. I’m very in touch with my emotions at all times, and music is my chance to fully just, without censoring anything, explore that.

#6650. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6649. Taylor Swift’s Yellow CMA Awards Gown Has a Dramatic High-Low Hem and Ruffles

This evening, Taylor Swift returns to the CMA Awards stage for her first performance in 13 years. But first, there’s the red carpet, and the singer just made a stylish entrance. Swift arrived at the Nashville ceremony in a bright yellow Oscar de la Renta gown featuring a dramatic high-low hem and ruffled details from the brand’s spring/summer 2027 collection. She completed the look with dangling earrings and gold high-heeled sandals. The singer walked the red carpet solo.

Swift has one nomination tonight: Single of the Year for her Toy Story 5 song “I Knew It, I Knew You.”

She last attended the ceremony in 2016, wearing a cutout dress by Julien Macdonald:

Last month, Swift was back in Nashville for her induction into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame. During her acceptance speech, she reflected on the city’s significance to her career.

“I started writing songs when I was a little kid and I knew from the time I wrote my first song that even if it couldn’t be my career, it would be my passion,” she said. “It would be what I centered my entire life around. Nashville is the place that I went to in my middle school daydreams. It was the place where all the wisdom that I wished to acquire existed in one place. All the lessons that I wished to learn existed in this magical place for me. And it ended up being all of that and more. It ended up being everything.

“Fame, that’s sort of a byproduct of my love for music,” she continued. “It’s kind of like songwriter plus Nashville equals fame. It’s why a lot of people know the words to my music, which is awesome. It’s also why there’s sort of like these daily random doses of chaos that just pop up in my life every once in a while, every couple of hours. That can be kind of weird, but I have tools in place in my mind that help me navigate that and get back to true north when life feels so bizarre. Those tools are my memories and the memories that I visit most frequently when I need to return back to some semblance of remembering what normalcy is and why I do this.

“I think back to when I first got to Nashville and I started writing on Music Row. I was lucky enough to get a publishing deal with Sony Publishing when I was 14, and I just hit the ground running. I started writing every single day. I learned so much. I was like a sponge and I have really curly hair and it was yellow, so I kind of looked like a sponge too. But I learned by repetition. I think you truly learn a craft when you do it over and over and over, and that is what the magnificent songwriters that work in this amazing town do. There is no music community like this music community. I know. I checked all the communities. There’s no one doing it.”

#6648. 2026 Earth Partner Prize: The Winners

Earth Partner, Art Partner's sustainability division, in collaboration with the Global Environment Facility (GEF) and Re:wild, has announced the winners of the 2026 Earth Partner Prize, the annual competition inviting artists aged 14–30 to explore different aspects of the ecological crisis through art.

The Grand Prize ($10,000) was awarded to 16-year-old Samuel Bird from the UK for THE GAS WORKS, a 2.1-metre-long linocut print exploring the climate impact of war and the lack of transparency surrounding military emissions. Two Runner-Up prizes ($5,000 each), five Third-Place awards ($2,000 each) and 20 Honourable Mentions were also awarded.

The 28 winning works are now on view in a virtual exhibition powered by Kunstmatrix. Spanning photography, film, poetry, performance, animation and textiles, the projects address issues ranging from retreating glaciers and disappearing pollinators to the environmental consequences of war and the loss of Indigenous knowledge.

All 28 works will also be showcased at the Climate Funds Pavilion during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, through the Prize's partnership with the GEF.

1st Place ($10k)Samuel Bird (UK), THE GAS WORKS

A 2.1-metre-long linocut print exploring the climate impact of war and the lack of transparency surrounding military emissions. At just 16 years old, Samuel draws on his experience of dyslexia to inform his distinctive approach to working in reverse when designing and cutting linocut prints.

2nd Place ($5k)Radoslav Sviretsov (Bulgaria-Iceland), VEINS OF A CHANGING LAND

As Iceland's glaciers continue to retreat, increasing volumes of meltwater are reshaping the country's river systems. Through his work, Radoslav reflects on the gradual transformation of landscapes and the danger of becoming accustomed to environmental loss.

2nd Place ($5k)Maewenn Bourcelot (France), ETERNAL EPHEMERAL

Through microscopy, colour and shifts in scale, Maewenn draws audiences into the world of pollinators, creating a photographic poem about their disappearance and the gradual, often unnoticed nature of ecological change.

3rd Place ($2k)Aakash Gulzar (India), THE LAST PATTU

3rd Place ($2k)Ishita Sharma (UK) — A WILD HOPE OF UNBOUNDED SEEING

3rd Place ($2k)Cristian Pǎsat and Oxana Capatina (Moldova), GUNOI SUB COVOR: SWEEPING UNDER THE RUG

3rd Place ($2k)Reza Javanshir (Iran), SALT WOUND

3rd Place ($2k)Kaanchi Chopra (India), THE EARTH LAUGHS IN FLOWERS

The artists were selected by an international jury, including Derrick O. Boateng (acclaimed artist and founder of the “Hueism” movement), Dr Robin Moore (photographer and Chief Communications Officer at Re:wild), Dr Musonda Mumba (Secretary General of the Convention on Wetlands), Giovanni Testino (Founder of Art Partner), Marina Testino (sustainability advocate), Hans Ulrich Obrist (Artistic Director of the Serpentine Galleries), Ferdinando Verderi (Creative Director), Marcela Villafaña (Indigenous Arhuaco filmmaker), and Shaway Yeh (pioneer of sustainable fashion in China).

The jury also awarded 20 Honourable Mentions and the Earth Partner Impact Award ($1.5K), recognising the project that best demonstrates the community impact of artistic initiatives led by young people, to ECO-ART BHUTA KALA: THE THIRD SPACE OF WATER GOVERNANCE (Bali), an interactive sculptural installation and community mobilisation project raising awareness of the hydrological challenges faced by local communities.

#6647. Noah Wrapped the Converse Chuck 70 in Menswear’s Favorite Tartan

When Converse and Noah collaborated for the first time earlier this year, the most surprising thing was that it’d taken so long for them to link up. The sneaker OGs and New York menswear mavens make as much sense together as peanut butter and jelly—both brands flow effortlessly between worlds, embraced by punks and preps and hoopers and skaters alike. Thankfully, the duo have been making up for lost time, kicking their partnership off with a couple of killer Chuck 70s in the spring before putting out an understated banger of a spin on the Louie Lopez 2 over the summer. Now, they’re capping off their banner year with one last go-round—another jazzed-up Chuck Taylor that’s about as holiday-ready as it gets.

Just in time for turkey season, Noah has wrapped the Converse Chuck 70 Low in one of the most beloved patterns in menswear: Black Watch tartan. The green, navy, and black plaid was originally worn by squadrons patrolling the Scottish Highlands in the 18th century, with its subdued tones meant to help wearers blend into their surroundings. Over the past several decades, it’s been embraced by fashion at large, but particularly Trad Ivy enthusiasts, who tend to sport the striking tartan on everything from sport coats and scarves during the colder months.

In addition to the sharp Black Watch canvas uppers, Noah made a handful of other subtle changes to the classic silhouette, adding its branding to the “license plate” on the shoe’s heel, removing the wing tongue stitch, and swapping in a woven tongue tag. The kicks feature the standard white laces but also come with a mustard yellow pair for an extra boost of color.

If you’re looking to dress festively but aren’t all that into freaky patterned sweaters, the latest Converse x Noah Chuck 70 Low might just be the ticket. The shoes drop tomorrow, November 19, for $112 via both Converse and Noah.

#6645. Why Men Are Posting Thirst Traps in Red Light Face Masks

Gonzalo Fernández Escribano knew all about the benefits of red-light therapy for his skin. Fewer wrinkles, a brighter complexion, minimizing acne—he’d experienced it all firsthand when he tried out LED masks during his facials. In March 2025, he purchased one for at-home use. Little did he know it would come with an extra benefit as a provocative prop for a sexy photo.

"I use my red-light mask right before bed, so I’m already shirtless,” says Escribano. “Let’s just say the sexy-looking picture is easily convenient to take.”

Escribano is one of many men online who’ve embraced the red-light thirst trap. More and more, image-conscious guys with followings built around some combination of beauty, fitness, wellness, travel, are pairing their red-light routines with the occasional shirtless selfie. The trend is especially prevalent in gay-male internet culture, where faceless torsos shots, sometimes featuring beefy chests and six-pack abs, have been part of the visual language of dating apps and social media for years. A shirtless red-light-mask pic is a variation on the theme: The body and the anonymity are still there—only now there’s a skincare routine attached.

Jayson Stacy, a celebrity groomer, noticed his friend wearing an LED in his Instagram profile picture three years ago. At the same time, Stacy had recently gotten a mask himself and decided to follow suit, posting a photo of his own after Mardi Gras under the guise of some much needed recovery.

“It’s almost like a sexy Halloween costume, but you don’t have to wait until October,” Stacy says. Escribano agrees, saying it makes him look like a superhero. Strong shadows, glowing skin, and a Sith-like red glow mix together in a thirsty trifecta meant to slow someone’s scrolling.

For Stacy, red-light masks strike the perfect balance between wellness and plausible deniability. “You’re supposed to use the mask after you wash your face, so most are fresh out of the shower before using,” he says. “It’s like, ‘Oh, look at my morning routine,’ which gives the perfect excuse to be mostly unclothed. Then you have the mask on, you feel like someone can’t see your face, so it can feel like a layer of protection.” In other words, the skin care routine becomes the reason for the thirst trap, even though it’s only half the motivation.

Red-light therapy is a noninvasive treatment that uses low-level LED light to stimulate cellular activity and boost collagen production. The technology has become especially prominent over the last few years thanks to its ability to reduce inflammation, soften fine lines, and promote skin and muscle recovery and hair growth. (That is, as long as you are willing to invest in high-quality equipment and use it every single day).

Celebrities have been documenting their LED routines for years, from January Jones to Kim Kardashian. But those posts were mostly framed around the masks’ intended purpose: improving your skin. Somewhere along the way, though, a certain breed of extremely online men—trainers, models, artists, content creators, and guys who simply know their angles—found a second purpose for the masks: as an accessory for a hot photo. The masks are turning up in bathroom mirror pics, bedroom shots, and buried several slides deep in otherwise unrelated photo dumps, often without any mention of skin care at all. And judging by the comments—fire emojis, heart eyes, and the occasional “yummy”—their followers seem to be noticing something other than the mask.

The thirst traps are also surfacing on social media at a time when curiosity around red-light therapy is booming. A 2025 study analyzing Google Trends data found that search interest across red-light-therapy-related terms increased 118% after February 2024. And by 2025, Google reported that searches for “red light therapy” had reached an all-time high. As these futuristic devices have rapidly flooded our feeds, maybe it was only a matter of time before they made their way out of the skin care selfie and into something a little thirstier.

In some ways these images are being ushered into well-trodden territory. In 2021, TikTok’s viral Silhouette Challenge had users transform themselves into barely distinguishable, body-forward silhouettes under a red filter, turning the color itself into a visual shorthand for sex appeal. Meanwhile, for gay men, shirtless photos are hardly a novelty, especially on dating apps like Grindr and Sniffies, where headless torsos are practically part of the experience. “The headless torsos definitely all blend together at this point,” says John Arthur Hill, who compares swiping through hookup apps to looking into “a lukewarm batch of Chili’s skillet queso” and trying to figure out what’s cheese, meat, or a bell pepper.

And even when the most impressive six-pack can get lost in an endless doom scroll, red light can add just enough intrigue to get someone to look twice. For Adam Pent, an OnlyFans creator who’s no stranger to posting thirst traps himself, that curiosity is part of the appeal. “It [a red-light-mask thirst trap] is definitely more interesting because I’d be curious about who’s behind the mask,” he says. To Pent, there’s something creative about the whole thing. “I guess it makes the photo a bit more artful too? ‘Art thot’ vibes I guess, unless it looks like sponsored content.” It also makes him want to shop. “I’m less focused on the body and more like, ‘Should I just get one already?’”

The red-light thirst trap also holds a certain mysterious appeal. “I’ve been posting ‘masked’ selfies for quite some time because I think it’s a really hot aesthetic and such a cool fantasy,” Michael Anthony, a celebrity makeup artist, says. For him, it’s not just about looking good in the photos. “The fantasy of anonymity and pleasure, while doing something for yourself that will make you look and feel better—it’s all so sexy.”

Tattoo artist Alvin Archibald sees a similar appeal. “There’s a subtle tension between vulnerability and control that makes it interesting,” he says. “The mask takes away your facial expressions, so the body becomes the focus. It creates this interesting dynamic where you’re both exposed and concealed at the same time. There’s something almost intimate about it, like you’re getting ready for an audience without necessarily admitting it.”

#6644. Watch Taylor Swift Perform ‘Our Song’ With ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’ at the 2026 CMA Awards

Taylor Swift embraced her country roots tonight, taking the stage at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years. The singer performed a mash-up of her Toy Story 5 song “I Knew It, I Knew You” and her 2007 country hit “Our Song,” making it a sweet, nostalgic homecoming.

She wore an embellished white sleeveless dress with a red skirt and bedazzled matching cowboy boots. Just like old times, she played along with a sparkly guitar. Swift’s performance began backstage, and she sang while making her way down the halls, nodding to fellow country music stars along the way. She was even joined by Keith Urban onstage.

“I Knew It, I Knew You” was nominated for Single of the Year, but Ella Langley ultimately took home the win with “Choosin’ Texas.” Swift received two Grammy nominations for the song last week as well: Song of the Year and Best Song Written for Visual Media.

During a virtual press conference for the Critics Choice Awards earlier this month, Swift spoke about connecting with Toy Story’s cowgirl Jessie, whose perspective shaped the song. She reflected on her own career trajectory and the ways she has reinvented herself as an artist over the years.

“It’s interesting because being in the entertainment industry, I’ve always just felt like it’s harder to hit a moving target,” she said of people’s changing tastes. “Once people feel like they’ve figured you out creatively and they’ve figured out what you can do, they usually move into the discardment phase and so that would always be where I would try to pivot and if they think you’re going to zig, you zag instead. Rather than looking at something as exhausting and daunting, I look at as just a new adventure. Once I’ve done one thing, I look for something else that inspires me.

“I feel like with Jessie, she’s always going on these adventures and she’s always trying to help someone new and there’s always something she feels really inspired by and some new challenge ahead of her and she takes them on with such fearlessness,” Swift continued. “Except we see her have this moment of crisis in this film, where she does feel hopeless and she does feel useless and she’s saying to herself, ‘Am I a bad toy? Does any of this matter?’ And it’s that moment that just breaks your heart because you’re like, ‘No, Jessie,’ and then you get that amazing resolution—obviously no spoilers—but in the film she reaches a place that was ultimately what inspired me to write the song I wrote.”

#6642. APC Just Dropped a Pair of Incredibly Clean Casios

We’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches. Timex is leading the way: its link-ups with Noah, Todd Snyder, and J. Crew are masterclasses in adding personality to classic designs without going OTT. But don’t count Casio out of the race. The Japanese giant has just followed up its 2024 collab with APC. The pair are perfectly matched: Casio watches are known for being beautifully functional and understated—adjectives that fit APC’s spartan aesthetic too.

The first collaboration between the two brands saw them rework the hallowed A1000 digital-display watch. That release stripped back a lot of the original’s markings and added the APC logo on the dial. This time around, it's the AQ-240 getting a makeover. The case is squarer than the rectangular A1000, and while there’s a narrow window for a digital display, the watch maintains the traditional analog format with hands and hour markers. Here, you get the best of both worlds. The watch is sold out on APC's website but still available through Casio, so act fast if you want one. The silver variant is $110, and the gold goes for $135.

What about the APC-ness of it all? That part is the opposite of loud: as with the previous collab, there isn’t much giving away the brand's participation. We’ve got the APC logo on the dial and the buckle, plus the brand’s guitar-and-dagger insignia engraved out of sight on the caseback. Casio already offers the regular A1000 in a bunch of different colorways, but these two new ones are made specifically for the APC collab. The release includes a silver case with a dark-green dial and another in gold on gold. Both of the pieces have a brushed sun-ray effect on the dial. The vibe is refined and stripped back; this is a fashion watch that almost feels anti-fashion.

Maybe the best way to think about it is as the reverse side of the coin to the excellent new G-Shock 2500 Series. Both come from Casio, and both are minimal and functional. But the G-Shocks are big and bulky, with a design that seems to tip its hat to Patek Philippe’s Nautilus. These new ones are slim and nearly dressy. Put the two new releases together, and you’ve got pretty much all bases covered. And if those aforementioned Timex collabs felt a bit too classicist for you, then the Casio-APC partnership takes things in a more modern direction. Far from just being a cash grab, the “fashion watch” is now one of the best routes into affordable, on-point horology.

“From that point on, it’s like her and her label are just working their ass off to make this one of the biggest releases of all time,” he added. “I’m just happy as hell for it because she’s happy with it. She’s proud of this and obviously I’m proud of her for going through the hoops to live out her dreams.”

#6640. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6638. Are You a Super Ager? This Competition Will Be the Judge of That

Alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart. Music booms over the speakers and other competitors shuffle around the cavernous room of the Armory Track in Washington Heights, New York, but Krepack stays laser-focused, thanks to years of meditation practice.

As soon as the volunteer says “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over. As he lands on the other side, he sprints to the beam, dropping down into an army crawl. “Take your time, take your time,” his son yells from the sidelines. Krepack reaches the far end, rushes back, and repeats the sequence again before crossing the line in 51 seconds. To cool down, he paces back and forth with his hands on his head. “I think I’m a sprinter, I’m a jumper, but then it’s like, fuck, no, I’m 73 years old,” he says, catching his breath.

The challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging. On November 7th, the inaugural day-long event drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries, and about 70% of participants were between the ages of 40 and 64. Krepeck agreed to let me shadow him to understand this new event through the lens of someone who is, in fact, aging, and would like to do so gracefully.

The name of the Games comes from a buzzword that originated in the longevity world: super ager. The term was originally coined by Northwestern University researchers to describe adults over 80 whose memories rival those of people 30 years younger. These days it’s thrown around on podcasts and in books to describe anyone who defies both the typical trajectory of both cognitive and physical aging.

The inaugural Super Age Games drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries.

From crawling across a cargo net to reading microexpressions, the challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill. At the end, athletes see where they rank among their age group and receive their “Super Age,” learning how their body’s physical fitness stacks up against the general U.S. population’s.

In an era where your average middle-aged midwestern dad is training for Hyrox, and a new, outlandishly extreme challenge is being invented every few months, the Super Age games are a low-key counterpoint to raw, stunty, athleticism, born from the metric-obsessed fitness subcultures who prize longevity above all. And now that fitness trackers like Whoop or Apple Watch can track VO2max, heart rate variability, and resting heart rates, that group continues to grow. Along the way, these stats have become status symbols on par with owning a Lamborghini. And now that overall health is quantifiable, fitness values have become less about just how fast you run or how much you lift, but how slowly aging.

It follows that, despite its name, Super Age Games isn’t just for aging athletes. The crowd there leaned middle-aged, and the youngest person at the competition was 21. As we stood by the dead hang station, Krepak pointed across the room at a brolic young man who looked like he could be an NFL prospect: “That dude’s a serious athlete,” he says, as we watched him run around the track cradling a sandbag on his shoulder.

Unlike competitions like Hyrox, where athletes race through a sequence of workouts against the clock, the Super Age Games allows competitors to rest as long as they need between trials. In fact, Junior Kennedy, the fitness program director for the Games, encourages it. “There's no rush,” he says. “The goal is to get through each event as intentionally as you can. We need to understand what it means to recover.”

Each trial was developed with a certain longevity marker in mind, and developed with input from researchers at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, a leading nonprofit research center based in Novato, California dedicated to understanding aging. The Over Under, for example, tests agility by judging how fast you can change levels and switch directions. Meanwhile, the Synapse, a challenge where participants track moving balls on a screen and identify them after they've been shuffled around, is meant to measure cognitive processing.

Challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill.

Krepack, a psychologist and lifelong athlete from Mill Valley, California, first heard about the event through its founder, David Stewart. Stewart is a media founder behind two niche longevity platforms, AGEIST and Super Age, where he writes about longevity, wellness, and redefining aging (one of his website testimonial’s says he has made aging “cool and aspirational.”). Krepack’s generally a skeptic of the profit-driven modern wellness industry—“I've always had a jaded view of all of that stuff,” he says—but he has followed both Stewart and the Buck Institutes’ work for years.

The competition appealed to Krepack, in part because he’s spent decades cultivating a consistent exercise routine he’s proud of. He played baseball in college and has spent much of his life skiing, cycling, and playing other sports. These days, his schedule revolves around a handful of rituals: bike rides on Mondays and Fridays, a Saturday hike with a friend, gardening, yoga, and Zen meditation most days. When he signed up for the Games in June, he altered his exercise routine, lifted more weights, practiced hanging from a bar, and experimented with the Neurotracker cognitive test online.

Yet all that training didn’t prepare Krepack for the biggest surprise of his day. After scoring well on both the Inferno (the assault bike VO2max test) and Synapse, next came the fourth trial: the “Tightrope,” a balance challenge that requires competitors to walk along a low beam while carrying a water-filled bag, taking as many consecutive steps as they can in two minutes without falling. He had expected to excel, thanks to years of skiing and yoga. Instead, he struggled to keep steady as the water shifted inside the bag. As his foot slipped off the bar, his eyes got wide. “I can’t believe my balance,” he says. “That’s my one disappointment in life now.”

Alan Krepack's sons Harrison and Aaron during the “tightrope” challenge.

Krepack was still hard on himself as we walked over to the dead hang trial. But after beating both his sons’ times, he seemed to get his competitive spirit back. He pushed through the remaining challenge determined to finish strong. And he did: By the end of the Games, he had placed second overall, with scores adjusted for age.

A few days after the competition, I checked in with Krepack to ask him how he’d processed the event. He responded with screenshots of his scores. His highest score came from the cargo net, which he credited to sheer determination rather than any particular finesse: “due to my will and overcoming an unconventional and desperate style!” he texted me, “Plus my sons were great support and focus partners.”

But the Games were also a reality check about aging: “I left there feeling both young and old,” he tells me on a phone call. As he watched his sons rocket through the obstacles, he was forced to confront how much of his athleticism he’d lost. “They just flew over it. They were so fluid, and so fast,” he says. “I’m not 30 or 40 or 50 or 60 anymore.”

Despite all the longevity industry's promises of maintaining youth, Krepack sees little value in denying the inevitable. Aging well, he says, is about “accepting, improving, and doing your best. It’s not a denial of who you are at this point in life.” The goal, he says, is to make the most of what you’re still capable of.

#6636. Lindsey Graham’s famous quote makes sense now

Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., talks with reporters in the basement of the Capitol on June 21, 2016. Back then, the late senator had a different view of President Donald Trump, Curtis writes. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

“If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed ... and we will deserve it.”

Reflecting on Tuesday’s midterm election results, a shellacking by Democrats that served as a rebuke to President Donald Trump, this quote deserves another look.

In 2016, in the midst of a heated Republican primary race, with assorted candidates jockeying to be the party’s presidential nominee, those words were posted by what now seems a surprising source: South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Of course, Graham himself had been one of the candidates in that bitter contest. Insults like “lightweight” and “jackass” were tossed back and forth, and Trump publicly shared Graham’s cellphone number. (Trump finally apologized for that stunt — at Graham’s funeral this past July. Better late than never, I suppose.)

By the time of Graham’s death this year, though, his earlier self would not have recognized the senator from South Carolina who had transformed himself into one of the president’s golfing buddies and closest allies.

In May of this year, after Sen. Bill Cassidy lost his Louisiana primary to a Trump-backed opponent, Graham reasoned on NBC News that Cassidy lost because he “tried to destroy” the president, and warned the same fate would befall any Republican who crossed Trump. “This is the party of Donald Trump.”

Why the switch? “He allowed me into his world. That’s great,” he told The New York Times.

Lindsey Graham stayed relevant, with a desired seat at the table — at a cost to his political reputation and legacy.

After he died, Graham’s sister was appointed to complete his Senate term and was then pushed to run for a full term by her brother’s onetime nemesis Donald Trump. The president’s endorsement pushed Darline Graham past a more experienced Republican, Rep. Ralph Norman, in the Senate primary.

That she played a part in the Republicans’ historic midterm loss is a full-circle moment that Shakespeare would relish.

Graham lost to Dr. Annie Andrews, as the state elected a Democratic senator for the first time in decades. It came as a big surprise, especially to those Republicans who, like Lindsey Graham, started out as skeptics of the inexperienced, cruel president before making peace with the man, his policies and his power.

MAGA swallowed the GOP, and voters who elected Trump in 2016 and 2024 followed.

What was the breaking point for the people who ignored millions of dollars in attack ads on their way to the polls?

In Ohio, was it the Vivek Ramaswamy ad that dredged up opponent Amy Acton’s childhood trauma, supported by Trump and Vice President JD Vance?

In the South, was it the seeming glee of Republican state legislatures as they gerrymandered districts with substantial African American constituencies, all with the blessing of a Supreme Court-weakened Voting Rights Act?

In Texas, did Hispanic voters who swung to Trump in 2024 realize that ICE’s definition of “the worst of the worst” included business owners, grandmoms and schoolchildren?

Did tariffs turn off farmers as it affected expenses and bottom lines?

Did Americans rebel when they saw their dollars buy less while the president gushed over gold trinkets, a ballroom and a reflecting pool his hand-picked contractors couldn’t fix, and made billions for himself and his family?

Did the Islamophobia and anti-Semitism, the racism and homophobia in the name of Jesus leave true people of faith or just plain decent people disgusted?

In South Carolina, Darline Graham didn’t explain her plans for the economy or for fighting corruption or foreign entanglements, except to say “national security is not my thing” on a debate stage.

But the candidate with a scant resume did manage at a South Carolina rally to call her opponent “bats — crazy” while standing next to an approving Trump, who coined his own anti-trans slur for Andrews.

Andrews responded by saying: “If name-calling would help lower gas prices and grocery prices, he can call me all the names he wants. But I don’t think that’s going to get the job done.” In a state with 14 counties “without a single OB/Gyn,” as Andrews has said, the emptiness of insults is hard to miss.

Whatever lessons they draw from Tuesday, Democrats should not get comfortable.

Angry, hurting voters expect results — fast.

But for now, it’s hard not to recall the warning issued and then forgotten 10 years ago, with the hope that Republicans realize the old Lindsey might have been right all along.

Mary C. Curtis has worked at The New York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on Twitter @mcurtisnc3.

#6634. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6633. Pride and Prejudice’s Rufus Sewell Is the Most Dashing Man on Television

It’s possible that Rufus Sewell is having too much fun right now. Between playing morally ambiguous Vice President (and husband to the U.S. Ambassador to the Court of St. James’s) Hal Wyler in Netflix’s frothy, prestige-y series The Diplomat and the beloved but deeply flawed Mr. Bennet in the streamer’s upcoming adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, he’s cornered the market on lovable rascals. He thrives on “exercises in gray” and relishes “when it goes wrong” for a character. “It’s the opposite of what you want in life,” he tells me. “You want drama, you want mistakes.” These roles offer plenty of both.

Wyler, of The Diplomat, is navigating how to work with the increasingly autocratic and bloody-minded President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) thousands of miles away from his wife Kate (Keri Russell), who is starting to exhibit some of his own manipulative behaviors she claims to abhor. Two centuries prior, Mr. Bennet is reckoning not with geopolitical crises and egomaniacal heads of state, but with the challenges his wife faces in marrying off five eligible, if dowry-poor, daughters.

Sewell sat down for a long chat with GQ about the two series, the value of blending high silliness with high stakes in the same scene, and how bodily functions are an under-appreciated key to unlocking a character’s specificity.

Rufus Sewell: The interesting question for me, for the second half of the season, was how much is Hal truly aware of everything that Kate and everyone else are noticing and concerned about with Grace's behavior. How much does he see? How much is he choosing to pretend not to see in order to stay in the room? He's always believed that access is all, but how much do you compromise in order to stay in the room? Where’s the point when you realize you stayed in the room too long without saying anything, and the moment’s passed, and you are just an accomplice? I found it very difficult to play his seeming unctuousness and obsequiousness with Grace this season, and to not be trying to protect my character in the wrong way, because I felt he was failing.

He’s overestimated his ability to effect change with Grace. Hal was prepared to appear to be supporting her, when he believed in his ability to steer her in a better direction, and I think he goes past that point. When I read the final episode script and saw where he ends up walking out, it gave me the courage to really lean into how much he goes wrong, by his own standards earlier in the season. He begins to lose his way in a way that he never has done before. But I embraced it, knowing that the real gift of the part was getting to play him going wrong and then seemingly correcting himself. We actually shot a speech that he made, just to give us a sense of where the scene was headed and for me to know how to play it. They might end up using some of it in the next season, or they could end up completely changing what was written. Hal coming out of the summit is a momentous decision in terms of what that does for the future and I've got no idea what’s next—I can't wait to start filming season five to find out.

I was always shocked when this show was described as a thriller because I always thought it was a kind of romantic sex comedy with extremely high stakes, because what it reminded me of firstly was some of the comedy of divorce screwball films of the 1940s. The characters may be divorced after a very tempestuous relationship, but they’re interlinked in a way that can never be undone. There's a romance to all of that history.

The other thing that it reminded me of was the kind of films that were made in the '70s—French films where halfway through an argument one of the characters would sit down on the toilet, you know what I mean? The people inside these films remind you of your own relationships. Your long-term relationship might not go to the same extremes, it might not be in the same setting, but I think people are people. What I love about their relationship is their shared wonkiness, and the getting into the nitty-gritty of the politics and taking someone down and hatching a plot whilst fighting over pastries and getting crumbs on the bed—all of that is part of their foreplay.

That is what the show is about, as far as I'm concerned. These are people who wear suits that might stand at a lectern and be on TV, but the fact is, how do you scratch an itch? Do you smell? Do you need to go to the toilet? These are the things that the script leans into a lot, and it might put some people off, but I don't care about that. That's the thing that makes it feel real, and it's so refreshing to play.

He'll flirt with anyone. We all know people like this. It's not even necessarily sexual, he just engages with people on that level and it's a natural thing for him.

I would say Hal’s flirtatiousness being a problem is open for debate, because a lot of what we understand of him is via Kate’s descriptions of him and his behavior. I can and often do see it in a different way. Part of the story of seasons three and four is Kate’s realization that a lot of stuff she thought of as his personality was in fact the mantle of the job that he'd taken on, because we see her doing the same kinds of things now that she is an ambassador. They both have a lot of the same qualities. They're both killers in a sense, and it's been very convenient for her and great for the show for her to introduce the public to Hal through her descriptions. And yet, every time it seems like he's changed character, in fact, it is revealing something from a different perspective.

We learned pretty early on that we were going to be doing some very, very long scenes, and we were given the advantage of seeing the scenes very early so we could slowly gestate the performances. We needed that because Windsor Castle in the show was comprised of several different buildings and locations, some of them with oceans between them, so we’d be shooting some parts the next day, and other bits in four months’ time.

Especially with a two-hander, with such long takes, you can go in and out of being relaxed, unrelaxed, free, slightly bound, and actually you get to the point where you stop worrying about it. It's like being on stage, because you end up too tired to be bad all the time and end up inhabiting the moment and things just happen. I love that all of it was a surprise to us.

I think what is most important in this particular iteration of the relationship between Mr. and Mrs. Bennet is that he comes to realize which ways he's failed his daughters. When Mrs. Bennet says to him in this version, it's easy for you to say that I’m silly or frivolous, but you try being a woman at this age with no means—this is the fight of their lives that he is making these jokes about. And yes, of course he's funny and right in certain ways, but he's also guilty of negligence of his family for the sake of an easy life for himself. The reason they have no money is that so much money has been spent on bonnets. Money could have been saved, but in order to have a quiet life, he's ducked out of fights in order to avoid responsibility.

Exactly. It was a gift in this role to have that moment when he feels that, admits that, and gets to be slightly humbled in this idea of himself that he's been cultivating. He didn’t actively or consciously avoid having this revelation, but that’s the effect of staying in his study, and now he’s facing the consequences. To use very modern terms, he has a revelation of what his pattern has been. It made sense!

One could be forgiven for thinking that Mr. and Mrs. Bennet are two people that used to be attracted to each other and now have nothing in common and don't like each other. I think it's born out in the book, though, the idea that there is still a love there, and especially a shared humor between them, and a bit of a spark remains.

I love the fact that we get to get drunk together and stuff like that. Olivia Colman and I worked on The Father together a few years ago with Anthony Hopkins, which was a very different kind of gig, but as is often the case with things that are very heavy and intense, we had a hoot doing it. I loved working with her, and was very excited about the chance to work with her again. I love the scenes between Mr. Bennet and Mrs. Bennet. They were such a treat for us.

#6632. Willy Chavarria Debuts His Dream “Bitchy Little Bags”

Are you a woman chasing the Willy Chavarria look? You’ll want to channel a Hitchcock heroine—Tippi Hedren is his favorite. Elongating skirt? Check. Strong-shouldered blouse or jacket? Done. Swooping french twist? Looking up Youtube tutorials now. But what about the classic handbag hitched up in the crook of your arm? Now, that can be yours, too.

Launched this morning on willychavarria.com, two new styles—the Bronca and the W Slouch—mark the New York designer’s official debut in the handbag space. Despite the pretty regular appearance of bags at his runway shows (both the Bronca and the W Slouch were seen at his spring 2027 menswear outing), introducing the category was a long time coming for Chavarria. “I’ve just been really timid about launching bags because it’s such a big thing,” he tells Vogue. “I never wanted to have a bag that ends up at the back of the store, doesn’t get the attention it needs—we just kind of pulled back and we said, okay, we’re going to launch this very soft bag that feels good.” Hence, only two styles, and direct-to-consumer only.

The Bronca is “sassy,” “a bitchy little bag,” even, and that’s just how Chavarria likes it. Available in pink, blue, black, and chocolate brown, it features a rolled leather handle with a set of keys dangling from the clasp. His dream girl to sport it is his forever muse Bianca Jagger; he’s fantasized about her pairing it with the iconic Yves Saint Laurent white wedding suit she wore to marry Mick in 1971.

In contrast, Chavarria says the W Slouch, available in green, chocolate brown, and black, is geared more towards his menswear customers. It comes with a detachable padded long strap, making it ideal for trekking across town with half of your belongings. To style it, he suggests following the wrong shoe theory. “I think it’s really cool with a tough look for a guy to have a bag that throws it off,” he says. “I always love those looks that just make you do a double take.”

Prior to today’s release, the designer has produced a W-embossed leather tote, some clutches, and a few coin purses, but he doesn’t look at those offerings in the same light. “This is more of me looking at [the category] as a business opportunity and building a plan and thinking about how I can grow this business,” he says.

It helps that with every collection, he’s dabbling in womenswear more and more. For his women customers, he sees a handbag as the perfect way in. “The brand is still small enough that I’m very careful about adding new categories, but as I’ve seen my womenswear business grow, it makes sense from a strategic standpoint to add a bag to the collection that actually enhances the full collection. And maybe she just buys the bag, maybe that’s all she wants.”

Though Chavarria is personally partial to a razor-sharp evening clutch, he doesn’t have plans to expand into additional silhouettes anytime soon. “I want to sit with these for a while,” he says. “I want to get these in the market and have people wearing them and get comfortable with them, and then maybe add on some little offspring, some little babies that go inside.” A nesting doll of handbag options await.

#6631. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.
