#6608. These former members are returning to Congress next year

Former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, here at a Oct. 20 campaign event near Ohio University in Athens, won his comeback bid Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Even in an election cycle marked by surprises and upsets, Capitol Hill observers will spot some familiar faces (identical twins notwithstanding) among this year’s midterm winners.

At least seven former members won comeback bids Tuesday.

The winners included alumni who dusted themselves off after election losses just two years ago. But other winners haven’t been in office in nearly two decades, their service predating the addition of a women’s restroom in the House (more recent than you may guess).

Here’s how these former members did on election night:

Carl lost a primary to fellow Republican Rep. Barry Moore in 2024 after a new map placed them in the same district. But with Moore running for the Senate in 2026, Carl had an easier path back to his old seat, which was redrawn again this year. He defeated his Democratic opponent Tuesday by 18 points.

It has been nearly two decades since Solis last served in Congress. She left in 2009 to serve as President Barack Obama’s first Labor secretary. Solis was in her sixth term as a Los Angeles county supervisor when she announced a bid for Congress after California voters approved a map that created five Democratic pickup opportunities.

Solis faced limited resistance on her path to victory in the 38th District, especially after Democratic Rep. Linda T. Sánchez opted to run for the redrawn 41st District.

Bean is making her way back to the House after losing her suburban Chicagoland seat in the conservative tea party wave of 2010.

A decade-and-a-half later, she won an eight-way primary for the 8th District seat Democrat Raja Krishnamoorthi vacated for an unsuccessful Senate bid. Winning the nomination all but guaranteed Bean a November victory in the deep-blue seat.

One of the cycle’s biggest comeback stories was in the Buckeye State, where Sherrod Brown was mounting a bid two years after Republican Bernie Moreno had unseated him. Positioning himself as an opponent of data centers, Brown defeated appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in a special election for the remainder of now Vice President JD Vance’s term. He could take office as early as December but would have to run again in 2028 if he wants another full term.

First elected in 2018, Allred left Congress two years ago after an unsuccessful Senate campaign against Republican incumbent Ted Cruz. After briefly launching a second Senate bid, Allred switched to a redrawn open House seat and won his primary over Rep. Julie Elizabeth Johnson, his successor in the chamber. Allred had no trouble winning his general election Tuesday for a fourth House term.

McAdams served one term in Congress representing a battleground Utah seat, before being unseated by Republican Burgess Owens in 2020. But after a state judge approved a new congressional map that created a heavily Democratic seat anchored in Salt Lake City, McAdams jumped into the race. He comfortably won his primary over more progressive opponents and stomped his way to a second term on Tuesday.

Once a high-ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, Luria lost her Hampton Roads seat in 2022 to Republican Jen Kiggans.

But a week after Virginia Democrats posted strong showings in the commonwealth’s 2025 off-year elections, Luria launched her House comeback bid and went on to oust Kiggans on Tuesday.

Former House Intelligence Chairman Mike Rogers left the House after the 2014 elections and made his first Senate bid 10 years later. He lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin but sought the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters the following year.

Rogers tried to take advantage of Democratic divisions between primary winner Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, even winning a late endorsement from the congresswoman. But it was not enough to stop El-Sayed on Tuesday.

Republican John E. Sununu served three terms in the House and one in the Senate before losing to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in 2008. With Shaheen retiring, Sununu attempted a comeback but ended up losing decisively to Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas.

Perriello won an upset victory in a Charlottesville-anchored district in 2008 before losing reelection in the tea party wave two years later. He launched a comeback bid this cycle for the current version of the seat, but the Republican incumbent, John McGuire, narrowly prevailed.

Two years after losing her at-large House seat to Republican Nick Begich, Peltola chose to challenge Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The race was rocked by late revelations by The New York Times that top aides to Peltola’s campaign were closely involved in recruiting a second candidate named Dan Sullivan into the race to peel votes from the incumbent. As of Wednesday afternoon, Peltola was clinging to a narrow lead as votes were counted.

#6607. The 5 Healthiest Fast Food Salads, According To Nutritionists

A drive-thru doesn’t have to derail your diet.

Fast food chains aren’t exactly famous for their salads. They usually fall into two categories: a sad bowl of lettuce added to menus as an afterthought, or a vehicle for fried, calorie-dense ingredients that offset any nutritional upsides. But some chains do make an effort to sell salads worth ordering.

To identify the best better-for-you fast-food salads, we asked three nutrition experts to weigh in. Here are the menu items they recommend, along with some tips and tricks for maximizing their nutrition.

First, we need to debunk salad’s diet-friendly reputation. “A salad isn't automatically the healthiest choice on a fast food menu,” says Kathy Levin, RDN, CDCES, dipACLM, LDN. “Once you add fried chicken, bacon, cheese, candied nuts, crunchy toppings, and a creamy dressing, some salads land in the same calorie and fat range as a burger and fries.”

Taking all of those components away isn’t always a solution either. A sad salad with just lettuce and a smattering of vegetables is more like rabbit food than a satisfying meal for humans. According to Briana V. Reamer, MS, RDN, LDN, the secret is getting enough fiber, which she says “will keep you satisfied and full until your next meal.” Take advantage of the restaurant's add-ons—like beans, avocado, and more vegetables—to make your salad more substantial.

Experts also recommend watching your saturated fat intake, specifically with your protein and dressing. Grilled chicken generally has fewer calories and less saturated fat than deep-fried alternatives. Consider your dressing options, too. “If you’re not sure what to pick, look for a vinaigrette or olive-oil-based dressing,” says Tina Sergi, MS, RD, CSSD, CSCS, TSAC-F.

And, as a rule of thumb, order your dressing on the side. It keeps your salad from getting soggy on the drive home, for one, but it also gives you more portion control. “Using only part of the packet cuts saturated fat and sodium, especially when they're already on the higher end,” Sergi adds.

Of course, the dressing is only part of the equation. With those tips in mind, here are the five salads that made the cut.

This regional chain is known for its fire-grilled chicken, and this salad packs plenty of it. Each portion contains a double serving of citrus-marinated chicken breast, sliced avocado, cotija cheese, salsa fresca, and tortilla strips over a bed of greens. It's served with a creamy Mexican-inspired Caesar dressing.

El Pollo Loco strikes the right balance between substantial and light with this dish. Before you add dressing, the entire salad contains 420 calories and 52 grams of protein. “The fire-grilled chicken makes it very filling, the avocado adds heart-healthy fat and fiber, and the salsa fresca adds flavor without much sodium or sugar,” Levin says.

Like with most salads, the dressing significantly raises the calorie count—in this case, it adds 440 calories if you use the entire serving. If you're closely monitoring your daily intake, Levin advises going easy on the dressing.

Culver’s may be best known for its ButterBurgers, but experts say you shouldn’t sleep on its salads. The Chicken Cashew Salad in particular is a great choice. It starts with a bed of mixed greens, topped with cheddar, grape tomatoes, cucumbers, and roasted cashews. You can also choose from several dressings to finish it off.

With grilled chicken, the salad comes in at 430 calories and 41 grams of protein before adding dressing. Culver’s also offers six dressing varieties ranging from 50 to 260 calories.

“This is a great fiber- and protein-packed option,” says Sergi. “Plus, the cashews add healthy fats, copper to support energy production, and magnesium for optimal nerve and muscle function.”

This Lone Star staple sells a Cobb salad that’s a lighter alternative to its lineup of burgers and sandwiches. It comes loaded with all of the essentials: greens, bacon, a hard-boiled egg, grape tomatoes, carrots, and shredded cheese. You can also choose from three chicken options (the grilled chicken filet is, naturally, lighter than the fried options).

Without dressing, Whataburger's Cobb with grilled chicken has 430 calories and 44 grams of protein. It's also a source of fiber and is low in sugar, according to Reamer. “Salads high in fiber help with weight management and satisfy hunger.”

Some of Whataburger's creamier dressings add 200 to 280 calories, while the balsamic vinaigrette has 180.

For a fried chicken chain, Chick-fil-A makes some surprisingly stellar salads. The Market Salad starts with mixed greens and is topped with strawberries, blueberries, red and green apples, blue cheese, roasted almonds, and the chain’s Harvest Nut Granola. Chick-fil-A also has the most protein options on this list. The grilled chicken can come in nugget or filet form, warm or cold, and spicy or regular. Talk about variety!

The different grilled chicken options provide between 26 and 32 grams of protein, according to Chick-fil-A's nutrition guide. Levin also says you can forgo chicken entirely for a meatless meal that doesn't feel like an afterthought. “Berries and apples bring fiber, antioxidants and natural sweetness, which makes it one of the most plant-forward options on the list.”

The Market Salad is typically paired with Chick-fil-A's Zesty Apple Cider Vinaigrette Dressing, which contains 230 calories per packet. But the chain is known for its sauces, after all, so you can swap it out for another option. There's a Light Balsamic Vinaigrette with 80 calories, Fat-Free Honey Mustard with 90, and Light Italian Dressing with just 25.

Zaxby's is the third chicken chain on this list, and it stands out by offering a salad with Asian-inspired flavors. The Asian Zensation Zalad (not Salad) adds shredded carrots, cabbage, wonton strips, and Asian Slaw to mixed greens, along with a drizzle of teriyaki sauce. It also comes with a vegetable egg roll on the side.

This salad is loaded with plant-based toppings, which is why Levin also recommends the garden version as a vegetarian option. Zaxby's lists that version at 390 calories, while the grilled chicken version comes in at 530 calories and 39 grams of protein, before adding dressing.

Alongside the teriyaki drizzle, Zaxby's offers Citrus Vinaigrette with the salad, which has 110 calories per packet. It's one of the chain's lighter options. But if you're watching your calorie intake, you can swap in Lite Vinaigrette, which contains just 30 calories.

#6605. 5 Restaurant Chains With Troubling Food Safety Records

Let's just say the health department had a few notes.

Not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day. Sometimes, going out really pays off. It saves you time in the kitchen, cuts down on effort, and most importantly, lets you relax while someone else does the heavy lifting. Many families turn to fast food when they want an easy, quick meal or when time is of the essence. But where you go can really make a difference.

Admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns. But beyond the macros, another factor to consider is cleanliness.

Cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location. You may have seen headlines concerning less-than-stellar hygiene reports stemming from certain fast food locations over the years. Kitchen cleanliness is paramount to food safety (just look at this year’s Cyclospora outbreak), and some chains have faced more than their share of troubling headlines. Here are five fast food chains with a disappointing history of food safety issues.

I hate to break it to burrito-with-extra-guac fans, but Chipotle has a history of high-profile food safety issues. The company paid $25 million to resolve criminal charges related to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks between 2015 and 2018. According to the documents, Chipotle was charged with "adulterating food in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act," resulting in the largest criminal fine ever imposed in a food safety case at the time.

Records cited at least five foodborne illness outbreaks across several states, including incidents involving norovirus, that sickened more than 1,100 people. These outbreaks "primarily stemmed from store-level employees' failure to follow company food safety protocols." Personally, I'd rather have a side of hot sauce than a side of stomach flu.

In February 2025, a Massachusetts store was cited for nine core health code violations—including insufficiently cleaned ice machines, improperly stored produce, and missing thermometers in a walk-in cooler—along with one priority foundation violation. Such issues can raise concerns about food safety and sanitation.

In 2022, a health inspector described another location in the state as "very unclean." A year before that, workers at a Springfield, Missouri, location staged a walkout over poor working conditions. A subsequent health inspection found that "the floors in the food preparation area (especially under equipment and near drains), walk-in refrigerator and freezer, and dry storage areas were not clean," leading to a follow-up inspection. (Don't even get us started on some of the issues found overseas!)

Sorry, chalupa lovers. Taco Bell has also faced its share of food safety concerns over the years. Reports include an E. coli outbreak along the East Coast in 2006 resulting in 71 illnesses (53 of whom were hospitalized), two Salmonella outbreaks in 2010 affecting at least 155 people across 21 states, and a hepatitis A outbreak in 2000 that sickened 23 people and hospitalized 15.

More recently, a customer’s viral video appeared to show a Taco Bell kitchen strewn with food, garbage, and old boxes near food prep areas. Some commenters suggested that it was filmed during rush hour while the restaurant was understaffed and that employees were too busy to clean. Still, it's not a great look for in-store hygiene.

Big Mac lovers, look away. The Golden Arches have faced numerous lawsuits over food safety issues over the years, including a class action suit (plus several personal injury suits) filed in 2024 following a multistate E. coli outbreak linked to Quarter Pounders. The outbreak ultimately sickened 104 people and killed one, with investigators identifying slivered onions as the likely source of contamination.

The Boston City Department of Inspectional Services found nearly 125 violations at seven different McDonald's locations between 2018 and 2019—everything from mismanaged storage to mold, rat droppings, and even live cockroaches. Complaints and lawsuits have also alleged undercooked meat and foodborne illnesses caused by cross-contamination.

Wendy's locations have racked up numerous health code violations, too (one Las Vegas restaurant in particular drew 27 demerits in a 2019 inspection for dirty soda nozzles, food left on the floor, raw food cross-contamination, and more). A 2023 "Dirty Dining" segment called out a Fort Lauderdale, Florida, location with an inspection that found insects all over the restaurant.

Perhaps most concerningly, a Michigan family filed a lawsuit in 2024 alleging their daughter developed hemolytic uremic syndrome following an E. coli infection they attributed to food from Wendy's. According to the lawsuit, the illness caused permanent brain damage, kidney failure, a seizure disorder, and other lasting health problems. Inspectors had found the location in violation of 17 different health and food codes just days before the family's visit, including moldy food, spoiled produce, dirty surfaces, and water leaks.

Even with these histories of violations, not every location should make you rethink your dining options—many restaurants are up to code and clean. While all this information is enough to convince me to stick to home-cooked meals for the rest of my life, I suggest checking your local restaurant's latest health inspection report before deciding whether or not to visit your chain of choice.

#6604. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

#6602. Florence Pugh Is Fed Up With Faces Being Scrutinized Online—We All Should Be

It can be tough, being a celebrity. Hear me out! Sure, it comes with money, acclaim, and unfettered access to luxury fashion. But it also tends to mean millions of people feel entitled to vocalize their opinion on your looks, which is when things inevitably tend to get a little trickier.

Particularly for women, of course. And particularly when self-appointed social media detectives start scrutinizing every inch of a woman’s face, speculating about what she may or may not have had “done.” Is it a facelift or filler? A little Botox or upper blepharoplasty? It’s safe to say that no tweak, tightening or treatment—real or imagined—goes unnoticed, or increasingly, unremarked upon.

One star who has found herself at the centre of online scrutiny this week is former Vogue cover star Florence Pugh. In an Instagram Reel titled, “Is it just me or does Hollywood hate round faces?” a writer compared an older photograph of Pugh with a more recent one, suggesting the 30-year-old East of Eden star’s face shape had changed in the interim.

Florence Pugh at the 2026 Governors Awards.

“People are saying that Florence Pugh has fallen victim to Hollywood’s war on round faces,” the writer says. “Don’t get me wrong, Florence Pugh still looks beautiful, but Hollywood seems to have this thing against softer features.” The reel goes on to discuss the “sculpted” and “snatched” look that has become the beauty ideal in the entertainment world, suggesting that women are increasingly pursuing sharper jawlines as a result. The clip caught the attention of Pugh herself, who commented on the post.

“Guys, I turned 30,” the actor wrote. “I’m a woman. [Bodies] and faces change. It’s not that deep, the fact that people can’t even tell between what’s aging and what’s surgery is disturbing. Sadly puppy fluff doesn’t last forever.”

Florence Pugh at the 96th Annual Academy Awards in 2024

Pugh’s exasperated response illustrates just how exhausting it is to be a woman in the public eye—a woman full stop—where you’re damned if you do and damned if you don’t. (Pugh sadly has previous experience with internet trolls, she memorably told online body shamers to “grow up” after they weighed in on her dress for the Valentino Haute Couture show in Rome.) On the one hand, women are celebrated for embracing the entirely normal aging process. (Take Olivia Colman and Sarah Jessica Parker, for example, who have been praised for their chic silver hair.) On the other, they risk being accused of “letting themselves go” if they don’t continue to look exactly as they did when they first entered the spotlight. And if they do choose to have a little help along the way, as is entirely their prerogative? That gets dissected ad nauseam, too.

Of course, celebrities shouldn’t be exempt from conversations about beauty standards, and the more we question the normalization of cosmetic procedures, the more we can make natural aging feel, well, normal. But there’s a difference between a healthy conversation about unrealistic beauty ideals and picking apart an individual woman’s appearance.

Speculating about what someone has or hasn’t had done is just as damaging as criticizing lines, wrinkles, or any other natural signs of aging. Both reinforce the idea that a woman’s face is fair game. What we’re really doing? Perpetuating the same impossible beauty standards that hurt us all in the long run.

Then there's the smaller Cantina Carne Asada Street Chalupa, which has a fried shell lined with crispy cheese.

Rounding things out is the Cantina Carne Asada Rolled Quesadilla, stuffed with steak, a three-cheese blend, and Spicy Ranch before being grilled and sliced. All six items also come with an Avocado Verde Salsa packet.

The rollout follows Taco Bell's push to give its Cantina menu more attention, including the slow-roasted chicken that's already made its way into items like the Cantina Chicken Mexican Pizza. This latest test could eventually put carne asada on the permanent menu, although there's no word yet on whether it'll expand beyond those two markets.

#6600. Too Busy for Breakfast? Make These Pumpkin Overnight Oats

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

I’m not going to tell you that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. Humans have been on the planet for hundreds of thousands of years and our ability to thrive simply isn’t rooted in whether we eat first thing in the morning. In fact, the cliché is barely a century old, stemming not from nutritional science but good old-fashioned advertising.

Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, advocates for breakfast cereal used religious rhetoric and maternal guilt to fuel their marketing efforts, while public relations executives at a pork company convinced doctors to recommend a heartier breakfast of bacon and eggs for sustained energy, aimed at working families.

Yet today breakfast is one of the most commonly skipped meals. So instead of wagging my finger at you about missing something so “important,” I think it’s worth asking: Why did you miss it in the first place?

On a jam-packed holiday like Thanksgiving, there are plenty of reasons. You have a turkey to roast. The table has to be set. Someone needs to pick up the wine. And oh, there’s still the pie dough to roll out! Maybe you even want to “save room” for the glorious feast you’re putting so much effort into.

But skipping this meal does come at a cost. Even if you aren’t ravenous, it’s metabolically valuable to eat in the morning. Breakfast stabilizes energy, and studies have shown that forgoing it leads to a reduced consumption of important nutrients like fiber, potassium, iron, and calcium, often found in morning staples like fruit, whole grains, and dairy. Without some food to start the day, you risk an energy dip, brain fog, and downright hanger. Which, let’s be honest, we don’t need in a kitchen overflowing with dirty dishes and extended relatives.

I have an easy solution. Making breakfast on Thanksgiving (or any day, really) doesn’t have to be a last-minute hassle. It can be quick to assemble and still feel special—like you’re really taking care of yourself, because you are. Take this overnight oats–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes the night before you plan to eat it.

Open up a can of pumpkin purée—odds are you bought extras that didn’t become a pie. Mix it with oats, maple syrup, and whichever milk you have in the fridge. A scoop of chia seeds adds bonus nutrition and prevents the oats from turning gluey as they hydrate overnight.

The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you. It’ll keep you full and firing on all cylinders for a day of turkey roasting, potato mashing, and vibe managing. It may not be the most important meal of the day—at least on Thanksgiving—but it will be delicious.

#6598. Papa Johns Wants Your Honest Opinion—And It's Offering Free Pizza In Return

They're asking for the good, the bad, and everything in between.

Opening a pizza box can bring out the critic in anyone. But whatever your reaction, whether it's about a pale crust or toppings piled onto one side, Papa Johns wants to hear about it—and your opinion could be worth a whole other pizza.

The chain has launched a two-week promotion called "Snap a Pizza, Get a Free Pizza," inviting customers to snap a photo of their orders and tell the company what they really think. You can praise it, complain about it, or land somewhere in the middle. Even a less-than-glowing review is welcome.

Before you start snapping pictures of every slice in sight, though, there's some fine print worth reading.

To participate, you'll need to spend at least $15 on an order placed through the Papa Johns website or app. You'll also need a Papa Rewards account with text messages enabled, since that's how the chain will contact you about submitting your review.

Papa Johns wants an unedited photo of your pizza, along with your thoughts on everything from the level of cheese and how it's cooked to the overall experience. Once the photo is approved, you'll receive an offer for a large one-topping pizza in your Rewards account.

That word "free" does come with a qualification. Redeeming your reward requires spending at least $5 on your next order, meaning you'll have to open your wallet twice. Still, if you've ever had strong opinions about the way your pizza arrived, you might as well get something out of sharing them.

Of course, Papa Johns is getting something out of this arrangement, too. All those pictures and reviews give the chain a closer look at what customers are actually receiving.

"We see the pizza pics, the unboxings and the hot takes online every day, and we know our customers aren't shy about sharing what they think," said Chris Lyn-Sue, Papa Johns' global chief marketing officer, in a statement.The promotion is part of Papa Johns' recently announced "Unbox Better" initiative, which focuses on things like food quality and the chain’s general service. It's also not the only fast food chain inviting customers to speak their minds. Earlier this year, Burger King went so far as to encourage customers to call or text its president directly with their feedback.

Papa Johns is offering a slightly different incentive, although I suspect a free pizza might convince a few more people to participate.

How can someone create a plaid nail look at home?

“Anyone can create a plaid look with just a few velvet polishes or jelly polishes,” says Kim. She says you just need to paint on a few stripes of one color in one direction, followed by a different color in the same direction. Then finish by painting on different sizes of stripes and colors in another direction for added dimension.

#6595. Best Kitchen Scales, Tested Over a Decade of Baking (2026)

I’ve been an avid home baker for well over a decade (my first stint in “food media” was a baking blog I started in middle school!), and I can confirm that there is no single tool quite as important to the outcome of your baked goods as a simple kitchen scale. Bon Appétit’s Test Kitchen team agrees, which is why you’ll see gram measurements in the baking recipes on our site.

Another bonus of a kitchen scale? In most cases, you can kiss measuring cups and spoons goodbye, which means far fewer utensils to clean once your bakes are in the oven.

Scales aren’t just for bakers, either. They make portioning burger patties and meatballs easier, streamline meal prep, and keep your Sunday morning pancake routine cleaner.

I’ve tested 16 models over several years and consulted Shilpa Uskokovic, former BA senior Test Kitchen editor and co-owner of Hani’s Bakery, to find the best kitchen scale for home cooks. The winner is just $27.

New in this update: I tested the new version of the Oxo Good Grips 11-Pound Digital Kitchen Food Scale. While it was easy to use and I appreciated the pull-out display, it was less accurate than the Escali—and over double the price. You can read my full review below.

Size: 8.5 x 6 x 1.5"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: 4 minutes 30 secondsPower: AA batteries (included)

This Escali Primo has held the top spot in our testing for over six years and has been a favorite in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen for far longer than that. “This scale has been with me for more than a decade of my career, staying faithfully by my side through 12-hour shifts in pastry kitchens, bouts of religious recipe testing, and weekly sessions of casual baking,” says senior Test Kitchen editor and resident baking whiz Shilpa Uskokovic.

It’s durable, accurate, intuitive to use, and affordable—pretty much everything we could ask of a kitchen scale.

What we love: The Escali Primo is lightweight, comes in a variety of fun colors, and has a simple two-button interface to turn it on, tare it, and toggle between ounces, pounds, and grams. In testing, it was responsive and precise, quick to tare, and delivered accurate readings every time. Its 4.5-minute auto shut-off is among the longest of any model we tested, so you won’t lose your measurements mid-bake. Plus, its 11-pound capacity is large enough to accommodate any task a home cook might ask of it.

Performance aside, the Escali Primo has several design features that helped it stand out. For one, the fact that the weighing platform is elevated and offset from the base means you can easily read the display or use the buttons even when measuring into a large, wide mixing bowl. The plastic body and sealed control panel make it a breeze to wipe down after a floury baking session and also keep stray crumbs from getting stuck in any crevices. Another detail we like? The four rubberized feet keep it stable on your kitchen counter.

The Escali Primo has proven quite durable as we’ve continued to test it long-term, another reason why it’s a perennial favorite among our Test Kitchen editors. Shilpa again: “It’s compact and easy to store, it’s easy to wipe clean, it toggles between grams and ounces seamlessly, and it’s reliably accurate."

What we’d leave: The Escali can only measure in 1-gram increments. While this was typical of most scales we tested, those looking to use their kitchen scale for dialing in their coffee routine will want something more precise (though coffee scales are kind of their own thing). Unlike some pricier models, the Escali’s display is not backlit, but we didn’t find this to be an issue. It’s also worth noting that the Escali is not a touchscreen device, so you’ll need to use a bit of pressure on the buttons.

Size: 8.3 x 7 x 1.3"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: NAPower: AAA batteries (included)

Amazon Basics products are not consistent across the board, but this scale is a certifiable hit. At about half the price of the Escali, it’s a good option if you’re not positive about this scale thing and want to spend as little as humanly possible to do so.

What we love: There are a lot of similarities between the Amazon Basics scale and the overall winner. The Amazon Basics scale has the same two-button setup, a similar elevated weighing platform that makes it easy to see the display, and the same 11-pound maximum capacity. It’s made of plastic with a stainless-steel platform that’s easy to wipe down and is just a touch larger than the Escali at 7 inches across.

In testing, I was impressed by the Amazon scale’s accuracy, considering its price point. It responded to weight addition or removal almost as quickly as the Escali and provided an accurate readout about 99% of the time. That 1% weight change inaccuracy happened when someone repeatedly added weight or switched back and forth between units of measurement, and when it did happen, the reading was off by a minor amount. The problem could be fixed by removing what was on the scale, taring it, and starting over. For $10 (at the time of writing), you’d be hard-pressed to find a better model.

What we’d leave: Unlike the Escali, the Amazon scale’s buttons lack any kind of laminated sealing to prevent crumbs or liquid from entering the crevices around them. As mentioned, this scale isn’t quite as accurate as the winner and it tended to overshoot an item’s actual weight at first (before correcting itself relatively quickly). And last, the stainless-steel platform is more prone to scratching or smudging than Escali’s plastic one.

You’ll notice there aren’t any other scales marketed as coffee scales on this list, and that’s because the Fellow Tally was the only coffee scale we thought could plausibly work as an all-purpose model too.

What we love: The Fellow Tally is one of our favorite coffee scales (especially for pour-over) thanks to features like a built-in timer and a “brew assist” that directs you on the proper ratio of coffee to water—but its 5.5-pound maximum capacity means it works for most home baking projects too. If you’re the kind of person who likes to nerd out over your brewing and baking techniques, this is your best bet unless you want to invest in two separate scales.

In testing, we quite liked the Tally’s design for its tactile controls and easy-to-read OLED display, and appreciated its ability to measure grams, ounces, pounds, and milliliters (that milliliter measurement is calibrated for water, so one milliliter equals one gram; if you're measuring a heavier liquid like milk it will be slightly off). The elevated 6-inch platform is large enough to comfortably hold a mixing bowl while allowing easy visibility of the display.

To find out how accurate each scale was, I used a set of calibration weights. I tested each scale’s ability to give an accurate reading for the minimum amount of weight it claimed to be able to accommodate (usually 1 or 2 grams), and its ability to detect small changes when there was already weight on the platform. I also placed weights in various places on each scale’s platform to determine whether they could give an accurate reading regardless of whether the weight was in the center or at the edge.

I coated each scale in a mixture of flour, water, and oil and let them sit overnight. I cleaned the residue off and noted which scales were easy to clean and resistant to any scratching or staining.

I distributed winning scales to staffers to see how they fared after long-term use in our homes and in the Test Kitchen and added any long-term testing notes to reviews as they came in.

I looked for consistently accurate measurements and a short response time when adding and removing items of varying sizes and materials from each scale. I took into account how weight distribution affected the readings, looking for scales that delivered spot-on results regardless of where on the platform we placed the weights. I also took note of how precise each scale could be in its measurements, but found our favorite all-around options tended to measure in 1-gram increments.

I looked for scales that were intuitive to use without picking up a manual.

I tested scales with weight capacities ranging from 1.65 to 16 pounds, but found that a maximum capacity of 11 pounds was more than enough for the tasks one might try to accomplish in a home kitchen.

I wanted a scale that felt durable, well-made, and stable on the counter and was also designed to be easy to clean.

Unlike a stand mixer, a scale isn’t the kind of kitchen gadget most home cooks are looking to keep permanently on their counter. Lightweight, compact models that could be easily stashed in a cabinet were better.

I took into account the relative price of each scale. After years of testing, we’ve found that you really don’t need to spend much to get a high-quality, highly accurate kitchen scale, so any models that were pricey needed to wow us with their design or extra features.

These scales didn’t quite make our list of top picks, but they still impressed us in testing and might fit your needs depending on what you’re looking for.

This is another scale from the makers of our top overall pick. It’s sleeker and slightly more advanced, with a four-button control panel that includes the typical on-off, unit change, and tare functions, plus a “hold” feature that keeps your measurement on the screen rather than automatically shutting off after a given amount of time.

We ultimately didn’t think the added feature and upgraded design merited spending an extra $10, but this is undoubtedly a good scale (and the rainbow of colorways available makes it easy to find a match for your kitchen decor).

This Oxo scale is a favorite among professional chefs for its easy-to-clean stainless-steel weighing platform and handy pull-out display design (great for measuring into extra-large bowls). I liked it a lot, but found it was often off by 1 gram, especially when the weight was placed in one of the platform’s corners. I ultimately didn’t feel its performance merited its price tag, which is more than double that of the winning Escali at the time of writing.

True to its name, this precision scale from Etekcity provides measurements in 0.1-gram increments as well as the option to measure in milliliters and fluid ounces (along with the typical grams and pounds/ounces). That said, we didn’t love that the instructions recommended using this scale with only the included plastic bowl and found that the stainless steel weighing platform scratched easily.

This rechargeable digital kitchen scale seemed promising, with its 22-pound maximum weight, easy-to-clean weighing platform, Bluetooth-enabled app connectivity, customizable auto-off function, and host of premium features. However, it was one of the least accurate scales we tested: Our 5-gram nickel weighed in at a low of 2 grams and high of 6. For that reason, we don’t recommend it unless you’re buying a scale primarily for meal tracking reasons.

The Zwilling Enfinigy Digital Food Scale was another promising option. It’s rechargeable via USB cord and has a sleek, buttonless design and 22-pound capacity. However, it wasn’t as accurate as we’d have liked, and despite how cool it looks, the lack of buttons turned out to be frustrating. We also disliked how the tab that switches the units of measurement is located underneath the scale.

MyWeigh KD-8000 Bakers Math Kitchen Scale

This scale is heavy-duty. It’s got a 16-pound max capacity, it can be charged with a plug-in A/C adapter, and it’s the size of a small kitchen appliance. It works well (and even allows you to measure using baker’s percentages), but unless you’re in a professional bakery setting, it’s overkill.

At less than 3-by-3 inches, this scale is truly tiny. It’s an impressive little kitchen tool, able to provide measurements in 0.1 gram increments, but its maximum capacity of 1.65 pounds is just too small for most cooking or baking projects besides making coffee.

This scale from Cuisinart has a glass weighing platform and removable stainless-steel bowl, but we ultimately didn’t love the idea of the bowl adding yet another piece of clutter to our kitchens. Besides that, this scale was less accurate than our top picks, had a short, 1-minute auto-off time, and was nearly double the price of the winning Escali.

This scale lost for a couple reasons: It was less accurate than our winners and one of the most difficult scales to clean in our most recent round of testing. The display panel was prone to trapping crumbs and bits of flour, and the scale itself required intensive scrubbing to remove leftover residue.

Joseph Joseph TriScale Compact Folding Digital Kitchen Food Scale

Like many of Joseph Joseph’s products, this scale has an interesting design. It’s made up of three prongs that fold into a small rectangle, making it easy to stash away when not in use. That said, this scale struggled in testing; it couldn’t detect small amounts of weight and was prone to reading the weight of your finger when you tapped its buttons.

I had high hopes for this dual platform scale from the makers of some of our favorite pizza ovens. It’s got a sleek, low-profile design, wide capacity range (0.1–22 grams if you take into account both platforms), and handy light-up display. Unfortunately, we found both the small and big platforms inaccurate: The small platform struggled with picking up small changes and was often off by multiple tenths of a gram, and the big platform was inconsistent, often fluctuating between two readings or off by a couple grams.

KitchenAid Dual Platform Digital Kitchen Scale

We noticed inaccuracies and inconsistencies with both of the KitchenAid’s platforms. The small scale is meant to be precise down to the hundredth of a gram, but it struggled to detect our .02-gram calibration weight and fluctuated between .19 and .20 when we weighed a 0.2-gram weight. The big scale was decidedly more inaccurate, off by 3–4 grams when we tested it with a 100-gram weight.

Like all of Smeg’s products, the brand’s take on a kitchen scale is very cute. Unfortunately, while the design is aesthetically pleasing, it didn’t prove to be very functional. The scale is very bulky because of the built-in bowl, which can’t be removed from the base (though the stainless-steel bowl insert can be removed for cleaning). The scale’s base itself is sensitive to weight, which means pressing on the buttons with force can cause a temporary spike in the reading—and, more important, if you drop any ingredients on the base, the weight of said ingredient will be added to the total. We also found that this scale struggled to accurately report small (1- or 2-gram) changes in weight.

ThermoWorks Gravitas Precision Kitchen Scale

I was very excited to test this scale from the brand behind our favorite cooking thermometers, but unfortunately it failed to impress me enough to merit a recommendation. The scale boasts the capability to measure down to the tenth of a gram, but according to ThermoWorks' product description, it does so with ±0.7 g accuracy. In testing, I found this to be true—readings were rarely accurate to the exact tenth. After testing the scale in his home kitchen for several weeks, senior commerce editor Noah Kaufman also noted that readings came in on the slow side, which made measuring ingredients that pour out quickly (like flour or liquids) tricky. I did appreciate the detachable display (helpful when using a large, wide bowl that might otherwise obscure the screen), but it wasn’t enough to outweigh the negatives—and besides, I’m of the opinion that there’s no reason for the average home cook to pay $120 for a scale when a $25 one performs incredibly well.

We also tested the Ozeri Pronto, Etekcity Multifunction Food Kitchen Scale, and GDealer Tempered Glass Kitchen Scale, all of which have been discontinued.

To use a kitchen scale, you’ll have to familiarize yourself with the concept of “tare.” Taring a scale allows you to reset the weight back to zero when you already have something on the weighing platform. This is particularly useful if you want to measure ingredients into a bowl (just place the bowl on the platform, click the tare button, and go on adding your ingredients), or if you want to measure multiple ingredients into that bowl without needing to add or subtract the existing weight in your head.

Baking is the obvious answer here, but the use cases for kitchen scales go far beyond the world of flour and butter. Use a scale to perfectly portion out meat for meatballs or burgers, aid in your meal prep for the week, or for any recipe where precise quantities are of the utmost importance.

Alaina Chou: Alaina has been testing products at Bon Appétit for over three years, which means she’s used dozens of air fryers, toasters, rice cookers, and—you guessed it—kitchen scales. She’s an avid baker who’s been a proponent of measuring by weight for the better part of a decade.

#6594. DoorDash Reveals The Thanksgiving Desserts & Sides Each State Loves

Somebody might want to check on the pumpkin pie loyalists.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

During a Thanksgiving food debate, everyone at the table likely has a strong opinion. DoorDash just added some numbers to the argument, and they might surprise you—especially if you assumed pumpkin pie was untouchable.

Ahead of Thanksgiving 2026, the delivery company went ahead and analyzed what Americans ordered during last year's holiday, and apparently, we've got some explaining to do. From an unexpected dessert taking the national crown to some questionable side-dish allegiances, the results make a pretty convincing case that no two Thanksgiving tables are exactly alike.

According to DoorDash's 2025 ordering data, chocolate cake was the most popular store-bought pie or cake purchased through the platform during Thanksgiving week. Apple pie came in second, followed by cheesecake. Pumpkin pie, arguably the holiday's most recognizable dessert, had to settle for fourth place, with pound cake rounding out the top five.

Things get even more interesting when you look at individual states. DoorDash also identified which desserts each state ordered at a higher rate than the national average, revealing some pretty distinct regional preferences.

Pumpkin pie still had plenty of supporters, with strong support in 14 states, including California, Washington, and Arizona. Hawaii was especially devoted, ordering it at nearly three times the national share. Meanwhile, New York, Connecticut, and Massachusetts leaned toward apple pie, while New Jersey and Pennsylvania showed a particular fondness for pound cake.

Cheesecake stood out in eight states, including Illinois, Michigan, and Ohio. Texas, Louisiana, and Tennessee favored pecan pie, while Maine and New Hampshire were among the states where chocolate pie stood out.

And then there's Georgia, where key lime pie was the surprising choice.

Mashed potatoes topped DoorDash's national Thanksgiving-week ranking, followed by corn, sweet potatoes, green beans, and gravy. Mac and cheese, stuffing, cornbread, carrots, and cranberries also made the top 10.

Regionally, though, things get a little more interesting. Cornbread stood out in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, while North Carolina and South Carolina showed a preference for mac and cheese. Tennessee's standout was biscuits, and Georgia, Alabama, and Florida leaned toward corn.

New York and New Jersey, two states that can barely agree on pizza, apparently found some common ground in carrots. Meanwhile, Vermont was the only state where stuffing stood out most, and neighboring New Hampshire went with squash.

It's worth remembering that these state rankings reflect what people ordered more frequently relative to the national average on DoorDash. They aren't necessarily each state's most popular dish overall, and they don't account for whatever Grandma was making from scratch.

Still, if someone tries to tell you there's only one acceptable Thanksgiving menu, you now have some pretty compelling evidence to the contrary.

#6593. 7 Best Shampoos for Hair Growth and Thickness, According to Dermatologists

I’ve been blessed with natural thick hair (thank you endlessly to my parents for passing along these genetics), but life happens and the effects of constantly being stressed, excessive hot tool use, and tight slicked-back ponytails are starting to manifest in a thinning hairline and some density loss. And I, like most people, have been wondering if all the shampoos that promise to help hair grow back are worth a spot in my hair routine.

The answer to that? It depends. If you’re wondering if these shampoos directly have anything to do with hair growing, then the answer, according to Y. Claire Chang, MD, board-certified dermatologist, is no. As Dr. Chang goes on to explain, hair growth occurs within the hair follicle, which is beneath the surface of the scalp. Since you are rinsing off shampoo, it only stays on your scalp and hair for a few minutes at best, which limits the amount of time that active ingredients have to interact with hair. “This is one of the biggest misconceptions in hair care,” she says. “Most shampoos marketed for hair growth may not actually stimulate hair growth.”

But this doesn’t mean these shampoos are completely ineffective. They do help in the grand scheme of your hair growth journey. You just have to think of hair growth shampoos as one piece in a very big puzzle for thicker hair. “Growth-promoting shampoos can play a meaningful part of a hair growth or regrowth journey,” says Kandice Bailey, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Skin of Color Society member. “However, these types of shampoos are a single asset within our arsenal, a single component of a larger plan.”

Dr. Chang agrees and goes on to explain that what these shampoos actually do is support scalp health, remove excess oil and product buildup, reduce inflammation, and strengthen hair to minimize breakage. “By reducing breakage, hair may retain more length and appear thicker and healthier,” she says.

So if you’re interested in just keeping your scalp as healthy as possible so that hair has the best environment to thrive in, we say to consider these seven shampoos.

Why We Love It: As New York City-based board-certified dermatologist Hadley King, MD, describes it, this is a scalp-focused cleansing system that comes with a shampoo, conditioner, and treatment to help hair look fuller and feel healthier. Inside, you’ll find key ingredients like salicylic acid, which Dr. King says helps remove excess sebum, dead skin cells and debris on the scalp, as well as peppermint oil and niacinamide to nourish hair. It also has panthenol, biotin, and caffeine to reduce breakage and boost the scalp’s circulation for increased hair growth. Though it may be drying to some (she says to be careful of the sulfates included), there’s nothing like a set to cut out all the guesswork, and this system makes your hair routine super easy.

Why We Love It: “This shampoo can help to strengthen and support hair growth,” says Dr. Garshick. “It’s especially good for those who regularly color, straighten, perm, or heat style their hair.” It contains nourishing ingredients like shea butter, castor oil, and rice protein that will give both your hair and scalp needed moisture and rebuild broken strands. She adds that castor oil has antifungal properties for extra nourishment. It’s also a clarifying shampoo that will give your hair a deep cleanse and get rid of buildup.

Why We Love It: Excessive hot tool use can wreak havoc on our hair. And worst case scenario, lead to thinning. So for the curling iron enthusiast, this is the shampoo for you.

“It helps maintain a clean, nourished scalp surface, which allows emerging hair strands to grow in stronger and [make them] less prone to breakage,” says Morgan Rabach, MD, board-certified dermatologist and co-founder of LM Medical NYC.

It contains peptides and caffeine to stimulate blood flow on the scalp and support the skin barrier, and biotin to strengthen hair. But what really sets it apart is its proprietary keratin alternative called Karmatin, which adds hydration, strength, and shine without heavy silicones weighing hair down. Dr. King adds that it can also improve hair conditioning and improve your hair’s appearance overall.

Why We Love It: How does Nutrafol’s shampoo compare to its storied hair-growth pills? Pretty well. “It works by balancing the scalp’s microbiome and gently exfoliating excess oil and product without stripping essential moisture,” says Dr. Rabach. “A balanced, hydrated scalp prevents follicle irritation and supports stronger, healthier hair.” It’s made with prebiotics, vegan protein, and antioxidant-rich Australian wild berry extract to strengthen the scalp barrier and promote healthy hair growth. It’s also made with biosurfactants, which gives you a thorough cleanse and a rich lather without stripping your hair of its natural oils. The end result is a clean scalp and added volume, which is all we ever ask of our shampoos.

Why We Love It: Of all the oils that are touted to help with hair growth, rosemary oil is the most promising; it has anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties to help create the ideal environment for hair to thrive in, and small studies even show that it can be as effective as minoxidil. This shampoo is centered around rosemary oil—mixes in plant proteins and ceramides to nourish the scalp and strands and promote healthy hair growth, which Dr. Garshick says it makes it a great option for anyone looking to keep their scalp healthy and strong. Plus it comes with a lovely rosemary scent that’s super refreshing.

Why We Love It: “This shampoo is a great option for those with thinning hair who want a gentle cleanse with added scalp support,” says Marisa Garshick, MD, board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology. It uses a special complex that combines biomimetic peptides and red clover extract to strengthen the scalp’s skin barrier, and pea sprout extract, which is rich in phytonutrients to help increase hair density and help the hair look fuller. It also has a compound called Redensyl to help reduce shedding (thank the beauty gods) and keep hair healthy overall. Plus, it works wonders in giving your hair a boost in volume, which is always welcomed.

Why We Love It: For when hair needs a full reset, we start with this shampoo. Dr. Garshick says that this is great for gently removing buildup from oil, dirt, and pollution, while also hydrating the scalp. It has hyaluronic acid to add that needed moisture and caffeine to boost circulation. But its special H2-Grow complex, which is made of a blend of apple stem cells, is what protects hair from future damage and helps give hair a ticker, fuller appearance.

What ingredients should you look for in hair growth shampoos?

“I would look for ingredients that support scalp health, reduce inflammation when present, and improve hair strength,” says Dr. Chang. “I would also prioritize shampoos with gentle cleansing agents and conditioning ingredients to avoid irritating the scalp or damaging the hair shaft.”

Some ingredients to look out for include:

Ketoconazole, zinc pyrithione, and selenium sulfide are known for their antifungal properties to control Malassezia yeast overgrowth and inflammation, per Dr. Bailey, and help create a healthy environment for hair to grow. She adds that ingredients like caffeine may help with hair growth by increasing blood circulation to the scalp, which will increase the delivery of micronutrients to your hair follicles.

Dr. Chang adds that ingredients like salicylic acid can help get rid of buildup, while ingredients like niacinamide will support the skin barrier. She also recommends ingredients like panthenol, biotin, and peptides can help strengthen the hair shaft and reduce the risk of breakage.

Are there any downsides to using a hair growth shampoo?

Hair growth shampoos are generally safe, but there are a few things to consider. Dr. Chang says that some formulations may cause scalp irritation, dryness, allergic contact dermatitis, or buildup. Those with sensitive scalps should especially be careful as it might cause more irritation, so she recommends prioritizing gentle, fragrance-free formulations. And if you’re experiencing persistent irritation, burning, or worsening flaking, you should stop using the shampoo and seek medical advice.

But the biggest downside, she says, is the unrealistic expectations. “Patients may spend a lot of money on products marketed for hair growth when they may potentially benefit more from medical treatment for an underlying form of hair loss,” she says. So remember that shampoos for hair growth may help, but they’re not the sole solution you should turn to.

Dr. Chang says that treatments such as topical minoxidil and PRP have much stronger clinical evidence when it comes to actual hair growth. But the most important part is trying to identify the underlying cause of your hair loss to figure out the appropriate treatment. “Because androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium, alopecia areata, and nutritional deficiencies all require different approaches,” she says.

When should someone see a doctor for hair loss?

Dr. Chang says that you shouldn’t be waiting several months to see whether your hair growth shampoo is working. Because hair loss can have many different causes (genetics, hormonal changes, postpartum shedding, stress, nutritional deficiencies, thyroid disorders, autoimmune conditions, certain medications, etc.), it’s always best to see a doctor to figure out the cause and come up with the right treatment.

She recommends seeing a doctor if you notice the following:

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity hairstylists—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to shampoos for hair growth, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, lather, finish, and the hair-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you. Read more about our testing methodology here.

#6592. Meet the history-makers of the 120th Congress

Democrat Annie Andrews, here addressing supporters at her election night party in Charleston, S.C., on Tuesday, is the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

The incoming freshman class of the 120th Congress includes several people who scored historic wins in their states and the nation at large.

Among them were women breaking glass ceilings in the Senate and trailblazers for Native American representation. Beyond Washington, a handful of nominees pulled off milestone victories in gubernatorial elections, including four Black candidates. Congress is also poised to witness history next year with New York Democrat Hakeem Jeffries expected to become the first Black speaker.

Here are some of the candidates who made history on election night, both in Congress and in the governor's mansions:

Alfonso, the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, is the first Gen Z Republican elected to Congress with his victory in Wisconsin’s open 7th District, a seat his father-in-law once held.

Andrews, a pediatrician, becomes the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina after defeating appointed Republican incumbent Darline Graham, the first female senator from the Palmetto State.

With her victory in New York’s 13th District, Avila Chevalier becomes the first Muslim person elected to Congress from the Empire State. She succeeds Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat, whom she defeated in the primary.

Benitez-Thompson, a former majority leader of the Nevada State Assembly, is the first Democrat elected to represent the state’s 2nd District since its creation after the 1980 census.

With his victory over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Colom, a district attorney, will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. He will also be the Magnolia State’s first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Conely, a Navy veteran, unseats Republican Rep. Mike Lawler to become the first openly gay woman elected to Congress from New York.

Dandiya, the daughter of Indian immigrants, becomes the first South Asian American elected to Congress from Florida with her victory in the redrawn 22nd District. She is also one of the first adherents of Jainism to be elected to Congress, along with Arizona's Amish Shah (see below).

With his victory over Republican Mike Rogers, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, becomes the first Muslim person elected to the Senate.

A member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, Flanagan becomes the first Native American woman elected to the Senate with her victory over Republican Michele Tafoya. The outgoing Minnesota lieutenant governor is also the first Native American to represent the state in Congress.

Ford, a state senator, unseated Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz to become the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Indiana.

Hamawy, a former Army surgeon who emigrated from Egypt to the U.S. as an infant, is the first Muslim person elected to Congress from New Jersey, with his victory in the state’s 12th District.

Killin, an Army veteran and onetime chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff, is the first Democrat elected to represent Colorado’s 5th District since its creation after the 1970 census.

Kiros, who upset Rep. Diana DeGette in the Democratic primary for Colorado’s 1st District, easily won the general election to become the first Black woman elected to Congress from the Centennial State. Kiros, who was born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and emigrated to the U.S. as an infant, is also the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress.

Koh, the son of a Korean American father and a Lebanese American mother, is the first Asian American elected to Congress from Massachusetts. The former Biden administration alumnus will succeed Democrat Seth Moulton in the state’s 6th District.

Letlow, the first Republican woman elected to the House from Louisiana, earns the same distinction in the Senate with her victory over Democrat Jamie Davis in the open-seat race to succeed GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy.

Limtiaco will be the first Chamorro woman to represent Guam in Congress after she unseated Republican Del. James C. Moylan. She previously was the first woman to serve as U.S. attorney for the Districts of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands.

McCann, a state senator, defeated Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga to become the first Native American elected to Congress from Michigan. McCann is a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation.

Moss, the president pro tempore of the Michigan Senate, keeps Rep. Haley Stevens’ 11th District in Democratic hands, becoming the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Michigan.

The grandson of a Mexican immigrant, Ojeda, who defeated National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, is the first Latino elected to Congress from North Carolina.

By defeating former Sen. John E. Sununu, Pappas, a fourth-term congressman, becomes the first openly gay man elected to the Senate.

The daughter of immigrants from Chile and Cuba, Powell is the first Latino person elected to Congress from Nebraska after flipping the state’s 2nd District. She is also the first Democratic woman elected to Congress from Nebraska.

Unofficial returns show Sarauw winning the open-seat race to succeed outgoing Del. Stacey Plaskett, making her the first openly gay person elected to Congress from the U.S. Virgin Islands.

The son of Indian immigrants, Shah is the first South Asian American elected to Congress from Arizona. The former state legislator is also one of the first adherents of Jainism to be elected to Congress, along with Florida’s Pia Dandiya.

A citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation, Valdez is the first Native American elected to Congress from New York. The New York State assemblywoman will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez.

Wiener, a state senator who succeeds former Speaker Nancy Pelosi in California’s 11th District, is the first openly gay person elected to represent San Francisco in Congress.

With her victory over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, Acton becomes the first woman elected governor of Ohio. Republican Nancy Hollister briefly served as the state’s top executive in the late 1990s but was never elected governor.

The son of Mexican immigrants, Becerra, a former congressman and Health and Human Services secretary, is the first Latino to be elected governor of California. He is the state’s second Latino governor after Romualdo Pacheco, who was never elected to the role but briefly succeeded an incumbent in 1875.

Blackburn, Tennessee’s first female senator, will soon become the Volunteer State’s first female governor after her victory over Democrat Jerri Green.

Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, will be the first Black person elected governor of Wisconsin after he defeated Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany.

Republican Rep. Byron Donalds will become Florida's first Black governor after he defeated Democrat David Jolly, a former GOP congressman.

Ford, the current Nevada attorney general, will become his state’s first Black governor after defeating Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo.

Haaland, a member of the Pueblo of Laguna, will become the first Native American woman to be elected governor in the U.S. after defeating Republican Gregg Hull. The former Interior secretary was also one of the first Native American women elected to Congress, along with Kansas Rep. Sharice Davids, in 2018.

Hinojosa, a state representative, will become the first Hispanic person elected Texas governor since statehood after she unseated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.

Klobuchar, the first woman to be elected senator from Minnesota, makes history again with her election as her state’s first female governor.

With her victory over Republican businessman Rick Jackson, Lance Bottoms becomes the first woman to be elected governor of Georgia. The former Atlanta mayor is also the state’s first Black governor and the first Black woman to be elected governor anywhere in the country, along with Del. Stacey Plaskett in the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Unofficial returns show Plaskett, the nonvoting delegate from the U.S. Virgin Islands, becoming the first woman to be elected governor of the island territory. She is also one of the first Black women to be elected governor in the country, along with Lance Bottoms in Georgia.

#6591. Patrick Schwarzenegger Says This Small Detail Makes All The Difference In A Great Martini (Exclusive)

Three years with one of vodka's oldest families will apparently teach you a few things.

Patrick Schwarzenegger knows a thing or two about a good martini. After three years working with Ketel One and spending time with the family behind the vodka, the White Lotus actor has learned that some people take their cocktails very seriously.

"I'm not that severe," Schwarzenegger told me, although he's developed a few preferences of his own. His biggest? "A frosted glass. A cold glass I think makes all the difference."

I caught up with Schwarzenegger in Schiedam, Netherlands, during a Ketel One-hosted visit to the historic Nolet Distillery, where the family has been making spirits since 1691. The trip was actually his idea. After hearing so much about the distillery from the Nolet family, Schwarzenegger wanted to see everything firsthand, even getting his hands dirty by shoveling coal into the distilling equipment.

According to Schwarzenegger, family members have gotten so particular about their drinks that they'll check where a bar stores its vermouth, olives, and white wine before ordering. If certain ingredients have been sitting out rather than refrigerated, they might opt for a drier martini.

Bob Nolet sees that same attention to detail in the way people order cocktails today. "Today's martini drinkers know what they want," he told Delish, whether that's a classic dry martini, something dirty, or an espresso version.

Of course, that hasn't stopped bartenders from seeing just how far they can stretch the definition of a martini. Schwarzenegger told me he tried The Corner Store’s viral sour cream-and-onion version largely because he'd heard so much about it, something he deemed “really good.”

The Tomatini was another story. He appreciated how convincingly it captured tomato flavor, but the novelty only went so far. "I think that I could have that for a few sips, maybe one max, but then I'm tapped out of that," he said.

His more dependable order is an espresso martini, something the Nolets know particularly well. Schwarzenegger revealed that the family even arranged for espresso machines to be sent to his wedding in Idaho, giving guests a way to enjoy his favorite cocktail during the celebration.

For Carl Nolet Jr., the connection goes deeper than a shared appreciation for espresso martinis. "Patrick comes from a family that is equally committed to their craft in the entertainment space," he told Delish. "You can see that commitment through his career and how he brings his legacy into a new generation."

Carl also credits Schwarzenegger with offering a younger perspective on cocktail culture, particularly how drinking has become part of the way people socialize, host, and celebrate.

For someone who knows his way around a cocktail, Schwarzenegger doesn't actually drink all that often. Between filming, fitness, and work, he's made a rule to keep alcohol to weekends. He's also taken an interest in the growing demand for better-for-you options, pointing to canned cocktails with less sugar and real fruit juice as examples of how people's drinking habits are changing.

That curiosity extends well beyond the bar. With his involvement in the protein snack company MOSH, Schwarzenegger has become the kind of person who considers wandering supermarket aisles a perfectly good Friday night activity. One of his first stops after arriving in the Netherlands was a grocery store, and he loves comparing what's available in different places, from Los Angeles to wife Abby Champion's home state of Alabama.

His Instagram algorithm isn't helping matters, either. Food, drinks, random syrups—if an ad catches his attention, there's a decent chance it'll end up on his doorstep. "I buy everything," he admitted.

Interestingly, all that enthusiasm for trying new things doesn't necessarily translate to elaborate dinners. He and Champion love exploring restaurants together, but they're equally happy cooking at home or keeping things simple. She's a fan of Chick-fil-A and In-N-Out, while he's perfectly content with a plate of chicken and rice.

After talking martinis with Schwarzenegger and the Nolets, I might start paying a little more attention to what happens behind the bar. I'll leave the vermouth inspections to the professionals, but keeping the rest of my martini on ice until I'm ready for a fresh, frosty glass? That's a level of service I could get used to.

#6588. Taylor Swift Returns to Her Roots at the 2026 CMAs

Taylor Swift hasn’t yee’d her last haw after all.

Tonight, the singer returned to the Country Music Awards for the first time in 10 years, where she is nominated for Single of the Year for her song “I Knew It, I Knew You” from Toy Story 5.

Swift returned to a longtime favorite house for the occasion: Oscar de la Renta. The singer hit the red carpet in Nashville wearing a strapless yellow gown with a billowing high-low skirt—plus pockets—from the brand’s spring 2027 runway. (One eagle-eyed Vogue editor suggested that the dress was an ode to Dolly Parton, whose favorite color was yellow.) While the house currently has no creative director since Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia exited over a year ago, she’s been loyal to the brand across leadership. She accessorized with strappy metallic gold Jimmy Choo heels and a pair of custom Lorraine Schwartz drop earrings with Paraíba tourmaline and white and yellow diamonds.

For her performance, Swift turned to one of her newer faves—Erdem. The singer plucked a minidress with a multicolored, bejeweled mock neck and a flouncy red drop-waist skirt straight off the spring 2027 runway. She countrified with a pair of matching cowboy boots and a rhinestone-encrusted guitar. Swift hit the stage once again to present Brooks & Dunn with the Willie Nelson lifetime achievement award. She brought a little disco to the Country Music Awards in another mock-necked mini from Taller Marmo: a blue and green sequined number with blue fringe hanging from her long sleeves.

The singer last attended the CMAs in 2016, when she was gearing up to release Reputation. The look, a departure from her sweeter look, matched the era’s tone: a slinky Julien Macdonald cutout dress with black sequined patternwork over illusion mesh.

But while it’s been a decade since Swift attended the CMAs, it’s been a whopping 13 years since she hit the stage. In 2013, the singer performed “Red,” for which she wore a classic black gown and strummed away on a rhinestone-encrusted guitar.

Swift performing at the 2013 Country Music Awards.

This year also marks the 20th anniversary of Swift’s first CMAs. The singer attended the awards for the first time in 2006, back when her most acclaimed song was “Teardrops on My Guitar.” For the occasion, she wore a black mermaid gown with matching evening gloves. Taylor Swift has come a long way, but she’s always known how to make a splash on the red carpet.

#6587. Don't Miss Starbucks Red Cup Day 2026—Here's What You Need To Know

It’s the most wonderful (and caffeinated) time of the year.

Starbucks has already unveiled its 2026 holiday cup designs, including an adorable miniature version for dogs. Now it's time for the humans to get their hands on something they can actually keep.

Starbucks Red Cup Day is officially back, and the multinational coffeehouse chain is once again giving customers a little something extra with their seasonal caffeine fix. But before you make a special trip for a little piece of festive plastic, a few things are worth knowing, as your usual coffee order might need some adjusting.

Circle Tuesday, November 17, on your calendar, as that's when Starbucks will be handing out its latest reusable holiday cups at participating locations across the country.

The catch is that it’s only happening while supplies last. And considering how much people love free stuff, I wouldn't recommend waiting until a 4 p.m. coffee run to try your hand at getting a cup.

Starbucks says it's bringing in extra baristas for the occasion, too, which should help with the inevitable rush of customers looking to add to their collections.

You'll need to purchase a qualifying handcrafted holiday or fall beverage of any size. Yes, even a tall gets you the same free 16-ounce cup as someone ordering a venti.

You don't even have to physically step inside a Starbucks, either. Orders placed at the drive-thru, through the app, or via DoorDash, Grubhub, and Uber Eats are all eligible.

And somehow, brewed Starbucks Christmas Blend and Starbucks Reserve Christmas coffee don't qualify, despite having Christmas right there in their names. Because apparently, even Christmas itself can't get you a free cup.

This year's version features coffee cherries and leafy branches tied together with a big red bow. There's also a green-and-white ribbon design around the outside that ties into the rest of Starbucks' holiday collection.

The reusable cup is made with 95 percent recycled material, and unlike the paper versions you normally toss after finishing your latte, this one is meant to stick around.

In fact, putting it back to work comes with a few perks. Bring a clean reusable cup to Starbucks on a future visit, and you'll save 10 cents on your drink, while Rewards members also get double Stars on their entire order.
