#6586. Bob's Chicken Salad and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

One of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#6585. Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake

This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling)

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

Place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

To serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

#6584. Upside-Down Apple Cider Cheesecake

If you feel there’s never enough graham cracker crust with your cheesecake, then this version is for you. The entire no-bake cheesecake is surrounded by crust, so there are buttery graham crackers and creamy cheesecake in every single bite. The exterior isn’t just hiding a silky-smooth cheesecake filling, but also a surprise syrupy apple filling. If you want to win the holidays this year, set this unassuming dessert on the table and watch everyone ooh and ahh as they cut in and discover the sweet, spiced, and completely delicious treat hiding inside.

How to make it upside-down:To achieve a double layer of crust, you need to freeze one layer so that it’s easy to place on top of the cheesecake. Before serving, you’ll flip the whole thing onto a plate, which puts the seam on the bottom and gives you a beautiful display of a solid crust. It’s easier than you think to flip it, and the parchment will ensure nothing sticks to the springform pan.

Make ahead & storage:I love to make this dessert during the holidays because you can prep and make it all ahead of time. The apple filling can be made up to 3 days ahead, and the assembled cheesecake can be made up to 2 days ahead of when you want to serve.

#6583. What Anthropic’s IPO Means for Fashion

Anthropic, the US artificial intelligence company behind Claude, will make its debut on New York’s tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange on Thursday under the ticker ANT, in a closely watched IPO that will test Wall Street’s appetite for — and potential of — the AI boom, amid concerns about the cost of developing the technology and intensifying competition.

The company priced its shares at $83, above the projected $70-78 range, raising $81.3 billion and valuing it at approximately $1.5 trillion. This positions it to be the biggest IPO in history, edging out SpaceX’s June debut. Early trading on Thursday will determine investor appetite.

“Anthropic’s IPO is an important bellwether for investor sentiment toward AI,” says Lior Prosor, managing partner at venture capital firm Deep33. “A successful listing would give the company significant capital and greater confidence in its ability to meet its enormous compute commitments. That should also give corporate customers more confidence in Anthropic as a long-term provider,” Prosor adds, forecasting that a successful IPO for Anthropic would signal strong investor appetite for an eventual listing for its biggest rival, OpenAI.

Anthropic’s ambitions extend far beyond the tech sector. In its IPO prospectus, the company says it wants to make Claude available “across every surface where work happens”, targeting a global “knowledge work” market (i.e., jobs that involve processing information, making decisions and producing content, rather than physical work) that it estimates generated more than $40 trillion in economic value in 2025.

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees, including CEO Dario Amodei, Anthropic has emerged as one of the industry’s leading developers of large language models, competing with OpenAI and Google. Unlike OpenAI, Google and Meta, which have positioned AI, in part, as a consumer tool for shopping and product discovery, Anthropic has focused more heavily on enterprise applications, from coding, research and data analysis, to workplace productivity and content creation. Though recently, it unveiled its first consumer-facing fashion partnership with J.Crew, in the shape of the brand’s “Style Advisor” AI styling tool, co-developed with Claude.

Anthropic’s market debut comes at a turbulent moment for the tech industry, amid a string of major US server outages, the scandal and resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — which is both an investor in Anthropic and a supplier of its AI chips — and mounting concerns about the AI boom. Amodei himself published an article in September calling for an industry-wide slowdown on AI development to ensure security risks and other AI doomsday fears didn’t spiral out of control.

For fashion, Anthropic’s debut offers another indication of how the AI market is evolving, as brands consider where — and how much — to invest in the technology. Luxury executives will be watching how Anthropic fares on the public markets, as they weigh their own investments in AI.

Luxury companies have been experimenting with AI across functions including customer service, merchandising, marketing and internal operations. The emergence of Anthropic as a publicly traded company marks a new chapter for the providers developing the technology behind those applications.

On the enterprise side, Anthropic has already found its way into the biggest luxury and beauty businesses. Earlier this year, LVMH group information officer Franck Le Moal said the group had strengthened its partnership with Anthropic and launched an internal platform built around Claude Code, designed to give its maisons secure access to AI tools. L’Oréal, meanwhile, uses Claude to develop specialized AI agents for workflows like conversational analytics across its business, while Kering has said it (occasionally) uses Claude Sonnet for software development, while mainly relying on Google Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

A successful listing could reinforce confidence in the long-term prospects of AI, although it doesn’t necessarily mean the industry’s sky-high valuations are sustainable. For brands considering large-scale investments in AI tools, the more pertinent question is whether AI providers can establish durable, commercially viable businesses while continuing to improve their products.

Anthropic’s own brand positioning could also prove significant. Unlike some of its competitors, the company has made AI safety and responsible development central to its identity. In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic acknowledges that AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” if developed or deployed without adequate safeguards. The company also operates as a public benefit corporation, a structure requiring it to balance shareholders’ financial interests with its stated mission, as per its IPO prospectus, of “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity”.

The IPO will put those commitments under greater scrutiny. Anthropic’s governance arrangements are designed in part to protect its mission, but going public also introduces new expectations around financial performance, sequential growth and shareholder returns. How the company balances those pressures could influence its reputation among corporate customers.

Not necessarily, according to creative agencies working with some of the world’s biggest brands. “We don’t hand clients one model,” says Gian-Carlo Lacanilao, director of creative innovation and AI at creative agency Made Thought, who explains that the agency often starts with Claude, then hand picks other AI models for different parts of a brief depending on which will do the job best.

Like Made Thought, Stephan Pretorius, chief technology officer at advertising group WPP, says WPP takes a “model-agnostic” approach, selecting AI tools from the different hyperscalers — from Google to Amazon to OpenAI — according to the task, their performance and cost.

Meanwhile, the listing could have implications for luxury’s customer base. At the valuation targeted ahead of the IPO, Anthropic’s founders, employees and early investors stand to hold substantial stakes in one of the world’s most valuable technology companies.

The flotation could contribute to a new wave of wealth creation in the US technology sector, particularly in Silicon Valley, at a time when luxury brands are seeking to strengthen relationships with high-spending clients with a focus on the US. Until now, much of that wealth has existed on paper, but now that the biggest companies in AI are hitting the public markets, analysts are poised for an influx of newly minted tech millionaires.

“The AI investment boom, accompanied by other factors, has been a major driver of global wealth creation in the last couple of years, and we expect tech’s share of the ultra-wealthy population to grow substantially over the next decade,” says Moira Boyle, global head of luxury, at wealth intelligence platform Altrata. “IPOs, acquisitions and secondary market sales are turning points, because they convert wealth on paper into wealth that can actually be spent.”

Altrata tracks how the newly wealthy allocate their money, from investments through to discretionary spend. Boyle expects luxury goods to be a firm part of the picture — and says the “smartest” luxury houses are already adjusting to the changing face of the high-net-worth individual. She cites Hermès, for example, as a brand that’s been opening boutiques beyond the classic fashion capitals to meet new luxury clients (many of whom will, in this case, be Silicon Valley-based) where they actually live. “This cohort will shop differently. The average ultra-wealthy individual today is 67, and this new generation is decades younger, at a very different stage of life, with different passions and priorities,” she says. “Every brand now has an unprecedented opportunity to build relationships with these clients before their tastes and loyalties are set.”

#6582. French Onion Croissant Strata

A breakfast strata is one of our go-tos when we want a hearty, shareable brunch dish, but it’s hard to put into words how good this French onion croissant strata is. It takes a few extra minutes to deeply caramelize the onions, but the extra flavor and richness make a HUGE difference.

Making it French Onion:Caramelizing the onions over medium heat helps them brown evenly and consistently. If the onions begin to stick or burn, add a splash of water to bring them back! Garlic, thyme, and black pepper are the aromatic unsung heroes in the onions, so you don’t want to skip them. Deglazing with white wine is essential in any French onion recipe, so use the one you’d sip! Once the wine has reduced, add some beef stock to impart meaty French onion soup flavor. The caramelized onions then get layered with torn croissants and Gruyère cheese, and topped with dollops of cream cheese.

Delish Official:Eggland's Best Eggs are the Official Eggs of Delish. That means they're the only eggs we're using in our recipe content.

Storage:The beautiful thing about a breakfast strata is that you can make it ahead. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 day and reheat until the internal temperature reaches 165°. This is also great to portion and store for breakfast at the office.

#6581. The Hidden Cost of a Hit Product

Between 2022 and 2025, Miu Miu was on fire. Driven by a string of viral product releases including the ultra-low-rise micro-mini skirt, a New Balance 530 collaboration and its logo ballet flats, the label saw rapid growth. In 2024, revenue grew 93% on the previous year. And by the end of 2025, it accounted for 31% of Prada Group’s retail sales, up from 25% a year earlier.

Now, Miu Miu’s explosive sales growth has normalized, recording a 2.4% increase in Q1 2026, against a 60% increase the year prior, according to Prada Group’s most recent earnings. This slowed growth was expected: during the first-quarter earnings call, Prada Group CEO Andrea Guerra said Miu Miu was dealing with a “disrupted environment, against the most challenging comparison base of the year”. In other words, Miu Miu did so well during its viral product peak that even a solid performance today looks like a slowdown (Miu Miu didn’t respond to request for comment).

The Miu Miu cropped jumper and mini skirt set as seen on influencer Caro Daur.

This isn’t an isolated example. Elsewhere, Hermès – which had remained a bright spot post pandemic as other brands faltered – recently recorded slower-than-expected growth over the nine months ending September 30, 2026. Ready-to-wear and accessories were down 2.1% on the previous year, weighing on overall performance. CFO Éric du Halgouët told investors during the earnings call that the decline is partly due to a contraction in “high-volume” categories such as footwear and non-handbag accessories like belts. Alongside many footwear styles, this category includes the Hermès Oran sandal, which offers an entry point to the house for more aspirational consumers, retailing at around $900. Hermès declined to comment for this story.

Viral hit products are undeniably a boon for brands, both for revenue and relevance. But there’s a downside once their star inevitably fades: difficult comps. In a challenging macroeconomic environment, where brands are seeking new customers and growth, they must strike a balance between sales spikes driven by virality and long-term brand desirability.

Regardless of the brand, “a single hit can keep sales strong while hiding [softer] demand elsewhere and failing to attract the next generation,” says Jeanel Alvarado, founder and editor-in-chief of RetailBoss. “When demand slows, the brand must replace lost revenue and build new demand, with less money available to do either.”

Sneakers are a key category for viral items. Alvarado highlights Balenciaga’s Demna-era Triple S sneaker as another hit piece that inflated brand sales after its release in 2017, before creating tough comparisons for the label once it fell out of fashion. “Its exaggerated silhouette connected luxury with the way people were dressing in everyday life,” she says. “The challenge comes when demand for those few recognizable products becomes stronger than customers’ interest in the wider collection.” A year after the Triple S hit the market, Kering’s 2018 report praised the “continuing exceptional momentum of Balenciaga”.

The Balenciaga Triple S sneaker was first shown in the FW17 menswear collection.

Likewise, McQueen’s entry-level Oversized Sneaker represented 80% of brand revenues at its peak in the late 2010s, according to Kering CEO Luca de Meo, during Kering’s full year 2025 earnings call in February of this year. According to analysts at Bernstein, the house’s turnover fell from €850 million to €200 million between 2022 and 2025.

“When sales are under pressure, brands [can] double down on products customers already understand and can more easily justify buying,” says Alvarado. Across brands, popular products are backed up by sales data, and begin to take more rail space and marketing attention, delivering short-term and easy wins. “The short-term need to protect revenue then leaves fewer resources to build demand for alternatives. That is how a sensible buying decision becomes a longer-term dependence.”

For brands, cashing in on a hit product makes immediate and obvious commercial sense. Done well, it welcomes new consumers into the fold, offering a short-term sales increase and the opportunity to convert them into long-term fans. But problems may arise when the entry-level product is pumped out without being replaced by another hit once demand fades.

“A breakout, viral product can lift a brand quickly, but once it’s everywhere, it loses the exclusivity that made people want it,” says Katy Lubin, VP of brand and communications at Lyst. Ubiquity is a problem for luxury brands, in particular. “It’s hard to spend a lot of money on something and then see it everywhere,” adds Marissa Lepor, managing director of The Sage Group. “The more prevalent that a luxury item becomes, the core customer of the luxury brand is less interested in it. They feel like it’s everywhere, or they already have enough of them.” Nowadays, this is happening quicker than ever. The rise of short-form video means that trends come and go much faster.

Conner Ives’s viral vintage robe from his SS27 collection.

If an item is too visible, it also runs the risk of being duped by more accessible contemporary or high street players, quickening its trend half-life and further reducing its appeal to luxury consumers. While many luxury customers won’t be interested in a dupe, other potential buyers may be tempted by a cheaper alternative. “It can really amplify the conversation around those hero products, but maybe doesn’t scale as much with sales,” Lepor says. “The person who’s coveting that luxury item might not end up buying it, they might end up buying something similar.”

One way to reduce reliance on a small number of items or categories is to reduce supply — something luxury houses have often employed. “Hermès and Rolex still sell less of their iconic products than their market would take,” says Luca Solca, managing director of luxury goods at Bernstein. For Hermès, its intricate leather goods production creates scarcity, rather than the brand holding back product, according to artistic director Pierre-Alexis Dumas, who told CBS’s 60 Minutes that “whatever we have, we put on the shelf, and it goes”, in 2024.

The Hermès Oran sandal seen on a guest at Berlin Fashion Week SS27.

When supply stays below demand, hero products never become ubiquitous and the market remains unsaturated, even if the product goes viral. “There has to be a balance between what a brand is known for, what products get mass scale and how to keep the scarcity,” says Lepor, “so that when you invest in these luxury items, you feel unique.”

Brands can avoid potential overreliance by using the exposure that comes with a popular item as an opportunity to introduce consumers to a wider brand universe. “It is good to have an iconic product that everybody wants, [but] it is better to follow-up with more products to build on this,” says Solca.

“If you have a few designs that become really popular, they become popular for a reason,” says Lepor. “It’s less figuring out why something went wrong, and more figuring out how to iterate upon it to do something like that again. Something I think is really important with the luxury world right now, is not just selling people one item, but getting them to covet the world of the brand.” Lepor points to Cartier’s Love bracelet, as well as the wider Love Unlimited collection that was built upon it, as an example of getting it right. “How can you stay true to a design that has been very successful, without just launching it in new colors?”

Emerging designers are also having to balance viral popularity with long-term growth. Lubin points to Conner Ives, who recorded a 49% rise in demand from the second quarter of 2026 to the third quarter, according to the Lyst Index. “The Vintage Robe led desire, but demand was also spread across scarves, dresses and shirts,” she explains. Other success stories according to Lyst include Bottega Veneta and Chanel, both of which recorded strong demand in multiple categories. “Strength across categories spreads commercial risk and protects brand value. It also widens a brand’s reach, because each hero product brings in a different shopper, from a bag collector to sneaker enthusiasts.”

Betting big on an already-popular product is a common path, whether it’s an oversized sneaker or a viral skirt. The brands that maintain that momentum and success, however, do so by looking forward. “Brands need to invest in the next reason to buy while the current hero funds the business,” says Alvarado. “The strategic advantage is building the next generation’s reason to purchase before the business loses the revenue supporting its current one.”

#6580. The Best Sparkling Water Maker, Based on Years of Testing (2026)

Dedicating some counter space to a soda maker comes with several benefits. For one thing, these appliances are a great way to cut down on single-use plastic and other waste by eliminating the recycling bags full of bottles, cans, and cardboard boxes you inevitably accumulate with a regular La Croix habit. But they will also save you some money in the long run, as carbonating your own water costs less than buying premade fizz from the store. One standard-size CO2 canister, which should cost roughly $15, can carbonate around 60 liters of water. Considering the $3 cost of a 2-L bottle of Canada Dry, that comes out to around three times as much soda water per dollar.

After years of testing soda makers, I’ve found models that make it quick and easy to make zingy, fizzy drinks (including juice, wine, and cocktails) with the push of a button. Find our top picks below and scroll further down to see what I thought of the machines that didn’t earn a top spot.

New in this update: For this update, I tested two sparkling water makers by Drinkmate: the previously discontinued (and now recontinued) Drinkmate Spritzer and the Drinkmate Lux, which in between testing and publishing was subsequently discontinued and replaced with the new Sparkleup, welp!

Drinkmate Omnifizz Sparkling Water and Soda Maker

Amazon (With 60-L CO2 Tank and Extra Bottle)

Height: 16.14"Machine material(s): PlasticBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Yes (size varies by retailer)Requires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years

Over years of testing, nothing has surpassed the Drinkmate Omnifizz’s mix of versatility and affordability. It is, full stop, the most affordable sparkling water maker that can also do other “fun” carbonating, like wine, cocktails, tea, and (pulp-free) fruit juice.

What I love: The Omnifizz has a well-designed detachable siphon with fast and slow pressure release tabs. It carbonates fast, delivering maximum sharp fizz in around two seconds. This gives you more control when carbonating anything with a syrup or other sugars (wine or cocktails, for example), which fizz up a lot more than plain water. The siphon design also offers a much more secure connection than the machines that require you to pop and/or twist the bottle into the base, which diminishes the likelihood of an accidental soda explosion to the face (which happens to the best of us!)

What I’d leave: In addition to being kind of meh in the looks department (especially in a world where so many brands have placed a focus on the aesthetics of their soda makers), this carbonator is made of all plastic parts, so it doesn’t feel as durable as some others I’ve tested. It also screams like a banshee when its done. Depending on the retailer you order from, it may or may not ship with a CO2 cylinder, so be sure to read the product descriptions carefully.

Height: 16.9"Machine material(s): Stainless steelBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Only if you buy the bundleRequires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years

Breville has cornered the market on high-end small kitchen appliances with its top-performing countertop oven, induction burner, toaster, and immersion blender. In 2024, the brand added a sparkling water maker to that list.

What I love: The Breville Infizz Fusion is a sleek, versatile carbonator, and like the Drinkmate Ominifizz, it will carbonate more than just water. The default setting on the carbonator cap is a slow pressure release that allows carbonation of fruit juice, wine, cocktails, and even creamy drinks if you’re feeling weird. You can manually release the pressure faster if you just need a bottle of fizzy water in a hurry. Unlike the soda makers I liked in the $100 to $150 range, which usually have all plastic parts, parts of the InFizz Fusion are made of durable, high-quality stainless steel, which is available in a variety of finishes, though options vary by retailer. It also comes with a handful of accessories (including a juice filter and silicone bottle brush) to enhance the experience of using and cleaning the machine and bottle.

What I’d leave: Compared to the Drinkmate, this machine is slightly more fussy to operate. Not by much, but I prefer the Drinkmate’s quick click to Breville’s twist-and-lock design. Countertop soda makers are simple gadgets, and this is one of the priciest ones you can buy. If it’s worth it to you to pay for quality materials, aesthetics, and the ability to wow your dinner guests by transforming a bottle of bad rosé into something bubbly and palatable, you’ll likely be very happy with this (FWIW the Drinkmate can also sparkle bad rosé, it just wont look as nice doing it). But do keep in mind that the base model, which is $249 at the time of publishing, doesn’t ship with a CO2 tank, so you’ll either need to buy one or spend $30 more on one that comes with the tank.

Drinkmate Spritzer Portable Sparkling Water

Height: 7"Machine material(s): PlasticBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Only if you buy the bundleRequires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years

What I love: When I first tested the Spritzer several years ago, it was my top pick. But then Drinkmate discontinued it, which was sad, but now, it’s back. At this point I can’t give it the absolute top spot (I’ll get into that down below), but in a more niche position of portable carbonator, I still recommend it.

The Spritzer has all the versatility of Drinkmate’s countertop model in a smaller, portable format. Seeing as the earliest carbonators were portable, it’s almost a return to form. Almost, because the Spritzer looks more like one of those guns that shoots money and not like something you’d see in the hands of an old-timey soda jerk. But much like a gun that shoots money, the Spritzer is very fun to use. In terms of user experience, I prefer the Spritzer’s trigger over the standard, button-on-top-of-the-machine design. It just feels like I have more control over the thing when I use it.

Beyond that, the Spritzer takes up less space and is easy to stow away, and it is also cheaper than the countertop version.

What I’d leave: The Spritzer is designed to use smaller 10-L gas canisters rather than the standard 60-L size. Unless you source them directly from Drinkmate, the 10-L canisters are difficult to find, so you end up being reliant on its exchange program. The Spritzer will still work with a full size canister, but I wouldn’t recommend doing that because it doesn’t fit well in the carbonator and gets a bit unwieldy. Drinkmate also originally had a docking station for it the Spritzer, but unfortunately the brand got rid of it. Ultimately, the reason I don’t give this the top spot is that its design is such a departure from what most people expect in a soda maker it has a much narrower appeal.

With every update I look at the most popular and highly rated countertop sparkling water makers, taking into consideration availability, price, and customer ratings. Then, I judge them on the following:

I first assess how easy it is to use and assemble each machine. Looks matter too, but they aren’t everything. And if a machine can carbonate more than just water (what's up Drinkmate and Breville), that’s a huge plus as well.

I used each machine several times to get a general sense of how long the machine takes to carbonate and the fizz level of each batch. For the first few rounds I follow the manufacturer’s instructions. After that I try pushing the machine to its maximum capability (usually until I hear the hissing of excess gas escaping). If the machine can carbonate more than just water, I’ll do a few rounds with juice and wine.

This simple, stylish carbonator from Finnish brand Mysoda is made from renewable wood composite. It’s beautiful, sturdy, and, when it comes to the level of carbonation, performs as well as any SodaStream. And if you want an aesthetically pleasing, sustainably made, budget-friendly soda maker, you’ll be very happy with this purchase. But there’s a catch to that: Most soda makers ship with a starter CO2 tank, and this one doesn’t. New tanks, not tank trade-ins, cost $30 to $40. So when you factor that into the cost, the initial investment is more than the cost of our top pick, which did perform a little better anyway. If you want to stay under $100 all in, check out the Philips Sparkling Water Maker below.

This Mysoda distinguishes itself from the others with a glass carafe. Anytime I encounter a soda maker that carbonates in glass, I'm suspicious, because I haven’t seen them work well in the past. This might be because soda makers that carbonate in glass tend to be designed with additional safeguards to minimize the possibility of the bottle exploding, and those safeguards are usually fussy. Often they take the form of some sort of cover that goes over the entire bottle during the carbonation process. In the case of the Glassy, the bottle is covered by a curved sliding door that you shut by hand, reminiscent of a changing room curtain or a shower stall.

To use the machine, you place the bottle inside and twist it onto the gas nozzle to lock it in place. Then you shut the door and press the top of the machine toward the front to inject the gas (the top is mostly one large button). After a couple of pumps, you’ll hear a hissing sound, which signals that it’s ready. You then press the top toward the back of the machine, which causes the door to fly open, presenting your carbonated water like a magician’s assistant doing a quick change magic trick. It’s all very dramatic, which is kind of fun.

As far as soda makers that carbonate in glass, this is the best I’ve tried. That said, I'm not sure how important it is to be able to carbonate in glass, especially with the risk (however small) that it will explode into shards with you close by. You can always just carbonate in a plastic bottle and pour it into a glass vessel for serving.

Check out our full review of the Glassy here.

The Philips Sparkling Water Maker is a handsome machine with a comparatively accessible price tag, and it’s easy to set up and operate with one button. More importantly, during testing, it made pleasantly sharp carbonated water. Like the Mysoda Woody above, it doesn’t ship with CO2, so you’ll still need to shell out for a standard screw-in 60-L CO2 tank. However, at the current retail price, even with the addition of a tank, it still comes in at just under $100.

The Aerflo is even easier to tae on the go than the Drinkmate Spritzer. There is a carbonator mechanism inside the lid, which you activate by pressing a button on the top. Instead of full-size CO2 canisters used for most sparkling water makers, it utilizes smaller capsules typically used for airsoft or BB guns. Because of the capsules small size, you will need to swap them much more frequently; one capsule has enough CO2 for about one day’s worth of sparkling water. It’s cool and convenient if you really prefer carbonated water over still. But this is a product for a smaller subset of people than a countertop soda maker. If it appeals to you though, go for it.

Check out my full review of the Aerflo here.

This is the model that came after the now-discontinued Aarke Carbonator II, and the main upgrades are materials. The Aarke Carbonator III has more stainless steel and fewer plastic parts than the II. Both models are highly aesthetic machines that are easy enough to use and make perfectly fine sparkling water. If you like the look of it, you’ll probably be very happy with it, but the Breville is in the same general price range and is more versatile. Plus, there are lower-priced machines that perform just as well.

Awa appears to be selling itself entirely based on aesthetics. Once you move beyond the body design though, this is a standard sparkling water maker with a single button for injecting CO2. It lacks a tilting nozzle or a slide-in lock, which makes it more annoying to use than the winning models. The build is also almost entirely plastic, save for a few metal details, which doesn’t really justify the premium price point. If you like how it looks, it will get the job done, but it’s not innovating on the form.

A frequent complaint people have about sparkling water makers is their reliance on plastic bottles, as many consumers are looking to avoid plastic entirely. The Fizzit is one of the few soda makers that uses metal bottles instead. Apart from that, its design and performance are similar to the other soda makers sharing the same standard design on the market. Were this the only machine on the market to carbonate directly into stainless steel, maybe that would be something, but Sodastream also offers stainless-steel carbonator bottles, and I imagine more brands will follow suit. Also sorry to Spärklï, but the branding on this machine is a bit of an eyesore. If you’re looking for a machine that comes with metal bottles and aren’t a fan of Sodastream though, this might be for you.

The Fritaire carbonator flipped the conventional soda maker design on its head. It’s the only soda maker I’ve tested so far that carbonates from the bottom up, with a fold-up gas nozzle that makes for a slightly more compact machine. The bottle is also different, with mechanical components built in at the bottom, and a wide curved carafe-style lip. Unfortunately I could not get this to produce a satisfyingly sharp bottle of seltzer, no matter how much gas I pumped into the bottle. Where other machines make a clear sound when the pressure has been maxed out, the Fritaire’s was not obvious. The instructions recommend pressing the button for three seconds until you “hear the sound of pressure building.” Each time I tried, the water came out under-carbonated. On top of that, the lid for the bottle dribbled water even when tightly screwed on. I really tried to give this machine the benefit of the doubt, testing and retesting to try and get it not to leak on me and to get a proper fizz, but each time I encountered the same problems no matter what I did.

Smeg is known for its retro-futurist luxury kitchen products that really sell for their looks. This machine worked fine. You twist the metal dial clockwise to carbonate, a clever hidden feature that sets it apart from other carbonators, but it lacks the ability to tilt the nozzle, which makes screwing on the bottle more tedious. For a soda maker made almost entirely out of plastic, the price point is well beyond what it’s worth, but if you’re a Smeg collector, this is another piece to add to your collection.

One of the few new electric sparkling water systems, the Carbon8 is quite different from other machines on the market. Instead of directly carbonating into the bottle, the Carbon8 has a refillable reservoir (much like a drip coffee maker) that instead, dispenses carbonated water straight into your glass. It has added flourishes, like a sanitizing UV light and a filter that remineralizes water while removing chlorine.

The brand implies superior eco-friendliness in their website copy because they don’t carbonate directly into a reusable PET plastic bottle; however, the reservoir and other parts of the machine are made of plastic, so I’m not sure they have much plastic-free ground to stand on. You could argue that since the plastic bottles of typical soda makers have to be replaced every couple of years, this system produces less plastic waste, but it’s a marginal difference in my opinion.

As a premium machine this Carbon8 worked fine, but had one shortcoming: There seems to be no way to control the carbonation level of the machine, and when I tasted the finished product, I found the level of carbonation to be far less than what you’d expect from store-bought seltzer, or what you can produce with the winning machines. If the Carbon8 gave you control over how fizzy you wanted your water, it would make this a much better machine.

Ninja is among the most prolific small appliance manufacturers with coffee makers, countertop ovens, blenders, ice cream makers, juicers, toasters, air fryers—the list goes on and on and on. So it should come as no surprise that the brand is now in the soda maker business too. Like many of Ninja’s other offerings, the Ninja Thirsti is a bit gimmicky while still being kind of cool. Out of the box, this electric soda maker (yes, you have to plug it in) reminded us of a Nespresso machine. The water tank sits off to the side and the carbonation happens inside the machine before coming out of a little spout. There’s an opening on the front to add up to two proprietary flavoring cartridges, which you can put in your bubbly water individually or combine them both. Currently there are 30 flavors available and the machine shipped with four of them. The control panel on the front of the machine allows you to choose between still water or three levels of carbonation, and four drink sizes (6, 12, 18, or 24 oz.). After testing, I have mixed feelings about this machine. Overall, it seems like a bit much for something to have at home. It could maybe be a great addition to a teachers’ lounge or a small office. But keep in mind that the water tank does require chilled, cold water so you’d also need a fridge or ice nearby whenever you want to use it.

If you’ve ever dreamed of having a club soda tap in your kitchen, this is probably as close as you’re going to get without cutting into your countertops. Like the Ninja above, the Glacier Fresh Sparkin Cold Soda Maker carbonates water in the machine, not in a bottle. Unlike the Ninja, the machine chills the water for you (though the manual still recommends filling the reservoir on the back of the machine with cold water). Once it’s filled, getting your bubbly water from the “tap” is a three-step process. First, you push a button to send water from the reservoir to the bubbling (and presumably chilling) chamber, then you push down on a lever to carbonate it. Once it’s sufficiently bubbly, you press another little lever on the front to dispense the water into a glass. It’s less complicated than it sounds, but with an 88-square-inch footprint, most people will be better off with a bottle-style carbonator. I will also note that when moved from the counter to a nearby table with the CO2 canister in place and some water still in the chamber (ill-advised, perhaps), it began to make a weird squealing noise.

The SodaStream Art is marketed as the company’s premium carbonator, because of its retro-inspired body. Though it produces the exact same carbonated water as other SodaStream models, it operates a little differently: Instead of pushing a button to carbonate, you pull the lever and you can pull it up to six times for the bubbliest water. But it’s made of lightweight plastic that feels cheap. If you want something that looks good on the countertop, there are prettier options that are also sturdier.

Aarke carbonators are really easy on the eyes, and this “pro” version doesn’t skimp on materials. Instead of the typical plastic bottles, this one uses glass, and the top of the machine (which is available in a matte black, matte sand, or shiny stainless-steel finish) covers the top of the bottle in case you were to over-carbonate and cause the glass to explode. Unfortunately, it’s not very user-friendly. I had issues getting everything to lock into place and ended up with an explosion—though, luckily, it was only water and not glass. I eventually got it to work, but for the price, it should be easier to operate.

I loved the sleek design of this soda maker in pictures, but in person, the materials felt cheap and flimsy. Also, because it’s so sleek and slim, the water bottles are really tall and didn’t fit into any shelves in a standard sized fridge.

Instead of using a CO2 tank to produce carbon dioxide, this machine uses citric acid and baking soda. The mechanism is just way more high maintenance compared to the machines that utilize a gas canister, and I struggle to see why this method is in any way better than the industry standard.

Currently, the Terra is SodaStream’s most basic offering, and functionally, it’s a lot like the original SodaStream, the Fizzi. However, instead of a screw-in CO2 cartridge, this machine uses the brand’s Quick Connect cartridges, which click in. Because the Quick Connect feature is proprietary, using this machine means being married to Soda Stream’s cylinder exchange program. With products like the Mysoda Woody or the Philips Sparkling Water Maker, you can and should get something with a universal connection.

This style of carbonator is a relic of the 19th century, and while it has an abundance of charm, it’s more tedious, fussy, and impractical than its modern counterparts. It relies on small, single-use CO2 cartridges—which negates the whole eco-friendly argument for carbonating at home rather buying seltzer from the store— and you have to use two cartridges per liter if you like your seltzer extra sharp. Frankly, the only people I’d recommend this to would be that husband and wife on TLC who pretend they’re living in the 1950s.

There is nothing inherently wrong with the E-Duo. Of the carbonators that use glass bottles, it is the easiest to use. It does require a few additional steps to lock the bottle safely into place (just in case that glass bottle explodes!), but I didn’t find the safety mechanisms to be overly fussy. However, as with the Ninja, this soda maker requires electricity. With so many excellent soda makers that function effectively without electricity, I don’t really see the need to use one that does.

#6578. Sticky Miso Chicken

Miso, soy, and honey are a powerful trio, creating a savory marinade that could make just about anything sing (cod or salmon, broccoli or zucchini, tofu). Do have a keen eye on your chicken (especially if you have a drawer-style broiler at the bottom of your oven), checking it every so often to prevent a completely blackened cook.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: My Go-To Marinade for Chicken Is 3 Ingredients.

Heat broiler. Whisk ¼ cup honey, ¼ cup white miso, and 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a large bowl to combine. Add 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (the miso and soy sauce are plenty salty, so no need to season the chicken) and toss to coat. Arrange on wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet lined with foil and spoon any marinade remaining in bowl over. Broil chicken, turning halfway through, until cooked through and deeply charred in spots, 10–15 minutes (keep a close eye on it). Thinly slice chicken. Serve over steamed white rice, topped with thinly sliced scallions, if desired.

#6577. Homemade Mac & Cheese

The perfect mac & cheese will have you dreaming about its cheesy goodness for days after you eat it. Obviously, the cheese has to be top-notch, but the real secret to the best version is the perfect crunchy topping. My recipe delivers on all of that and more, so you won't even think about reaching for another mac & cheese recipe for the rest of your gatherings. From weeknight dinners to potlucks and holidays, this is the classic side dish everyone will be reaching for.

What People Are Saying:"Always a huge hit with friends and family! This is my go-to if I'm bringing a dish to a holiday dinner with friends. I've rarely had leftovers to take home!" - Zafire_Shadows

"This is exactly what mac and cheese dreams are made of. Love the gruyere funk and the mustard powder (so clever!)." - Pastagofer

First, you’ll boil the pasta. Start with a big pot of salted water (and I mean super salty, it should taste like the ocean), then add your pasta and cook it until before al dente—I’m talking still-has-a-ring-of-hard-white-pasta-in-the-middle-when-you-bite-in uncooked. You want it to meld and absorb with your cheese sauce in the oven, not turn into mush. Undercooking now guarantees the perfect bite when you pull it out of the oven.

Then it’s cheese sauce time, and that means making a béchamel. You’ll start by melting your butter in a pan over medium heat, then sprinkling the flour over the top and stirring everything together until it starts pulling away from the pan slightly. You’re looking for what’s called a “blonde roux,” which has a slightly yellow tint and should smell a bit like baked goods. You don’t want it super dark (so keep an eye on the heat!), but you definitely don’t want it as light as it started.

Next, add the milk in slowly, stirring constantly so you don’t get thick lumps. Want to shortcut this process a bit? Heat your milk ahead of time to room temperature or even slightly warm. You’re going to cook it until it’s thick and bubbly (about 2 minutes), so having your milk warm will help you get there faster. It’s going to get a LOT thicker when you add the cheese, so if it’s still a little thin but you want to get on with it, that’s okay too.

Once you’re ready to add the cheese, it’s very important to take it off the heat before so that the sauce doesn’t start to separate. That said, if you’ve been at it for a minute and are still having trouble getting your cheese to melt, pop your pot back on the heat for just a few seconds to bring the temperature up and help the process along.

Once it comes together, you can stir in the macaroni until every noodle is coated.

At this point, you could eat this mac & cheese right now, and it would taste wonderful. But! If you want exceptional mac & cheese, you’ve gotta bake it. So pour it into a pan, then get ready for the best part—the topping. To make it, you’ll combine some breadcrumbs and the remaining half cup of Parmesan in a bowl, then add the olive oil and mix it all up. Sprinkle it on top of the mac and cheese in the casserole dish.

All you have to do is pop it into your preheated 375° oven and bake it until it's golden brown on top. Go ahead, snag a bite before it's fully cooled—you'll really be able to taste all your extra effort.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

If you’re looking to make this dish ahead of time, prepare the mac & cheese up until step 4, then cover it in your baking dish and refrigerate it up to 3 days (or freeze it up to 2 months). When ready to serve, add the Parmesan and panko mixture, bake, and serve. If baking from frozen, allow to thaw in the refrigerator overnight before baking.

If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for around 3 days.

#6576. Kering Hires Group Pricing Director: Why It Matters

Kering has appointed Francisco Ochando to the newly created role of group pricing director, the company confirmed on Wednesday. Ochando, who took up the position on November 16, reports to Marilyne Trebus, Kering’s chief product officer, who in turn reports to Carlo Mocci, the group’s chief client officer.

According to his LinkedIn profile, Ochando previously worked at Inditex, Calvin Klein and Nike, most recently as director of planning in charge of lifestyle footwear at the sporting giant, based in the Netherlands. In his new role at Kering, and according to his LinkedIn, he will be “leading the group-wide pricing strategy across all Kering houses and geographies, driving sustainable revenue growth, brand value creation and pricing excellence”.

Pricing architecture is typically the remit of merchandising teams at the brand level. What, then, is the rationale for having someone oversee it at group level?

As part of the “ReconKering” strategy unveiled at the group’s Capital Markets Day in April, CEO Luca de Meo said he would build a “streamlined group platform”, organized around five “hubs”, including a client hub led by Mocci. “It is not a question of centralization. It’s a rebalance,” de Meo said.

This strategy makes sense in the short term due to the need for greater discipline and alignment after years of underperformance, according to Goldman Sachs analyst Erwan Rambourg. “This nomination [of Ochando] comes across as quite consistent with what the group is trying to achieve,” he says.

During an interview with Vogue Business in October 2025, de Meo also outlined his ambition to take a more strategic approach to managing the group’s brand portfolio. “We need to ensure there’s no cannibalization between the brands, and strategically target different types of clients with each brand based on what we’ve achieved so far,” he noted.

The French luxury group’s new CEO attended fashion week in Milan and Paris. He shares his first take with Vogue Business.

At Capital Markets Day, he explained this further by saying that Balenciaga is best positioned to capture the Gen Z audience as “one of the brands that better understands the vibes of the new generation”, while Bottega Veneta should have a different positioning with a higher-end clientele. And pricing is a big component of this strategic approach.

Ochando’s appointment comes at a time when the industry is grappling with pricing challenges, amid criticism of so-called “greedflation” — the idea that many luxury brands raised prices too aggressively, and too quickly, during the post-Covid luxury boom.

“Pricing has been an issue for the industry in the last three years, as aspirational consumers have been priced out,” Mario Ortelli, managing partner of Ortelli & Co, says. “There’s a disconnect between the perceived value and the cost of the product. Appointing a pricing director is an organizational attempt to address the situation. This new role can help in fine-tuning the pricing architecture across brands, and centralize intelligence on the pricing of competitors.”

As Kering’s largest brand Gucci navigates a turnaround, it has taken selective price cuts, according to Bernstein analyst Luca Solca. He notes that global prices for Spring/Summer 2026’s Mercato tote bag were reduced by 20% to 25% (from €2.600 to €1.950 for the small version, in leather, in France). “Our data indicates that Gucci continues to work on increasing brand accessibility,” Solca wrote in a note in July. For example, Gucci unveiled at its resort 2026 show the Giglio, a tote bag whose large canvas edition is priced at €1,800.

Ochando will need to support brands in their efforts to win back middle-income consumers, either by introducing new product lines at more accessible price points or by selectively lowering prices. Both approaches will need to be carefully done to ensure affordability while preserving the brand equity.

“Gucci has lowered prices, notably on products from previous designers that will be discontinued, and the sector overall has come out with more palatable price points throughout,” Rambourg says. He notes that efforts to appeal to more price-sensitive customers are not unique to Gucci. “It holds true for Chanel, Dior, Burberry and many others, hopefully gradually reversing the negative impacts of post-Covid greedflation on end demand.”

#6575. Anchovy-Garlic Pasta

Even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

#6573. How Luxury Brands Should Show Up for UAE’s National Day

December in the United Arab Emirates begins with one of the country’s most significant celebrations: UAE National Day, officially known as Eid Al Etihad. On December 2, 1971, six emirates (Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah) formally united to establish the United Arab Emirates, under the vision of the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan. Ras Al Khaimah joined the federation on February 10, 1972, completing the union of seven emirates.

As the luxury industry invests more in the Middle East, holiday shopping moments around Eid and Ramadan have ranked high on brands’ priority lists. To expand their reach, brands should look beyond these two tentpoles, starting with National Day, which this year marks the 55th anniversary of the UAE’s formation on December 2-3.

For those who live and work in the UAE, the occasion carries a significance that extends well beyond a public holiday. “What makes the UAE particularly special is that its national identity is strong enough to embrace people from all over the world without losing its own character,” says Ahmad Al Gergawi, an Emirati and founder of UAE-based creative agency Dyemension A, which has worked with brands ranging from Cartier and Vacheron Constantin to Birkenstock. “It is a country where Emirati heritage and global perspectives coexist, and where people from different backgrounds are able to contribute to its story.”

In 2025, Birkenstock collaborated with Dyemension A for their National Day celebrations, employing Emirati talent across their production.

This year’s celebrations come after a particularly challenging period for the region, shaped in part by the US-Israeli war on Iran and its wider economic repercussions. For the retail industry, the impact has been felt through increased costs of transporting goods and a slowdown in tourism.

Against this backdrop, the importance of the local consumer has come into sharper focus, particularly as UAE residents have continued to support the market and luxury brands. Firras Alwahabi, founder and managing director of Faux Consultancy, a Dubai-based public relations company whose clients include Loewe, Guerlain and Zegna, says, “I think this year’s National Day will carry particular significance. The UAE has experienced a challenging year, and I think there will be an even stronger sense of appreciation, pride and solidarity among those who call the country home.” But how should brands show up?

For luxury brands, this presents an opportunity to consider how they participate in the country’s national celebrations. But, as Alwahabi points out, National Day is not necessarily an easy occasion for fashion brands to interpret. National Day is different from Ramadan and Eid, Alwahabi says, where occasion dressing is more clearly defined around the religious holidays. It is not an occasion where people typically dress a particular way, which makes it more challenging for fashion brands to translate into a capsule collection or a specific product offering. “National Day is less about shopping for the occasion and more about the experience and connection people are looking for. Customers want to celebrate, express their pride and share meaningful moments with their families and communities,” says Reda Keddaji, general manager of Tryano, the luxury department store at Yas Mall in Abu Dhabi.

Alwahabi’s advice is for brands to rethink their approach. “Rather than creating another product or collection for every occasion, I think the opportunity lies in finding more meaningful and relevant ways to participate,” he says.

Samara Punjabi, CEO of Timeless Group, which owns Palm Angels, Temperley London and Kat Maconie and distributes labels including Off-White, Judith Leiber and Dunhill, believes localization needs to go beyond adapting a global campaign with local colors or messaging. “The UAE is a significant market for international luxury brands, but understanding its cultural identity goes far beyond commercial opportunities. National Day is deeply personal, and brands need to recognize the emotional connection people have with the country,” she says.

In celebration of UAE National Day, customers will be able to personalise their Off-White pieces with UAE-inspired motifs through an exclusive heat-press patch bar.

For Timeless Group, National Day is an opportunity to spotlight existing offerings rather than launch new products. Palm Angels’ Dubai-exclusive capsule and Judith Leiber’s Dubai number plate clutch and bag inspired by the Dubai chocolate and pistachio croissant are available all year, but are being presented as National Day edits. For this year's celebrations, Off-White is developing exclusive artwork featuring Dubai landmarks and cultural references such as karak tea and the falcon. Customers will also be able to personalize T-shirts through an in-store heat-press experience. “The biggest opportunity for international brands is to move from simply marketing to the region to actively creating with the region. That is where meaningful cultural connections and long-term brand loyalty are built,” says Punjabi.

Palm Angels collaborated with Dubai-based creative community SNS to curate looks featuring pieces from the brand.

For Al Gergawi, the distinction between referencing a culture and genuinely involving its community is key. He points to Birkenstock’s National Day collaboration with his agency last year, which involved Emirati talent across the production, from actors and the director to the set designer and crew. “It’s not about placing an Emirati face in an advertisement or incorporating cultural references for the sake of relevance. It’s about genuinely investing in the people, creativity and communities that make this region what it is,” he says. “Birkenstock isn’t simply speaking to the UAE community. It’s creating with them.”

At Tryano, the emphasis is on experience rather than product. Its National Day activation will run from November 27 to December 6, with the main in-store experience on December 1. The program will bring Emirati hospitality into the store through a Talli demonstration by an Emirati artisan, an Emirati-inspired Majlis setting and henna painting. Homegrown brands, Keddaji notes, often have a closer connection to local heritage, craftsmanship and identity. International brands can also participate, provided their contribution feels relevant, respectful and authentic.

Not every initiative needs to be a public-facing campaign. Etoile Group, which operates boutiques across seven countries in the region, including brands such as Chanel, Etro, Ralph Lauren, Valentino, Tod’s and Aquazzura, says it will send National Day gifts to its UAE national VIP clients across its brands and celebrate employees.

While National Day remains an underexplored moment on the UAE cultural calendar for international brands, Al Gergawi believes cultural engagement cannot be confined to a handful of occasions. “UAE consumers are increasingly discerning. They can tell the difference between a brand that engages with the culture organically and one that appears only for a seasonal campaign. Culture is rooted in values, and those values should not be confined to activations around Emirati Women’s Day, National Day or Ramadan. Brands need a year-round strategy that carries cultural understanding through their communications, identity and commitment to community empowerment,” he says.

Miral Youssef, president of Kering Middle East, Africa and India, says this approach is reflected in the group’s work in the UAE. “Our relationship with the UAE and its communities goes well beyond National Day. It is built throughout the year, through meaningful collaborations, shared experiences and the people we work with. UAE National Day is an opportunity to celebrate these relationships, rather than create them for the occasion,” she says.

Bottega Veneta spotlighted Emirati weaving traditions in parallel with the house intrecciato weave.

She points to collaborations across Kering’s Houses with regional creative talent. This year, Boucheron hosted “Hug My Land” with Emirati photographer Hussain AlMossawi and homegrown café Inner Child. Pomellato’s “The Art of Iconic Craftsmanship” brought its Iconica collection together with five women designers from the region, including Emirati studio One Third Studio. In October, Bottega Veneta’s “When Your Own Initials Are Enough” at Keturah Cactus Park in Dubai brought Emirati weaving traditions into dialogue with the house’s Italian intrecciato technique through its collaboration with Irthi, a Sharjah-based organization dedicated to preserving and reinterpreting the UAE’s traditional crafts. Other Kering brands are marking National Day with dedicated activations: Bottega Veneta will welcome guests to its boutiques at Mall of the Emirates, The Dubai Mall and Abu Dhabi for artistic experiences led by Emirati artists, while Saint Laurent will draw on the UAE’s tradition of hospitality through intimate in-store activations.

Earlier this year Boucheron collaborated with Hussain AlMossawi, presenting his photography of UAE’s architectural heritage as collectible postcards.

Youssef’s advice to brands is to collaborate rather than decorate, giving local creatives, artisans and designers a genuine role; invest in local talent beyond a single celebration; and be present throughout the year. “Meaningful relationships are built through consistency, mutual respect and a long-term commitment to the community,” she says.

As brands begin planning their calendars for 2027, National Day should sit alongside other important moments in the UAE’s cultural calendar, including Emirati Women’s Day and Ramadan, as well as events such as Art Dubai. The opportunity is to build a calendar that reflects a deeper understanding of the UAE, its people and its cultural landscape, rather than approaching each occasion as a one-off marketing opportunity. As Al Gergawi adds: “When the cultural connection is genuine, the commercial value will often follow naturally.”

#6572. On the Front Lines of the Advent Calendar Wars

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the mysterious hackers hitting refrigeration systems.

I’m starting today’s Open Tab with my favorite thing in the world: a morsel of exclusive news. In chatting with BA alum Alison Roman about First Bloom, her soon-to-open NYC storefront (more on that from me very soon), she told me she’s releasing a new podcast that will be officially announced early next week.

I’m mostly sworn to secrecy until Roman drops the trailer, but I can tell you there will be cooking, there will be guests, and there will be banter. But, she said, this project will be distinctly different from her earlier work. “I’m not going back to Home Movies. I’m just not,” she told me over the phone earlier this week.

Also in today’s Open Tab: How much more ridiculous can advent calendars get? Was this NYC gay bar actually designed by AI? And how is Andy Baraghani thinking about his first restaurant?

Gone are the days when advent calendars were essentially manufactured cardboard inside of which you could find some of the most unfortunate tasting chocolate ever produced. These days we’ve moved beyond chocolate. Some advent calendars open to reveal tinned fish, others jewelry, and still others skin-care products. Google Trends data shows search interest for advent calendars has grown steadily for the past five years, and as writer Emily Bloch reported for Bon Appétit, the global advent calendar market is expected to grow to $2.47 billion by 2033.

Part of the appeal, as Bloch mentions, is the little-treat-culture of it all. It’s nice to open up a little surprise each day. But another element, surely, is the content that’s made around advent calendars. There are the unboxings—tailor-made for the short-form vertical video format which rewards reveals—and there are the scandals. Who could forget (everyone except me, realistically) the backlash against Chanel’s $825 advent calendar in 2021 when customers declared the included products decidedly lackluster? This year Skims faces a similar backlash for its $148 advent calendar for which it is now offering refunds.

But drama and outrage gets attention, which in turn fuels more content. And as the Kardashian clan knows better than most, no matter what the public is saying, at the end of the day they’re still talking about you. Thus, the advent calendar cycle continues for another year, growing ever greater. Will we ever summit the peak of the advent calendar craze? So far, the data say no.

If you’ve read—or even skimmed—this column in the past, you’ve likely gleaned that I often point out the many fumblings of AI—one could argue I make a sport of it. That’s why, when I saw grumblings online that a new gay bar in New York City’s Hell’s Kitchen looked like it had been designed by Chat-GPT, I felt a morbid curiosity begin to bubble. The bar, commenters said, was so deeply on-the-nose gay-bar-coded, it simply couldn’t have been made by a human brain. It was named Pride Bar x Lounge (a bit first thought, right?), and its decor is essentially just rainbow flags. It kind of looks like how they’d design a gay bar in a Netflix show, which is to say: almost impressively bland.

In a report from The New York Times, the two co-owners say that they did not in fact use any AI in designing the bar, which has cost about $5 million so far to come to fruition. On the other hand, the posters released to promote the bar, which had also received some heat, were in fact made using AI.

The saga is an interesting data point in the public’s perception of what is an appropriate way to use this tech: making a grocery list? Sure. Using it to help you figure out what exactly you like about your own child? Absolutely not. Asking AI to help you plan a trip? I guess. Using it to design a gay bar? Hard no.

Former Bon Appétit food editor Andy Baraghani is likely familiar to readers of this publication. But now, after years of cooking for others—on the line at Chez Panisse, here in the Test Kitchen—he’s opening his own restaurant, Ditto, in Union Square. “There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see,” he told Ella Quittner, who profiled him for BA. Read on to see how Baraghani’s vision comes to life at his first ever restaurant.

#6571. We Found The 6 Strongest Drinks At Starbucks, Ranked By Caffeine

Each of these bevvies delivers a serious buzz.

I would love nothing more than to be the type of person who jumps out of bed with the sunrise—without the lure of a steaming hot and very caffeinated cup of coffee waiting for me. But I need to smell the freshly brewed espresso before I can muster the strength to get out from under the duvet.

In the spirit of staying fueled, I analyzed the Starbucks menu and narrowed it down to the most caffeinated bevvies you can buy in a grande size. However, everything is customizable and may differ slightly in caffeine content—you can always ask for more or fewer espresso shots, or opt for a larger size.

There’s a reason you might feel extra jittery after a morning Cold Brew. It’s packed with caffeine because it uses almost twice as many coffee grounds as regular brewed coffee. It is diluted with water, though, to temper the buzz.

A Caffè Americano—hot or iced—packs a similar punch as a Cold Brew. It’s not all that different, TBH, except instead of brewed coffee, it combines water and espresso to give it a littleeeee more edge.

If you love a sweet latte but want more caffeine, the Iced Brown Sugar Shaken Espresso is your ticket at roughly 255 milligrams for a grande.

If you’re craving a Cold Brew with a kick, go Nitro. It uses a higher coffee-to-water ratio in the cold steeping and dispensing process, and it is served without ice (so, again, less dilution). The result: bold flavor and about 280 milligrams of caffeine.

There’s a reason I’m a drip-coffee loyalist, and it’s not just the flavor. It’s also about the 310 milligrams of caffeine that a grande Pike Place delivers, which earns the medium roast coffee a solid second spot on this list.

Drumroll, please! The most caffeinated beverage on Starbucks’ menu is the Blonde Roast Brewed Coffee at 360 milligrams. Why does it differ from the medium and even the dark roast? It’s pretty simple: Blonde usually tests higher because Starbucks brews it with a little more coffee, and lighter roasts can pack more grounds into the scoop. That means more caffeine makes its way into your cup.
