#6469. The Best Air Fryers For Faster, Crispier Cooking (2026)

Buzzy as they’ve become over the past several years, air fryers are really just small ovens with fans built into them, i.e., convection ovens. Their fans to circulate hot air around your food, theoretically to but not all of them are created equal. Our years of testing air fryers (and we’ve used over two dozen in that time) have taught us that there are plenty out there that can give you crispy-enough results—but the very best air fryers churn out not only golden brown french fries and crispy-skinned chicken wings, but tender fillets of salmon and even whole roast chickens at the touch of a button.

Air fryers can take a few forms; the robot-esque basket-style models are probably what come to mind when you think of an air fryer, but there are versatile countertop convection ovens that add bake, broil, toast, and slow-cook options to the air fryer functionality. Some even dehydrate and steam too. And most recently more bowl-style air fryers have started to hit shelves, which swap a slide-in basket for a glass container and top-down, air-frying lid.

The best for all varieties of air fryer needs are below.

New in this update: We tested five models in the growing category of glass air fryers, i.e., those with slide-in glass baskets or glass bowl bases with an air fryer lid. This included new reviews for air fryers from Cuisinart, Chefman, Kisimile, and Magnifique, plus retesting the Ninja Crispi against this new crop of similar products.

Most air fryers fit into one of three categories: oven, basket, or bowl.

A countertop convection oven, or air fryer–toaster oven, combines most of the crisping power of the basket-style air fryers you know and love with the multifunctionality you get from a toaster oven or countertop oven. Generally, the “air frying” function is achieved with a perforated slide-in rack, which usually means lots of cooking surface, but the racks are usually shallow and can require careful tossing or flipping of whatever you’re cooking, depending on the dish. But air fryer ovens, like the Breville Smart Oven Pro with its 13 different cooking modes, can do a lot, making them bona fide do-it-all kitchen appliances.

Basket-style air fryers aren’t as versatile as air fryer ovens, but they’re also less expensive and take up less space. They also tend to deliver better final results on traditional air fryer stuff like crisping up small foods that require shaking (tater tots, french fries, or brussels sprouts), for which a handled basket is far easier to maneuver. Minuses are that they can be hard to clean and limited on square inches inside the basket. They’re also sometimes made of plastic or nonstick coated materials, which may not appeal to some consumers.

Bowl air fryers offer some of the best (and worst) of both worlds and also some unique benefits. Most of these include a heat-resistant glass bowl acting as the basket. Some models operate much like basket air fryers, with the glass container sliding into the base unit, while others opt for a “lid” that sits on top and houses the air frying mechanism. The glass baskets make these very easy to clean (included crisping trays are another story), however their functionality for shaking and pausing to flip foods can be cumbersome. But many come with lids for the glass containers, letting them double as prep and storage containers too.

Capacity: 6 qt.Wattage: 172510 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Roast, Broil, Frozen, Preheat, Reheat, Dehydrate, Proof, Bake, and Keep WarmColor: WhiteWeight: 11.5 lb.Dimensions: 11.8" x 14.4" x 11.9"Warranty: 2 years

What we love: The 6-Quart Cosori Turboblaze Smart Air Fryer impressed us in every test, producing evenly browned and crispy frozen sweet potato fries, juicy chicken breasts, and perfectly cooked brussels sprouts. It has a straightforward digital interface that allows you to easily set the time and temperature and an impressive array of preset programs (Air Fry, Roast, Broil, Frozen, Preheat, Reheat, Dehydrate, Proof, Bake, and Keep Warm).

A few things set the Turboblaze apart from the competition (including the previous longtime winner of this test, the Instant Vortex Slim). Most notably, it consistently produced the crispiest food of any air fryer we tested in record time. That may have something to do with the fact that there’s more space between the crisper plate (where the food sits) and the bottom of the basket than there is in some of the other top-performing models we’ve tried, which allows for better air circulation.

Another standout feature is its variable fan speeds, which adjust automatically depending on the cooking function. Unlike most air fryers that use this tech behind the scenes, the Turboblaze shows you the fan speed right on the display. Air Fry, for example, is one of four “turbo modes,” running the fan at full blast (speed 5), while Bake uses a gentler speed 3 to avoid disrupting delicate foods. Low-temperature settings like Dehydrate and Proof drop all the way down to speed 1.

The Cosori Turboblaze is also a real value pick. The top performer in its price range (100–150) by a wide margin, it’s powerful, versatile, quiet, lightweight, and easy to clean (the brand says both the nonstick basket and cooking tray are dishwasher-safe, though we recommend hand-washing anything with a nonstick coating).

The model we tested includes smart features, meaning you can control it remotely or use voice commands via the VeSync app. If that’s not your thing, Cosori also sells a non-smart version for about $10 less.

What we’d leave: Our gripes with this model are minor. It’s slightly annoying that you have to press a release button to pull the basket out. And while the greater amount of space between the crisper tray and basket bottom contributes to better airflow (and thus better browning), it means food is more likely to fall through while cooking.

Capacity: 2.1-qt.Wattage: 9004 cooking functions: Air-Fry, Bake, Roast, ReheatColors: Gray, red, white, greenWeight: 4.9 lb.Dimensions: 10.1" x 8.3" x 10.5"Warranty: 2 years

If you’re on a tighter budget, have very little counter space to spare, or are mostly crisping up food just for yourself, consider the Cosori Lite 2.1-Quart Mini Air Fryer.

What we love: This compact air fryer did a beautiful job crisping and browning small servings of frozen tater tots and fries, sliced zucchini, and veggie burger patties (two at a time, max). Depending on where you buy, it will only costs $50–$60 (as of publish time)—not at all bad for a lightweight, quiet, digital air fryer with four easy-to-use presets (air-fry, roast, bake, and reheat). It’s easy to tuck into a cabinet and to clean. Like the Cosori Blaze, the Lite has a nonstick basket. Again, while the manual says the nonstick basket is dishwasher-safe, we always recommend hand-washing anything with a nonstick coating.

What we’d leave: Per its name, it’s quite small—don’t expect to be cooking enough food for more than two people in this thing. It also won’t remind you when it’s time to shake your food, so you’ll need to keep an eye on the timer yourself (luckily, the digital display makes this pretty easy).

If you want an air fryer with maximum versatility and have some counter space to spare, spring for the Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro. Breville makes a few different models (which can be found in the kitchens of many of our editors), but this one is the best combination of performance and value.

What we love: This midrange model has been our top pick for years now because of its versatility, build quality, intuitive design, and consistently strong performance in testing.

In testing, the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro delivered reliably great results. It excelled at foods that need to be laid in a flat, even layer across the crisper tray (think veggie burgers or salmon fillets), but also handled frozen fries, tots, and sweet potato fries well. Its interior is roomy enough to fit a quarter sheet pan or 13x9" casserole pan, which means it can effectively double your oven space (or eliminate the need to turn on your full-size oven altogether).

This model is also a favorite among BA staffers and Test Kitchen editors, as well as award-winning cookbook author Nik Sharma, who developed some of BA’s favorite air fryer recipes. “I prefer toaster-oven-style to basket-style air fryers, because they’re easier to use for more common tasks like baking, toasting bread, and roasting more efficiently,” Sharma says.

What we’d leave: As with most oven-style air fryers, it’s harder to toss or shake small foods mid-cook compared to a basket-style machine. We also found that, in general, food benefited from a higher cooking temperature (and often slightly longer cook time) relative to the basket-style winners.

Capacity: .5 cubic feetWattage: 18005 Cooking functions: Toast, Bagel, Broil, Pizza, Bake & Roast5 Air-frying functions: Air-Fry, Fries, Wings, Bacon, Crispy ReheatColor: Stainless steelWeight: 15.8 lb.Dimensions: 15.7" x 16.9" x 10"Warranty: 2 years

If you like the idea of going the air fryer–toaster oven route but (1) don’t have the space for the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro or (2) don’t want to shell out $400 in pursuit of crispiness, here’s some good news: Breville offers the Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact, which is essentially a smaller, cheaper version of our top pick.

What we love: As with most Breville products, the Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact feels thoughtfully designed, with stainless-steel finishes and a solid build. There are fewer niche modes than the Pro—no Dehydrate or Proof—but it does include four air-frying-specific presets in addition to a standard Air Fry setting.

We found using the Compact intuitive (the guide printed on the inside of the oven door helped). We also appreciated the “bit more” button, a feature borrowed from Breville’s toasters that adds a touch of extra cooking time when your fries are looking just a touch underdone.

This model performed comparably to the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro in most of our tests, producing juicy chicken, evenly browned cubes of tofu, and crispy veggies. We still prefer the larger model for its versatility and additional functionality, but this little oven would make a worthy addition to any smaller kitchen.

What we’d leave: While the Compact did well in most tests, it struggled a bit with frozen sweet potato fries. This largely came down to overcrowding due to the smaller capacity: While we tried to fit an entire bag’s worth on a single tray, the unevenness with which the fries browned is a good example of the fact that, unlike a basket fryer, countertop oven-style air fryers are best used to cook things in a single layer.

As mentioned, there’s a guide to oven inserts and placement on the inside of the oven’s door, but this is easy to miss, and these suggestions did not appear in full in the manual. Because of this, one tester accidentally cooked chicken with no tray underneath the wire basket to catch the drippings, which resulted in a smoking-hot mess.

It’s also worth noting that one of the major benefits of opting for an oven-style air fryer tends to be capacity, but the Compact wasn’t able to fit more food than our top basket-style pick.

The Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact (L) is much smaller than the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro (R).

Capacity: 4 qt.Wattage: 16005 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Bake, Broil, Recrisp, Keep Warm, plus custom settingsColors: Black, Toasted Oat, Sage, TahiniWeight: 12.75 lb.Dimensions: 13.75" W x 12.75" D x 11.25" HWarranty: 3 years

New on the market in 2026, Cuisinart’s ClearView series of air fryers truly delivers on its name with the introduction of a glass basket model that also sports a viewing window on the top of the unit (the line also features a larger, 9-qt. non-glass model). Unlike other glass air fryers we tried, this one operates more like the basket-style most people expect when they think of an air fryer.

What we love: The ClearView got high marks across the board in our tests comparing glass air fryers head-to-head, almost always offering up the winning results. The controls are easy to navigate, and the functions are intuitive with beeps to remind you to flip or shake your food when your cook is halfway through. In addition to the usual Air Fry, Bake, and Reheat functions, Cuisinart’s also offers a Keep Warm. Plus, there are two programmable custom presets if you’re cooking the same foods frequently.

The crisper plate is nonstick, coated in PFAS-free ceramic, making it a breeze to clean with a little soap and water (or just throw it in the dishwasher). The glass basket is also dishwasher-safe. The ClearView doesn’t have any kind of mesh or grate covering the heating mechanism. We’ll continue to see how this fares over time, but in the meantime it’s nice not worrying about another greasy, perforated plate to clean. Lastly, the ClearView 4-Quart Glass Basket Air Fryer also comes in four colors—Black, Toasted Oat, Sage, and Tahini—and, as with all countertop appliances, it’s nice to have some kind of choice behind black plastic and stainless steel.

What we’d leave: The cord wrap post noticeably sticks out from the back of the unit. While this is probably great for airflow safety, it adds inches to a machine that’s also tall. And unlike some of the other glass air fryers we tried, Cuisinart’s bowl is oven or microwave safe. Granted, the point of the bowl is to air-fry, but if you’re using to carry your lunch into the office after cooking the night before, reheating is a little trickier.

Capacity: 6.5 qt.Wattage: 17256 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Roast, Bake, Dehydrate, Proof, and ReheatColor: Stainless steelWeight: 14.1 lb.Dimensions: 11.8" x 11.8" x 11.6"Warranty: 5-year limited

We won’t go down the PFAS rabbit hole and get deep into the concept of “nontoxic” cookware right here and now (we've got other articles for that), but given the way the concept has come front and center we know some people want an air fryer with a PFAS-free nonstick basket—and for that, we recommend the Cosori Iconic.

What we love: It has similar features and produces similar results to our top pick, the Cosori TurboBlaze, churning out crispy-skinned salmon and beautifully browned Brussels. Like the TurboBlaze, the Iconic allows you to choose between five different fan speeds, which means it's equally adept at turning delicate kale into crispy chips without blowing them around the basket as it is cooking hefty bone-in chicken breasts to bronzed perfection.

And for those looking to eliminate PFAS from every inch of their kitchen, it has both a PFAS-free ceramic nonstick-coated basket and crisper plate.

What we’d leave: Aesthetically, it may not be for everyone as this stainless-steel air fryer looks a bit spaceship-like. But the real downside is the price, which is practically double that of the TurboBlaze.

In the long run: The Cosori Iconic has seamlessly fit into the life of BA’s head of video, Dan Siegel. The speed is what won him over: “I shave 25% or more off any package-recommended cooking time and achieve perfect browning and crisping on every cook. The nonstick surfaces of both the basket and the included rack are remarkably easy to clean, making this my go-to appliance. My toaster oven probably misses me.” He mostly uses it for his two kids, occasionally scaling up to cook chicken breasts for his family of four, which takes two batches. (“It’s not huge.”) Despite the mirror-like stainless-steel finish, upkeep has been simple: “I haven't had any issues; I really only touch the top and the basket.” And then there’s the look. "It looks grown-up, like an actual appliance and not a big plastic toy without looking industrial. The MacBook of air fryers."

We have spent hours and hours over the past few years researching, testing, and retesting popular air fryers from top-name brands, including Breville, Cuisinart, Ninja, Philips, and Cosori. Here's how we put each appliance to the test:

When evaluating each model, we looked for a few key qualities:

This model from Instant Pot is a great option if a full-size (6-qt. or more) air fryer feels too big for your space or lifestyle, but our winning mini model (2-qt. limit) is too small. There’s a lot to love here, including the intuitive controls and presets, the viewing window and built-in light, and the ceramic nonstick interior coating. In testing, we found it did a decent job crisping everything we threw at it, though its performance didn’t quite match the winning Cosori Turboblaze.

This model from Instant was a previous top pick, and we still think it’s an excellent air fryer. Its design, although compact, offers a significantly larger cooking surface area than comparably sized air fryers thanks to the shape of its basket. In practice, this meant our tester was able to fit an entire extra veggie burger patty (six total) compared to models of a similar size and generally cook more food in each batch without sacrificing any of the airflow that makes air-fried food so crispy.

If a basket-style air fryer is what you’re after and you like the idea of being able to monitor what you’re cooking, the Instant Pot Vortex Plus ClearCook is definitely worth considering. This model performed nearly identically to our old top pick, the Instant Vortex Slim (probably because it’s a very similar build). The major difference—besides the ClearCook’s dimensions—is that it has a cooking window located at the front of its basket, plus a button that switches on an interior light, sort of like a traditional oven. This makes tracking the progress of your tots, fries, or chicken wings possible without removing the basket and disrupting the cooking process. Considering that providing a certain level of brownness is one of the chief concerns in air fryer cooking, this really comes in handy. A few more bonus points for the ClearCook: It adds Dehydrate to its list of functions and can hold temperatures as low as 95°F (the low end of the Vortex Slim’s range is 120°F). The ClearCook also happens to be $30 cheaper than the Slim at full price. On the downside, the square shape of the ClearCook’s basket fits one less veggie burger patty than more elongated baskets. It’s also a bit bulky.

The Typhur Dome 2 is notably spacious compared to other basket-style fryers, with 139.5 square inches of cooking surface that fits a 12" pizza, 20 chicken wings, or 11 large chicken thighs per batch, and a digital panel with 15 presets plus a companion app offering more settings, self-cleaning, and one-touch recipes. We used to recommend the original Typhur Dome as a top pick for extra-large capacity, but after testing the Dome 2, which replaced it, we felt its performance didn’t quite merit a spot on our top picks: When filled to capacity, it took much longer to properly cook and crisp food than most other basket air fryers, and 11 bone-in chicken thighs took upward of 45 minutes to get truly golden, a major red flag given that cutting cooking time is a big reason to choose an air fryer over the oven. That said, the Dome 2 cooks food evenly and does eventually get very crisp, so if you’re feeding a large family and have counter space to spare, it may still be worth the investment.

The Philips almost took a top spot—almost. It’s got a generous capacity, the control panel is easy to navigate, and it performs well with minimal user intervention. In other words, you won’t have to do a lot of shaking or stirring to get crispy fries from the Philips. This model did have a smaller yet heavier basket, and it’s loud and harder to clean due to a bunch of interlocking parts. It’s a good air fryer, but with its higher price tag, we feel like there are better deals on this list.

This newer model from Philips has a lot going for it: sleek touchscreen interface, helpful viewing window, and a whopping 16 settings. It did very well in our testing, producing crispy tots, tofu, and fries, but we preferred the design and the interface of the Cosori and Instant models. If you’re looking for an air fryer with a window feature, we’d recommend going with the Instant ClearCook (slightly cheaper at the time of writing) unless you find this model at a discount.

The Dreo ChefMaker isn't just an air fryer—it's also got probe cooking capabilities and app compatibility that make cooking proteins pretty effortless, and is a personal favorite of senior editor Olivia Tarantino. For the purposes of this article, though, we mainly tested its air frying abilities. We found that while the Dreo performed well, the winning TurboBlaze produced crispier, more evenly-cooked results all while ringing in at a third of the price. That said, if the probe cooking feature intrigues you, this fryer might be worth a try.

Our Place partnered with James Beard Award–winning chef and cookbook author J. Kenji López-Alt on this updated version of the Wonder Oven, which features eight cooking functions, a touchscreen interface, and a roomy three-tier 30-liter capacity. Like all of Our Place's products, this little oven is an aesthete’s dream—but looks aside, it impressed us. It’s incredibly powerful, able to crisp brussels sprouts, tofu, and fries up to twice as fast as the winning Breville. It produced tender salmon with potato-chip-like skin in just seven minutes. Despite its smaller footprint, it’s large enough to fit a quarter-sheet pan, making it a good option if you want to save a few inches of counter space.

All that said, while the Wonder Oven Pro is generally well-designed, a few features were annoying to use. The touchscreen isn’t the most responsive. But the bigger issue we had was with the preheating cycle. Preheating this oven to 400°F took 8–9 minutes from cold, which is already slower than the Breville’s 4–5. But more importantly, the Breville (like most regular ovens) takes less time to preheat when it’s already at temp. The Wonder Oven Pro, on the other hand, seemed to kick off a whole new several-minutes-long preheat cycle even when it had just been heated, only after which the timer would start.

Cuisinart Air Fryer Oven 6-Qt Basket Stainless Steel Air Fryer

The Cuisinart was easy to use, didn’t whirr too loudly, included a nice preheat feature, and was about the same price. We also really liked the viewing window you could use to check the progress of your food. However, its deeper square-shaped basket has less surface area than something like the Instant Vortex Slim’s rectangular one, which limits its capacity.

Ninja SL401 DoubleStack XL 2-Basket Air Fryer

The DoubleStack takes the idea of a dual-basket air fryer to a whole new level—literally. Like the Vortex Slim, the DoubleStack’s design prioritizes using vertical space. It’s skinny with the baskets stacked on top of each other instead of side by side like most other dual models. This makes it narrow and tall instead of wide, but not so tall that you can’t nestle it under your cabinets. Despite its space-saving design, you don’t lose out on actual cooking space. The baskets are big enough to fit a chicken, and the wire racks in each mean you can really maximize how much you’re cooking. (Though you do need to remain mindful of not overloading it with food, otherwise you’ll block the airflow and mess up the whole air-frying process.) You can also program the baskets separately and utilize the machine’s Smart Finish feature—which delays the start of the basket with the shorter cook—to have a whole meal ready at the same time. The one thing we didn’t like was the somewhat confusing interface.

Like the Cuisinart ClearView we recommend above, this glass air fryer operates like a traditional basket air fryer, in fact even more so as it features a front-mounted basket handle with slide-in operation. It’s a sleek-looking machine with a glossy top that illuminates when powered on with all of your touch-surface buttons. And we like that’s is relatively compact at just over 9.5" tall, making it great for in-cabinet storage. In the glass category, it performed nearly as well as the Cuisinart across the board with just a few cases of less even results, but we’re really nitpicking. What we didn’t like was the mesh-style crisping plate, which is tedious to clean and sits awkwardly on some jutting posts inside the basket, (though its design does offer a high and low position for maximizing space or airflow). That mesh is repeated on the underside of the heating element, something we don’t look forward to cleaning after a few dozen oil-evaporating cooking cycles. The internal light is intended to help you see what you’re cooking, but it glows red, which isn’t so helpful when you’re trying to keep an eye on browning.

Of the lid-style glass bowl air fryers we tested, this one was the easiest to maneuver with a fold-away handle that makes removing the top easy for flipping or shaking in the middle of cooking. With fine-tunable controls, it nailed crunchy skin on chicken thighs and crispy brussels sprouts with tender centers. More delicate dishes like salmon didn’t get where we wanted on the first try, and tofu cubes required more time than the recipe allotted to get anywhere near crispy enough. It fell short, as a lot of the glass bowl fryers did, on frozen fries, yielding uneven results and underdone portions when using the settings suggested on the back of the bag. We wish the “flip” alert was more than just a light, and it’s a little odd that the “Dehydrate” setting is listed as a bonus because you have to long-press another button to use it. The attached feet also mean the glass bowl can’t be put in the oven or microwave, but it is dishwasher-safe and comes with a lid. Plus, the whole fryer and basket setup is designed to nest inside itself for storage. And of this style of meal-prep-friendly air fryers, it’s the best version.

This Instant Pot air fryer model is if you need something with a smaller capacity. The rectangular shape of its basket made it easy to fit plenty of food inside. It is sleek and has a short profile, which are nice features too. The Vortex Slim just offered better performance.

This is Ninja's basic basket air fryer. It’s lightweight and simple to use, and it does a nice job crisping up fries. The round shape of its basket, though, makes it less versatile than other models on this list. If you’re trying to cook raw proteins or a tray of vegetables, you give away a lot of space with a round basket.

While the Dash looks cute with its retro silhouette and poppy colors, it just didn’t perform that well. Sweet potato fries came out soggy and greasy. Tofu cubes got crisped on one side but were raw on the other, and the round basket could only fit one veggie burger. The two dials, controlling time and temperature, also prevented us from getting more specific in the cook settings.

Panasonic FlashXpress Air Fryer Toaster Oven

This oven-style air fryer from Panasonic performed well in our testing, but we found it frustrating to use for a few reasons. It has 12 different functions, but they come with very little on the display as to what each of these functions truly means. The Air Fry mode only allowed us to select temperatures between 410℉–445℉, which seemed quite high for certain foods. We also disliked the automatic preheating period that we couldn’t bypass even if the oven was already hot (this was particularly annoying when we just wanted to tack on an extra few minutes after finishing a cooking cycle). If you want to do that, you have to take the extra step of once again pressing the start button after the preheating process in order to start the timed cook cycle.

Like all of DTC darling Our Place’s products, the original Wonder Oven is cute. Unfortunately, it failed to impress us enough to earn a recommendation here. While it did fine at cooking tater tots and french fries, it produced unevenly browned, ultra mushy zucchini and tofu that never quite got the crisp exterior we were looking for. The analog controls are aesthetically pleasing, but make selecting an exact temperature impossible (and knowing when the unit is at temperature impossible too). It did, however, make a shockingly good fillet of crispy-skinned salmon.

Rather than a typical basket system, the Crispi consists of a glass container and a PowerPod that sits on top. The idea is that you can store your food directly in the glass containers, and Crispi sets include as many as three basket sizes (with more available). While most food did get crisp in the Crispi (you’d hope so with a name like that!), it took longer to do so than in a standard basket air fryer, and we found that food cooked somewhat unevenly. We tested this unit twice, the second time head-to-head with other glass air fryers, and our biggest gripe remains that there’s no precise temperature control—instead, you must choose between four preset modes (Max Crisp, Bake, Air Fry, and Recrisp). We thought that lack of precision made this model less versatile, and remembering which mode to use for which temperature number recommended on the bag of frozen fries or other foods wasn’t very user-friendly.

The Typhur Sync has lots of bells and whistles, like a wireless probe thermometer (with a built-in charging port), app compatibility, a PFAS-free basket, and nine total programs (including the three found only in the app). In testing, though, it failed to produce as impressive results as the winning Cosori. The fries browned, but many remained soggy, the salmon skin failed to crisp, and the Brussels sprouts didn’t quite get as golden as we’d have liked. While some of this might be solved by tinkering with time and temperature, at $160, we just didn’t feel this air fryer was worth the splurge.

In its defense, Magnifique’s Glass Air Fryer has some thoughtful features: two sizes of glass baskets (4.5-qt. and 2.5-qt.), each with lids, and a silicone base that’s easy to remove for cleaning and oven or microwave cooking (something Cuisinart and Ninja can’t match). It’s also the only glass air fryer we tested in this round that could possibly hold a small pizza with an 8.5" diameter crisper plate. However, there are more than a few aspects that weren’t as user-friendly. The stainless-steel crisper plate (no nonstick coating whatsoever) was the most difficult to clean by far, not only because of that lack of coating but because of the perforation pattern as well. The instructions specifically say don’t use scouring pads, but a gentle scrub with a plastic pad was the only way we could remove all the residue. There’s no reminder to flip or shake your food halfway through, a pretty standard-issue beep on many other units, and when you do take the lid off, you have to actually hit Start again to keep going, something other fryers do automatically. Results, especially with frozen foods like fries, were uneven, and fine-tuning is near impossible as its interface only allows for four preset cooking modes with no customization. If you’re following a recipe, you’ll have to remember which mode gets to which general temperature range and hope for the best.

What is an air fryer? Is it just a convection oven?

An air fryer is a countertop oven that uses hot air, circulated by a fan, to give foods crisper textures than you can achieve in a regular oven or toaster oven. What makes an air fryer a “fryer” is a built-in convection fan that blows the hot air around the food to crisp it up. It’s the combination of heat and moving air that produces the kind of crispy exterior you’d otherwise get from deep-frying or pan-frying. But unlike a deep fryer, an air fryer requires far less oil to achieve the desired effect—and it doesn’t leave your house smelling like a grease trap for days or weeks. So, technically speaking, yes, air fryers are just small convection ovens, but the most classic form of air fryer isn’t usually oven-shaped, rather more like egg or block with a slide-out basket on the front.

Whether you’re a purist and only consider products that contain baskets to be true air fryers, or you find the term air fryer to be stupid marketing jargon for a convection oven is up to you to decide. For the purposes of this review, we’ve included both toaster ovens that contain convection or “air fryer” settings and basket or bowl air fryers.

What accessories should I buy for my air fryer?

There are a few extras you can buy to optimize your frying experience—things like an olive oil sprayer (so you can crisp without spilling oil on the heating element), parchment paper liners, and an instant read thermometer. For more of our favorite air fryer accessories, head right this way.

Alaina Chou: I’ve been testing air fryers and other small appliances for Bon Appétit and Epicurious since 2023. In that time, I’ve cooked countless batches of salmon, brussels sprouts, and frozen fries in pursuit of an air fryer that delivers on the lofty promise of deep-fryer-level crispiness without the need for a vat of hot oil. And I’ve blown out the power in the Test Kitchen numerous times in the process (sorry, Test Kitchen editors).

#6468. Astrophysicists Cross Another Dark Matter Candidate Off Their List: Stupendously Large Black Holes

If cosmologists ever identify what dark matter actually is, it may be because of a process of elimination.

There are many potential candidates for dark matter, including WIMPs and axions, which are both hypothetical particles. But one of the most intriguing candidates are primordial black holes (PBHs) that formed in the early Universe. They're hypothetical too, but are massive objects, so their presence should be detectable in a way that particles aren't.

All dark matter candidates have their supporters and their dectractors, and PBHs are no different. But PBHs have fairly well-defined search strategies that should detect them if they exist. If they exist, then cosmologists should find evidence of them in the cosmic microwave background (CMB).

The CMB is relic radiation from the Big Bang itself, the oldest detectable light that exists. It was released when the Universe was only about 380,000 years old. For the most part, the CMB appears smooth and uniform, or isotropic. But increasingly powerful detectors let cosmologists examine the CMB for minor fluctuations. Those could show the presence of PBHs, or at least a subset of them called stupendously large black holes, or SLABs. SLABs, if they exist, are truly stupendously massive, with masses up to 10 billion billion solar masses. Yes, that's two billions one after another.

This is a temperature map of the CMB created with data from the ESA's Planck spacecraft. The CMB can only be measured from space, and Planck's job was to measure anisotropies in the CMB. The different colours show temperature differences, and those differences correspond to where the first galaxies formed. Image Credit: NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=130789180

New research published in Physical Review Letters says that SLABs can't be dark matter. It's titled "Closing the Mass Window for Stupendously Large Black Holes," and the lead author is Christopher Gerlach. Gerlach is a theoretical physicist at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, and its PRISMA++ Cluster of Excellence.

âA possible solution to the puzzle of dark matter was that it might have collected shortly after the Big Bang in giant black holes with masses ranging from 100 million to 10 billion billion times that of the sun," said lead author Gerlatz.

This work is largely based on the ESA's Planck satellite. The Planck satellite ended its mission in 2013, but researchers are still generating new insights from its data. Part of that is because of more raw computing power. But it's also because they can cross-correlate it with new data from sources that didn't exist back in 2013. Physicists also have better ways to filter out interference, like that from the Milky Way.

âThat we are still generating new insights into the universeâs evolution and structure 13 years after it was shut down only emphasizes how important the Planck satellite was and is to physicists," explained Gerlach.

âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â - Nicholas Leister, Johannes Gutenberg University.

SLABs, if they're real, formed from overdensities of matter after the Big Bang. They didn't need to form massive stars, burn their fuel, and explode as supernovae. They skipped that step, and are too massive for that, anyway. Since they're theorized to have formed so early, before massive objects like galaxy clusters, they should be the only things that left such an imprint on the CMB.

âIf these SLABs had existed in large numbers and contained significant amounts of dark matter, they would have left a characteristic imprint on the CMB through their unique perturbations, or, in a word, making it grainy," said study co-author Nicholas Leister, also a JGU physicist.

This image is an artist's interpretation of what primordial black holes could look like. SLABs, Stupendously Large Black holes, a hypothetical sub-type of primordial black holes, would be far more massive than these. Image Credit: NASA

Previous work has all but eliminated the possibility that regular primordial black holes could account for all dark matter. But what about SLABs? Have they survived the process of dark matter elimination, unlike their less massive cousins?

To find out, the researchers first modelled SLABs and how they would affect the CMB. Then they compared the modelled effects to the actual CMB. The result was clear: the CMB doesn't have the characteristic graininess that SLABs should have imprinted on it.

"In this work, we have shown that the production of stupendously large PBHs would generate large DM isocurvature perturbations, tightly constrained by CMB and BAO data," the authors explain.

"We show that primordial black holes (PBHs) in the Stupendously Large Black Hole mass range (Mâ³1011Mâ) produce isocurvature perturbations exceeding current Planck Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) limits, thereby excluding them as a significant dark matter component," the authors conclude.

This artist's impression depicts a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole surrounded by an accretion disc. SMBH are massive and they're real. But they're still dwarfed by the hypothetical SLABs. Credit: ESO, ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser

The results also counter some other thinking regarding PBHs and dark matter. When the JWST discovered its notorious early massive galaxies, galaxies so massive that they challenged models of galaxy formation, it set the astrophysical community in motion searching for explanations. Astrophysicists cast their net wide, and one explanation they caught concerned PBHs. One 2022 study, titled "Accelerating Early Massive Galaxy Formation with Primordial Black Holes," suggested that PBHs make up a fraction of dark matter and were behind the JWST's early, massive galaxies.

But that's unlikely to be true, according to these results.

"They also challenge scenarios attributing the early massive galaxy candidates observed by James Webb Space Telescope to PBH-induced fluctuations," the researchers write.

SLABs were also potential explanations for another unexplained phenomenon. A gravitational wave background hum pervades the Universe, sensed by Pulsar Timing Arrays, and some researchers asked if SLABs could be responsible. "These questions are also unlikely to be answered by SLABs, since our findings show that they didnât exist in large numbers," said Nicholas Leister. âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â

So the search for dark matter candidates continues. It's possible that no one type of object or particle makes up dark matter. Dark matter may be a collective effect generated by different particles, objects, or phenomena.

But it looks like SLABs are no longer in contention.

Julie Elie, an ethologist at the University of California, Berkeley, tells Live Science's Kenna Hughes-Castleberry about using AI to decode the vocalizations of zebra finches.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bird calls are far more than pleasant sounds in nature. They are complex forms of communication that can reveal how birds think, learn, cooperate and respond to their surroundings. From intricate songs used to attract mates to alarm calls that warn others of danger, vocalizations offer valuable clues about avian intelligence and social organization.

Julie Elie is an animal behavior researcher and associate project scientist at the University of California, Berkeley. She recently won the 2026 Coller Dolittle Challenge for Two-Way Interspecies Communication for her work in studying and deciphering zebra finch communication.

For more than a decade, Elie observed the social behavior of birds, recording thousands of sounds and using machine learning combined with behavioral experiments to decode specific calls.

In this interview, Elie discusses how zebra finches learn and use vocalizations, what their calls reveal about intelligence and social relationships and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to decoding birdsong.

Dr Julie Elie is a computational neuroethologist who studies how social animals communicate. Her research combines behavioral experiments, neuroscience, and computational tools to reveal how animals produce communication sounds, what information they transmit in their vocalizations and how they perceive the meaning of vocalizations.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: What made you study birds and birdsong?

Julie Elie: The beginning of my work with birds dates from my Ph.D. I've always been super interested in animal behavior in general. But I think as a young person, I was more attracted by animals that we relate more easily to, which are mammals, right? Dogs, cats, horses.

I wanted to do a Ph.D. on animal behavior and, more specifically, on relationships between animals. I was interested in how animals interact with each other and what kind of social organization they establish.

[Someone suggested I] work on the zebra finch, and I said, "OK, I've never taken the time to really observe birds very well; might as well start now."

I realized that it's difficult to observe birds because they're not close to you. They can fly wherever they want. When you are out and about in town, in the countryside, and you see birds, they're here, and then they're gone. You don't get to see a lot of their vocal interactions or a lot of their social interactions.

So here I was, studying the zebra finch in cages where they were fully interacting with each other. And the question was, what kind of social organization do they have?

I realized quickly that they were not doing a dominance hierarchy [which was previously thought to be the case], but instead, the most important thing in their life was their partner. They were doing pair bonds, and that's the core of their social organization, [with] males and females pairing for life.

Studying birdsong can help researchers like Elie better understand how the birds navigate their complex environments.

KHC: Why is it important to study birdsong, and what can it teach us about intelligence and behavior?

JE: A level of complexity we were trying to understand was, what are the neural mechanisms that enable those birds to do this process of listening to something and copying it, and reproducing it, and doing a comparison between what they're producing and what they're hearing?

The zebra finch is a just-right middle ground level of cognitive ability that is interesting, where you see this pattern of copying vocalization and producing it. But you can look through the avian kingdom, and some species show more complex behaviors.

We know that there are some species that are able to not only imitate their own vocalizations from their own species, their dad, but they're able to copy other species. So, here in California, for instance, a mockingbird is a bird that is really known to be able to reproduce a bunch of different sounds and is actually incorporating this in their vocalizations.

Parrots are also well known for that because we have them as pets, and they're able to reproduce our own vocalizations as humans. This is kind of crazy, when you think about it, because they don't have the same vocal tract as we do. It's smaller, and they have a different system. I think a high cognitive level is when an animal is able to reproduce a sound that is not in their "native language," let's say, and use it for a goal. We do see this in parrots ‪—‬ they're able to ask you for something or even ask the dog to shut up sometimes, which is interesting. They're able to really use those vocalizations, such as "This is not mine, but I communicate with another species this way."

It shows you how smart they can be, and by studying vocal communication in animals, we are getting a window of what cognitive abilities they have and how the usage reveals their level of smartness.

KHC: Could you walk me through how you ended up decoding bird vocalizations?

JE: I spent countless hours observing zebra finches, and I realized that I could progressively do a match between the social context and the acoustic characteristics of the sound produced. I could recognize these sounds and understand what they "mean."

It's like at home with your cat or dog: Within a couple of months, you figure out every time the cat is doing this kind of sound —‬ "meow" — ‬it means he wants to get out or he's hungry, or he wants to cuddle. Same thing with the dog. It's the same process, but instead of doing this with cats or dogs, I did this with birds and constituted the first acoustic dictionary of zebra finch calls.

However, how do you know you are correct? That you correctly identified the sounds that correspond to the "words" in that species?

Pet owners can often differentiate between different vocalizations in their pets, such as different meowing noises for their cat.

I thought that the best confirmation of whether I was right or not could only come from the zebra finches themselves. Up to now, nobody had found a way to systematically go through the vocal repertoire of an animal and confirm if each identified call type was indeed perceived as a word in that species' language.

To achieve this somewhat impossible discussion with a bird, we designed an operant conditioning experiment where the bird is asked to classify vocalizations that were previously recorded from other zebra finches. The game is simple and relies on two rules. The first one is that every day, only the recordings corresponding to one call type are rewarded by seeds, while the recordings from the other call types in the repertoire are not rewarded. The second rule is that the bird can interrupt recordings and skip to the next one whenever they want, like how you skip through songs on your favorite music app.

The bird is placed in a cage that has a button or a little infrared sensor that it can activate with its beak. Each time it does so, the recording of a vocalization randomly drawn from the library of call types is played. Four out of five times, birds trigger the playback of a call type that will not give them access to seeds. Because they are slightly food deprived, they only really want to listen to the rewarded playback, so they interrupt the nonrewarded calls and only listen for the calls that are going to be rewarded.

Every day, the bird has to find out which call type or "word" is rewarded. They usually figure it out pretty rapidly and then start interrupting the playback of all the other call types. Using this task, we could test a different call type every dayIf they had not been able to do it, it would tell us that the call type we had identified was in fact not existing in their language. If they were able to do it ‪—‬ and spoiler alert, they were! ‪—‬ it meant that we had correctly identified that call type.

The birds told us yes, basically —‬ the organization that you're proposing is correct.

But then we made a surprising discovery. We noticed that birds were making some rare and systematic mistakes. We wondered if these mistakes were coming from the acoustic similarity of the call types — how you might mistake, for instance, the word "glove" for "love" or "hurt" for "heart." Or if they were coming from the semantic similarity of the call types — you could maybe mistake "love" for "heart" if you are remembering about the general meaning of the rewarded word today, which is "love.".

In that last case, it would mean that birds truly have an understanding of their call types' meaning. We found out that birds' errors could be better explained by the meaning [the semantic similarity] of the call types. That is a big discovery in the field of animal communication.

I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird.

KHC: Do you think we are headed toward actually being able to communicate with birds, or do you think it's more that we're still testing the waters and we still need to learn the rest of the language before we get there?

JE: When we say "talking with birds," I think we need to understand that it's not going to be a language. Right now, I am studying the zebra finch; it doesn't mean that I would be able to communicate with a crow once I have a repertoire. So there's this component of when we talk about birds, there are many different species.

I think there's more traction in this particular part of the animal kingdom than in other parts, just because birds are really talkative. Birds use a lot of their vocalizations to communicate with each other. So because of that, I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird, just because they are very talkative.

For now, I found all those words. But we need to understand how those words are [strung] together. So it's not necessarily the case that we need to understand the rules of the dynamic exchanges between individuals or how fast you're responding, but how you are responding and whether that makes sense or not.

They [also] have [body] postures. They have specific displays at the same time they're producing the vocalizations. And if we really want to achieve full communication with another species, we need to get to that level.

It's not tomorrow for sure, it's probably not next year, but I think in the range of 10 years we should get there. Especially with how fast the domains of AI and robotics are. I have some hope that we should be able to get to that point.

KHC: Is there one takeaway you would want our readers to know about your work?

JE: Just one. The most important thing for readers that are not specifically scientists is to realize that, by studying animal behavior more generally, researchers are discovering the intelligence of animals. This is opening our eyes to other species and realizing that we're not the only species that is intelligent on this planet.

This is a lesson to us as another species on this planet, that we are not the only ones that are smart and we need to take this into account in how we are evolving.

We need to realize how we're affecting them and realize that they also have their own internal lives, and maybe we should start to respect them a little bit more.

Editor's note: Some of this interview was conducted via email as part of a follow-up conversation. The interview has been edited lightly for clarity and length.

#6466. When Einstein's Gravitational Waves Meet Newton's Tides

In 1687, Sir Isaac Newton released his magnum opus, PhilosophiÃ¦ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), in which he described his theories of motion and gravity. His theory of the latter accurately described the motion of the Earth's tides, something that scientists had been wrestling with for centuries. For over three hundred years, Newton's work remained scientific canon and the last word on gravity, until Albert Einstein introduced his Theory of General Relativity.

According to a recent study from the Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories. While the pull of the Sun and Moon and their influence on the tides can be predicted very accurately using Newtonian gravity, GR offers a fuller description that includes gravitational waves (GWs). The new study merges these two theories into a single model that could offer a new way to test our understanding of gravity.

The study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB. His work extends the classical model of lunar tides to include the cross polarization of gravitational waves, one of the key ways GWs can deform spacetime as they pass through. As he explained in a FUB press release:

Isaac Newton explains the tides extremely well. Albert Einstein shows us that gravity is also dynamic and that changes in spacetime can propagate as waves. Our work brings both perspectives together and asks what traces of this might be found in high-precision measurements.

GWs were originally predicted by Einstein's Theory of General Relativity and refer to ripples in spacetime caused by the merger of massive objects. To date, thousands of GW events have been detected, the majority of which were caused by the merger of black holes or neutron stars. However, GWs can also result from smaller gravitational interactions, such as those produced by the interactions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.

One issue addressed by Eser's study is the difficulty of distinguishing possible additional signals from measurement errors, the choice of reference frame, and uncertainties in calculating the positions of the Sun and Moon. By identifying which influences must be accounted for, Eser shows how a signal could be isolated and the possible physical effects identified. The study therefore presents a quantitative basis for future studies of tidal patterns that deviate from what Newtonian Gravity predicts. Said Eser:

We are not claiming to have discovered a new gravitational effect. What we show is how one could look for it in a targeted way. The EarthâMoon system is particularly interesting for this because we can already describe and measure its tidal effects very precisely.

Further Reading: Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin

#6465. Baby, She's Back! SpaceX Catches a Starship From Orbit for First Time

SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.

The 171-foot-tall (52-meter) space vehicle, known as Ship 42, settled between a giant pair of mechanical arms extended from the South Texas launch tower where its journey began 22.5 hours earlier. The arm-capture system, nicknamed "Mechazilla," had been used three times previously to capture Starship Super Heavy boosters during suborbital flight tests, but this was the first time for a second stage coming in hot from orbit.

"Mechazilla has caught the Starship â we've been waiting to hear that for a long time," SpaceX launch commentator Dan Huot said.

In addition to the first orbital catch, this week's test marked the longest Starship flight to date, besting a three-hour orbital flight in September.

Years of development â including 15 full-scale flight tests since 2023 â led up to today's orbital catch, which Huot called "the Holy Grail of spaceflight." The achievement took the sting out of the previous day's aborted effort to catch the rocket's booster using the same system, minutes after liftoff. SpaceX said the booster was diverted when its onboard system detected a fuel-system alarm. The root cause of the alarm is under investigation.

SpaceX plans to use the launch-pad arms to recover Starship's boosters and second stages on a routine basis, achieving company founder Elon Musk's goal of creating a fully reusable, orbital-class launch system.

This 15th flight test proceeded almost in textbook fashion, aside from the boosterâs offshore splashdown on launch day. During the first hours of its 14-orbit flight, Starship deployed 26 more next-generation satellites for SpaceXâs Starlink broadband internet network. All of the satellites were in good health and beginning to raise their orbits to operational altitude, the company said.

At the end of the trip, the second stage fired a single engine for roughly 10 seconds to start its descent through the atmosphere. As the temperatures rose, a brlght glow surrounded Ship 42âs leading edges. The craft executed a bellyflop maneuver to maximize its deceleration. Then it righted itself, and fired its engines a final time to sink into Mechazillaâs arms.

SpaceX employees around the country and hundreds of onlookers near the Texas launch site cheered, while âBaby, Come Backâ played on the soundtrack for the webcast. âBaby, sheâs back,â Huot joked.

Bringing Starship into full operation is expected to speed up deployment of Starlink satellites. More importantly, Starship is slated to serve as a landing system for NASA's crewed moon missions starting as early as 2028. Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system are scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA's Artemis III mission.

In a post to X, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated Musk and the SpaceX team on today's successful catch. "It was almost magic ... Making more believers by the day," he wrote. Using emojis, Isaacman said the achievement brought the United States "one step closer" to putting an American flag once more on the moon.

SpaceX's team will analyze the data gathered about Starship's performance, including the ability of Ship 42's heat shield to stand up to the rigors of atmospheric re-entry. The company is gearing up to expand Starship operations to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and yet another Starship launch site is in the works for Louisiana.

In the long term, Musk envisions creating a fleet of Starships that could offer point-to-point rocket travel on Earth, as well as mass transit to Mars and other off-Earth destinations. Cryptocurrency investor Chun Wang has already announced his intention to take Starship trips around the moon and Mars.

"I donât think you guys understand," a software engineer named Will DePue wrote in a post to X. "You will get the chance to go to space in your lifetime. New era."

#6463. The Best Frozen Lasagna, According to Our Taste Test

Frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you. For when you need the comfort of pasta, cheese, and sauce, but you’re not prepared to spend hours boiling, sautéing, and layering. And that’s okay. A great frozen lasagna might not hold a candle to BA’s Best Lasagna, but at the very least it should hold together, with distinct layers, plenty of sauce, gooey cheese, and bouncy pasta.

For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters. Three stood out: Trader Joe’s tasted the closest to homemade, Marie Callender’s was a solid backup, and Rao’s was our favorite for a single serving.

After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.

Why it won us over: Trader Joe’s frozen lasagna had a homemade vibe. There were distinct layers of pasta, cheese, and meaty sauce. The cheeses—ricotta, mozzarella, Romano, and Parmesan—each pulled their weight. And the noodles had a fresh bounce. “There’s a whole tomato!” exclaimed senior editor Kelsey Jane Youngman upon finding a chunk of diced tomato in her sample. Other tasters complimented the bright aromatics—fennel was prominent, backed up by oregano and basil. The evenly distributed ground beef and pork were the cherry on top.

Trader Giotto’s Family-Style Meat Lasagna, 32-oz.

More great frozen foods at Trader Joe’s →

Big Lasagna would have you believe you’ll always want to cook a frozen lasagna for a crowd, but sometimes it’s about you and you alone. The 9-oz. Rao’s Made for Home Meat Lasagna is just enough for a single serving—and it doesn’t sacrifice flavor.

Why it won us over: Our tasters were excited to report that Rao’s delivered on structure. While other lasagnas were soupy, floppy, or otherwise unbalanced, Rao’s stayed intact, layer on top of layer, as we ate. It had sturdy (but not tough) noodles, a tomato sauce that was full of umami, and herbal accents that didn’t overpower. Some tasters noted a robust beefy flavor; others were more focused on the garlic and onion. Everyone went in for a second bite.

Maybe you don’t live by a Trader Joe’s—our condolences—and Rao’s proves elusive. You still deserve a serviceable frozen lasagna. Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce offers a sweet and tangy tomato sauce punctuated by well-seasoned meat and noodles that hold their shape.

Why it won us over: This contender avoided many of the pitfalls other brands fell into. It had a solid tomato sauce that was just slightly sweet and tangy, and the meat—both beef and sausage—was flavorful and varied enough in size to give each bite some dynamism. The pasta sheets were springy, not gummy. And while it wasn’t drowning in dairy, there was enough cottage cheese and mozzarella to make itself known.

Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce, 10.5-oz.

We cooked each lasagna from frozen according to its package instructions. While most contenders offered both oven and microwave directions, we stuck with the oven. Tasters sampled each lasagna without knowing which brand they were trying, evaluating each for flavor, texture, and structural integrity. Although Giovanni Rana’s Meat Lasagna is sold refrigerated, we froze it before baking, following the brand’s instructions for cooking from frozen.

The best frozen lasagna should deliver on the fundamentals of structure, flavor, and texture—a tall order for many of our contenders. That meant distinct layers; sheets of pasta that were bouncy, not flimsy; tomato sauce with concentrated flavor and enough body to cling to the pasta; meat that stood out instead of getting lost; and cheese—or many cheeses—that added milky flavor and melty cohesion.

#6461. ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

We tested the brand-new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus, an all-in-one smart telescope for beginners and hobbyists that makes astrophotography accessible to everyone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing

2K image quality is better than we expected

Editing controls could be a little more responsive

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas

Why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

With 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

It comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

On the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

The set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.)

The Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, plan a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

The Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

There's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a new target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

The AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

We had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release on November 10, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd ideally have aimed for longer in some cases.

Nov. 16, 2026: Lunar, solar and Heart Nebula images and information added.

Now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

The Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

The Eastern Veil Nebula and Heart Nebula are also lovely targets for the Seestar S30 Plus. In the Eastern Veil Nebula in particular, you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

Planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

Solar and lunar imaging is easier than ever thanks to the Seestar S30 Plus. The included solar filter is easy to attach to the front of the telescope (and should be used for every solar session). Solar mode is ideal for viewing sunspots and creating a timelapse of a solar eclipse — we captured the total solar eclipse with our S30 Pro back in the summer. Similarly, lunar imaging gives you the option to capture images, video and timelapses of the moon, and we were impressed with the detail we got on a crescent moon, particularly at 2x. On both solar and lunar modes, you can shoot at 1x, 2x and 4x.

The Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced users will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ review

With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.
